Vue compiler upgrade remakes every dump that holds a .vue file.
Dumps with no .vue file read as before. The same key can map a
React library's components; this step reads it in Vue templates
only. definePageMeta's keys other than title, layout and middleware
print a line until a key maps a project's own metadata, such as a
permission.

**Insight:** @vue/compiler-sfc is the parser Vue's own tools split a component with, so it accepts what Vue accepts; its parts are MIT, BSD and ISC, and its SBOM scan is clean. Keeping every character's position lets the facts cite the .vue file a person opens, with no source map to carry, and lets the checker resolve the script's imports and types as it does any file. Template expressions are written by their syntax only, since the checker does not see the template; a name there is not resolved, and what it would give is a question. A component binds a field only where the project says so: guessing from a tag's name (anything with v-model) would write fields for a date picker and a tag cloud alike. The key names the component and what it binds once for every screen, as permissionChecks names a check once for every route, and it is checked by both validators. A component used with no import is matched by its name because Nuxt and a global registration supply it without one, and the implementation file is the project's own statement of which components those are. Nuxt injects its helpers with no import, so a name is all the syntax gives; a project that shadows one is read wrongly, which a test of the result shows. Middleware that a page runs gives it a permission only when every one the page runs is read and they name one permission between them; several, or one unread, are asked, since a page checks one permission and an unread middleware may check another. Every screen and route is read from one dump with no build and no browser, so a result shows early and each guess is a question at its line.

### ADR-092: extract dart reads a code-facts dump the analyzer package's parseString wrote, resolving no package, and turns its facts into screens, models, routes, clients and settings in Go

Status: accepted, 2026-10-09.

Context: Step 21 of docs/extraction.md reads Dart and Flutter, the last
language of the plan. The analyzer package is the parser of the
Dart SDK's own tools. A resolved unit needs pub get and the pub
cache, which no commit holds; parseString gives syntax alone.
Flutter declares screens through go_router, MaterialApp and
Navigator, forms through form fields and their callbacks, models
through json_serializable's and freezed's annotations on classes a
code generator reads, clients through retrofit's annotations, dio
and http, and servers through shelf_router and dart_frog's routes
folder. In Dart 3 a switch case may be a pattern.

Decision: readers/dart is a Dart package that pins analyzer 14.4.0 exactly
with pubspec.lock committed, and writes the code-facts dump of
ADR-075 with the language dart: imports, classes with their
annotations, fields, constructors and methods with their
parameters, enums with their values' annotations, calls and
instance creations with their arguments as values (a closure by its
parameters and what it returns, an assignment by its target), the
comparisons of a request's method and the branch of one a call is
in, and reads of Platform.environment. specarch pins the same
version and refuses a dump another one made. A file a code
generator wrote is listed and not read. In Go, the screens,
models, routes, clients and settings are read as extract.yaml
lists; the implementation file's permissionChecks names a Dart check
by the path of its file from the folder read, without .dart.

Consequences: A Flutter app or a Dart server is read from a committed dump; making
the dump needs the Dart SDK and fetches the analyzer once. An
analyzer upgrade remakes every Dart dump. Flavour files and the
configuration a --dart-define-from-file gives are not read yet;
joining a client's call to its operation by method and path waits,
as for every reader.

**Insight:** parseString needs nothing but the file, so the dump is made from a commit with no pub get, and a package's types are known only by the names the code writes, which is what the idiom table keys on. Pinning the analyzer holds the facts to one parser, as SwiftSyntax and the TypeScript compiler are held; its tree is BSD-3-Clause and MIT and its SBOM scan is clean. A model is read from the class the generator reads, not the generator's output, because the output is generated and says so; the annotations are the statement. A field a form saves is named by the property its onSaved assigns, the one place the syntax ties a control to a model; a controller names a variable, not a property, so it is asked. A validator's empty or length test is a rule a page's field cannot hold, so it is a line for the entity's field, not a page key. A redirect is code, and only its question names it, since syntax cannot say whom it lets through. dart_frog's folder is its router, read like the other file-system routers, and its handler's comparisons say which methods it serves; what a default branch serves is asked. A check called in a switch case gives only that case's method its permission, which the branch of each call records. Every surface is read from one dump with no build, no device and no emulator, so a result shows early, and every guess is a question at its line.

### ADR-093: generate --check compares a page's schema built by hand as a value in the object-literal subset, and a file built by hand without the generated header

Status: accepted, 2026-10-11.

Context: generate --check compares every file byte for byte. A project that
brings screens built by hand wants to know, page by page, whether
the generated schema and page match its own, and to see the
difference without the noise of formatting (Q9 of
docs/ui-nextjs-carbon.md). A file built by hand never carries the
header, draft notice or problem marks every generated file starts
with, so a byte comparison can never find it equal.

Decision: A plug-in marks, in its answer, each file that is one object
literal of data with comparison: object-literal; the Next.js
generator marks every page.schema.ts. When such a file on disk
differs, both sides are read in the subset of TypeScript that is
also JSON5: line and block comments, import statements, one
export const holding an object literal, optionally followed by
satisfies and a type name; inside it objects, arrays, strings in
double or single quotes, numbers, true, false and null, keys bare or
quoted, trailing commas allowed. They are compared by value: the
imports, the constant's name, the type it satisfies and the
literal. A difference is printed one line per value, by its path in
the literal. Anything else, such as an identifier, a function or a
template string, makes the file not comparable, named with its
line, never equal. A file on disk with no line that starts the
generated header is built by hand: it matches when it equals what
the target writes without its header, draft notice and problem
marks, or, for an object literal, when the values are equal; a match
prints a line and is not counted as differing. A generated file is
compared byte for byte as before, and its value difference is
printed below the line that says it differs.

Consequences: A project points --out at its folder of hand-built pages and reads,
file by file, which match and which values differ; a page it has
not built is reported missing, as any missing file is. Reformatting
a generated file is still reported, since generated output is
byte-identical by rule. A plug-in that marks no file keeps the byte
comparison everywhere, so the plain JavaScript generator and every
other target are unchanged.

**Insight:** JSON5 is the subset because it is the part of ECMAScript object literals that is plain data, with a specification of its own, so a value comparison has a definition both sides can be held to; a parser of all TypeScript would have to decide what an expression is worth, which is not data. Refusing what lies outside the subset keeps ambiguity an error (docs/principles.md): a file that cannot be read as data is never declared equal. The plug-in says which files are data, not their names, so specarch knows no stack's file layout. The header decides between a generated file and one built by hand, because it is the one thing every generated file has and no file written by hand does; dropping it only for files without it keeps the check that generated output is current exactly as strict.

**Note:** From The JSON5 Data Interchange Format, 1.0.0: JSON5 extends JSON with the object-literal syntax of ECMAScript 5.1: unquoted keys, single-quoted strings, trailing commas and comments. <https://spec.json5.org/>

### ADR-094: Meta-model 0.3 is built around the caller in five steps, and the version moves with the first, which reserves the name caller

Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.

Context: Specifying a running identity service from its sources found three
things the meta-model cannot say: a route open only to named
machine clients or closed to everyone, a signed request as a gate,
and the claims and lifetimes of the tokens the service issues. The
library example carries a fourth in words, in its member role's
why: a member sees only loans whose memberId is their own. 0.2 left
all four out together because each needs the caller as something
an expression can name (ADR-052).

Decision: docs/meta-model-0.3.md is the plan. The caller is one declared
record, and a role's rows rule, machine clients with a proof and
the gates callers and nobody, and token formats are built on it in
five steps: the caller and rows in both validator builds, row
security in generate sql, clients and gates, tokens, then the
readers. Step 1 reserves the name caller wherever an expression's
names come from, which refuses a 0.2 file that has a field,
property or input of that name once it says 0.3, so the version
moves with step 1 and the trees in this repository move with it; a
file that stays on 0.2 is read with the meta_model_version warning
until 1.0. Every later keyword is an addition. Left out of 0.3:
seed data per profile, which two extractions and merge compare;
data held in a cache and tables kept but unused, which are the
implementation file's; more than one deliverable per
specification, which is a second implementation file; the roles or
the client in an expression; a route both people and clients call;
a shorthand for a tenant scope; and rows rules on a view's own
fields.

Consequences: A rule that names the caller can be written as soon as step 1
lands, and the library's member rule moves from a why into the
role. The migration of this repository's trees is one version line
per root file, since none has a field named caller. A 0.2 file
keeps validating with one warning. The three concepts share one
name and one expression form, so a generator that learns to render
caller.<property> once renders it for rows, token checks and
whatever comes after.

**Insight:** Semantic Versioning moves a version for what breaks its users, and the reserved name is the only change here that makes a valid file invalid, as the missing-test rule was in 0.2. It comes first rather than last because every other step writes caller.<property>, and a step that adds an expression form no file may yet use would be building on a version that does not exist. The migration is cheap enough to run first: a version line, not a derived test per subject. The concepts stay together for the reason ADR-052 gave: designing the caller three times would give three ways to name it. Each candidate left out is left out with the reason the plan records, and each is taken only when a real system asks, which is the roadmap's rule for the meta-model.

### ADR-095: The caller is a declared record, caller.<property> is the one field access an expression may use, and a role's rows rule limits an entity's rows after PostgreSQL's row security policies, with a record outside the rows not found

Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.

Context: A member sees only their own loans, and a tenant's staff see only
their organisation's records. The meta-model names the permission a
caller must hold and the roles that grant it, and nothing about the
caller beyond that, so the rule could only be written in words. The
expression subset refuses field access with a dot, lists and
macros, so that every name in a rule is a column of the one record
the rule is about (docs/conventions.md, Expressions).

Decision: caller is an object of the design stage with the properties of a
value object. In an expression, caller.<property> names one of
them, checked against the declared properties and typed as a field;
a dot anywhere else, an undeclared property, and a field, property
or input named caller are refused. A nullable property compares as
false when it is null. A role's rows maps an entity to one bool
expression over the entity's fields and the caller; a holder reads
and changes only the rows it holds for, an entity with no rule is
reached whole, and a caller with several roles reaches the union.
A list shows only the rows, a read by key outside them answers not
found, a write that would leave them is refused, and a job acting
as the role sees the rows only; each is a derived case. generate
sql writes a policy per rule on PostgreSQL and marks the entry on
an engine without row security; generate openapi is unchanged. The
roles a caller holds and the client they come through are not
properties.

Consequences: The library's member rule is a rule the validator checks and the
techspec's matrix shows, and its derived cases are tests. A tenant
scope is the rule written on each entity that carries the
organisation's key. How the caller's values reach the query is the
implementation file's. A rule comparing a property the caller may
lack needs no null test to be fail-closed.

**Insight:** CEL has field access because its values are messages, and SpecArch refused it so that a generator renders every name without a join and the validator types every name against a declared field. The caller is one more declared record, so caller.<property> keeps both guarantees, and CEL's own form is taken rather than a prefix on flat names, which would be a second naming idiom. The rule sits on the role because it says who reaches which rows, as PostgreSQL's CREATE POLICY is granted TO a role, and its permissive policies, combined with OR, are the one widely used model for several roles on one table; the permission stays what may be done. Not found rather than forbidden for a record outside the rows, because answering forbidden tells the caller the record exists, which the OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet and the object-level authorisation failure of the OWASP API Security Top 10 warn against. The engine without row security gets a mark and not a silent drop, because a rule dropped is a rule the specification claims and the schema does not keep. Roles and clients stay out of expressions because no rule needs them and taking them would bring sets into the language.

**Note:** From Common Expression Language, language definition, 2024: Field selection with a dot reads a field of a message or a key of a map. <https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/master/doc/langdef.md>

**Note:** From PostgreSQL documentation, Row Security Policies and CREATE POLICY, 17: A policy is granted to roles, permissive policies on one table are combined with OR, USING filters the rows read and WITH CHECK refuses rows a change would create or leave outside the policy. <https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-rowsecurity.html>

**Note:** From OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet: Deny by default, enforce authorisation on every record a caller names, and do not reveal through the answer whether a record the caller may not reach exists. <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html>

### ADR-096: Machine callers are clients that hold roles with a proof per request after RFC 9421, an operation says callers clients, and nobody is a reserved permission for a route closed on purpose

Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.

Context: An identity service serves routes open only to named machine
clients by client identity, routes that also require a signed
request header, and a route deliberately closed to everyone. Each
had to be written as a permission with prose, which loses the
default-deny caller list and the signature, and the closed route
needed a placeholder role because a permission no role grants is a
fail-closed error.

Decision: clients is an object of the design stage keyed by kebab-case name:
a program that calls the system, with the roles it holds and a
proof, how it proves its identity on each request: signedRequest
with an algorithm RFC 9421 registers and the covered components it
signs, mutualTls, or a token format. An operation or command may
say callers clients, which refuses every person's session and
admits only a declared client holding a granting role; left out,
it admits people and refuses clients. The validator refuses a
callers clients operation whose permission no client's role grants,
a proof with an unregistered algorithm or a covered component that
is not a request part, and a client naming an undeclared role. The
permission nobody is reserved beside public: a route with it is
served and refuses every caller, no role is asked to grant it, and
nobody with enabledBy is an error. Derived cases: refused for a
signed-in person, refused with a bad signature, refused for every
caller.

Consequences: A machine route's caller list is the clients whose roles grant its
permission, read from the specification, and the signature it
needs is on the client. A route closed by intent and a permission
forgotten in the roles are told apart by the word, so the
fail-closed error keeps its meaning. A route both people and
clients call is two operations with one handler. The key a client
signs with is a secret and is never in a specification.

**Insight:** A client holds roles rather than being named on the operation so that what may be done is said once, through permissions, and the fail-closed rule stays one rule; the default-deny list the handoff asked for is then the clients holding a granting role, with callers clients keeping people out. RFC 9421 is taken for the signed request because it is the published form of signing named parts of an HTTP message, with a registry of algorithms and the covered-component names, so a specification does not invent a signature scheme; the algorithm is design because the client cannot sign without knowing it, the interface boundary's test. A closed route is written with a reserved permission rather than a switch on the operation because public already says the open end of the same scale, and a second keyword would be a second way to say who may call. It stays served, in the OpenAPI document and the techspec, because a client that still calls it should get the declared problem document and not a 404 that looks like a wrong path.

**Note:** From RFC 9421, HTTP Message Signatures, 2024: A signature covers named components of an HTTP message, such as @method, @path and a header field, using an algorithm from the HTTP Signature Algorithms registry. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421>

### ADR-097: Tokens are declared formats with a lifetime, a signature algorithm, claims as properties under the one wire-name rule, and checks over the claims, after RFC 7519, RFC 7518 and RFC 8725, and a claim fills the caller property of its name

Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.

Context: An identity service issues access, refresh, step-up, delegated and
machine tokens, each with its own claims and lifetime, and the
claims were only in prose, so a requirement such as the actor
claim never equals the subject could not be checked against the
binding. The caller's properties need a declared source.

Decision: tokens is an object of the design stage keyed by camelCase name.
Each has a format, jwt or opaque; a lifetime; for a JWT a
signature naming an algorithm of RFC 7518, with none refused;
claims as JSON Schema properties, camelCase like every property
and on the wire as info.wireNames says, the registered claims of
RFC 7519 written as the RFC names them and carrying its types
without being retyped; and checks, bool expressions over the
claims, each a derived red case wherever the token is accepted. A
claim fills the caller property of the same name, null when the
token carried has no such claim; a claim and a caller property of
one name and different types are refused. Exactly one token is the
default, which every operation accepts unless it names another
with token; an operation naming an undeclared token, two defaults
and a check over an undeclared claim are refused. Every operation
accepting a token derives denied with expired <token>. generate
openapi writes the bearer scheme the default token gives. A
specification with a session and no tokens writes none of this,
and the session fills the caller's properties at sign-in.

Consequences: A claim's rule is checked where the token is accepted, and the
caller's properties have a declared origin per token without a
mapping between the two. Refresh, step-up and machine tokens are
formats like any other, told apart by lifetime, claims and the
operations that accept them; a token exchange is an operation
whose response is the token. The signing key is a secret and is
never in a specification.

**Insight:** RFC 7519 defines the claims and their meanings, and its registered names are single lower-case words, so the one wire-name rule of info.wireNames (ADR-062), covers a token as it covers every body: a name per claim would be the second way to say a wire name that 0.2 refused. RFC 7518 names the algorithms and RFC 8725 says a verifier must refuse none and pin what it accepts, so none is refused at validation rather than left to each verifier. The algorithm is design and not stack because the verifier is often another service, the interface boundary's test. A claim fills the property of its name rather than through a mapping, because a mapping would be a second place to name the same fact and most claims are the property. One default token rather than a token on every operation, because a service accepts one token nearly everywhere and the exceptions are what is worth writing. The expired case follows the session's, so that a specification with tokens and one with a session derive the same shape of red case.

**Note:** From RFC 7519, JSON Web Token (JWT), 2015: A JWT carries claims as a JSON object; the registered claim names iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat and jti have defined meanings and types. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519>

**Note:** From RFC 8725, JSON Web Token Best Current Practices, 2020: Verifiers must reject the none algorithm and must only accept the algorithms they are configured for. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725>

### ADR-098: A dump committed outside the code's repository names the code's repository as a gitlink of its own, and is read at the commit that gitlink records

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Every dump reader checks that the dump is committed in the code's
repository, beside the path it was made from, so that its commit
is a real edition and a stale dump is refused. A team that may
only read the code of an estate of modules cannot commit there;
the dumps it makes would live on a local branch, an edition that
exists on one machine only. Point 1 of docs/estate.md asks for the
dump to be committed in the team's own repository instead.

Decision: Every dump format (catalogue, route table, permission table and
the three code-facts dumps) takes an optional key, repository: the
folder of the code's repository from the root of the repository
holding the dump, a slash-separated path with no . or .. part. It
must be a gitlink there (mode 160000 in git ls-tree HEAD), and the
commit the gitlink records is the reference. The dump's path is
then from the code's repository's root, and its commit must be the
last change to that path at the reference (git log -1 <reference>
-- <path>), or the dump is stale and the refusal names the dump's
commit, that last change and the reference. The code's checkout
must be a full clone with nothing uncommitted under the path, and
its files under the path must be the reference's (the same tree
object), or it is refused with the git submodule update that
checks the reference out. A folder that is a plain folder or file
and no gitlink, a gitlink that is not checked out and a reference
the code's history does not hold are refused with that reason,
before anything is read. The code source's edition is the dump's
commit and its url the code's repository, as for a dump committed
beside the code; no commit of the dump's own repository appears in
the tree. A dump without repository is read as before. Every dump
script writes the key by itself when the dump file's repository is
not the code's, and refuses a dump file in a repository that does
not hold the code's.

Consequences: An extracting team commits its dumps in its own repository, which
holds each module as a submodule, and a change on the code side
reaches the specification by moving the gitlink and running the
script again, without a change request to the code's owners. Two
machines at the same commit of the outer repository read the same
files and write the same bytes, and the output equals the output
of the same dump committed beside the code. A code checkout moved
ahead without touching the path reads as before; one that changed
the path is refused rather than read at the wrong commit.

**Insight:** A gitlink is git's own record of which commit of another repository a repository uses, committed with the rest of it, so it pins the code's commit as firmly as committing the dump beside the code does. A plain checkout in the folder would pin nothing: what was read would depend on where that checkout stood on the machine. The reference is the gitlink and not the checkout's HEAD for the same reason, and the readers keep reading the checkout's files only because the check makes them the reference's: refusing a checkout that differs under the path is cheaper and clearer than a second way of reading files out of git objects in every reader. The key is optional and changes nothing for a dump without it, so no 0.2 dump or specification breaks, and a problem with it is a refusal naming the dump and its reason, as every other dump check is.

### ADR-099: A specification names how its roles go on the wire with one rule, info.roleNames upper_snake, which the validator, the two readers of grants and the generators apply through one function

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 4 of docs/estate.md, build item 2. A role's name is kebab-case
in a specification, and the token's roles claim and the permission
table of the systems the estate holds write it in upper snake case
(DESK_SUPERVISOR). extract permissions and extract go left out every
grant whose role is not kebab-case, so a module whose roles are all
upper snake came out with no role at all. A property had the same
split, settled by info.wireNames (ADR-062).

Decision: info.roleNames takes one value, upper_snake; left out, every role
goes on the wire as written. Under it every role goes on the wire as
its kebab-case name with each hyphen an underscore and each letter in
upper case: desk-supervisor is DESK_SUPERVISOR, level-2-clerk is
LEVEL_2_CLERK. The mapping is one function in each build
(internal/wirename's Role, and roleWireName in WireNames.swift).
The validator refuses two roles that go on the wire under one name,
as wire_name, the rule that already holds for properties, reported
at the second in the order the roles are written.
extract permissions and extract go read a source's roles in upper
snake case when the source names no role in kebab-case and at least
one in upper snake case (capitals, digits and underscores, a capital
first). The tree then says info.roleNames upper_snake, each such
role is written by its kebab-case name, and every citation keeps the
source's own name. A name the mapping would not give back (two
underscores in a row, an underscore last) prints a line and is a
could question, left out as before, and so is a name in another
form. A source that names roles both ways is read as before: its
kebab-case roles are read, and each upper snake one prints a line
that says the source names its roles both ways. merge writes the
rule when a tree names it.
generate go-dxlib writes each role's name id in the wire form, since
dxlib_module's role table holds the name the token carries, and says
so in the comment above the roles. The techspec's Permissions
section says how a role goes on the wire and lists each role with its
wire name. The OpenAPI document and the UI's session carry no role:
an operation names the permission it needs, and the session the
permissions its holder has, so neither writes a role's wire form.

Consequences: A module whose permission table and seeds write DESK_SUPERVISOR is
extracted with its roles, info.roleNames upper_snake, and no line for
them. A table with kebab-case roles, the lending desk's among them,
extracts byte for byte as before. A specification that names its
roles in upper snake case keeps its roles' names in kebab-case, and
its generated dxlib seed and techspec show the wire form.

**Insight:** One rule rather than a name per role, for the reason of ADR-062: a system names its roles one way throughout, and a wire name on every role would be a second way to say the same thing on each. One value only, since no source has shown another convention, and kebab-case named explicitly would be a second way to say what leaving the key out says. The mapping is one to one on kebab-case names, so two valid roles never meet; the rule matters for a name the schema refuses, such as desk_staff beside desk-staff, which the validator still reads, and would give the token one role where the specification holds two. A roles claim holds each role as a string (RFC 9068, section 2.2.3.1, after SCIM's roles attribute), and a check compares the strings, so two roles meeting on the wire are one role to every check, and the validator refuses it rather than let a generator pick one. The error is reported at the second role, as a property's is, so it is not hidden as an echo of the schema error at a name the schema refused when that name comes first; when the refused name comes second, its schema error is the one shown, and renaming it settles both. A reader reads the upper snake form only when no role of the source is kebab-case, because a source that writes both has no one rule that gives back every name; reading it as kebab-case keeps today's result for the roles it already read, and a line says why the others are left out. The round trip is the reason ADR-062 gives for properties: a reader that renamed a role whose name does not come back the same would generate a seed or a token check that differs from the source it read. Only a reader of grants (the permission table, a seed) sees roles as the wire writes them; a workflow file or a document names roles its own way, so merge takes the rule from the tree that states it. The token claims of meta-model 0.3 carry roles in this form too, since a claim is a property under the one rule (ADR-097); no claim is written by this build. Compiler test: a role the rule cannot map is still a line and a question, never dropped, and a collision is an error at the role. Acceptance test: one key in info answers it for a whole system.

### ADR-100: A permission may imply others, every check of what a role grants counts the implications, and extract permissions reads a policy of path patterns into permissions named by a fixed rule

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 5 of docs/estate.md, build item 3, and the owner's decision 1
there. Some systems check a policy of rows, each a role, a path
pattern and a method or `*`, matched by the library's path matcher,
and name no permission anywhere. A printer that made names by a rule
of its own had to grant a role with a `*` row two names, since
nothing said that one permission covers another. A permission
computed from a pattern was declined in the plan: rows overlap by
design, so one operation would have several permissions, and a
pattern would reach a route added later without anyone writing it,
which is the fail-open that fail-closed access refuses.

Decision: A permission may list `implies`: the permissions a holder of it
holds too, transitively. The validator refuses, as `implies` at the
entry, a name that is not declared, `public` implied (everyone holds
it already) or implying (it would give the implied permission to
everyone), and a permission that implies itself through the
implications, reported at every permission on the cycle with the
way round, the shortest one, following each list in its order. Every
check of what a role grants counts what its permissions imply: the
grants check, separation of duties, workflow approvals, a picker's
list, a flow's pages, the role chosen for a derived "denied without"
case, and merge's line for a permission no operation checks. The
techspec's matrix and the site's write "through" and the permission
a role holds an implied one by, and the techspec lists what each
permission implies when one does; generate go-dxlib writes a role's
privileges with the ones they imply after them, since the check
reads each privilege by its name.
The permission table gains `rules`, beside `grants` and `gates`, and
a table without it reads as before. A rule is a role, a pattern, the
methods (a list of methods in capitals, or `*`) and the matcher:
`colon`, where a segment `:name` is one segment, or `brace`, where a
segment `{name}` is; in both `*` as the whole last segment is the
rest of the path after the slash before it, slashes included. The
rules give one permission per distinct pattern and method pair, the
parameters' names aside, named by the fixed rule: the literal
segments' words in lower case joined by dots, then `all` for `*` or
the method in lower case; `/v1/*` with `*` is `v1.all`, and
`/v1/items/{id}` with `DELETE` is `v1.items.delete`. Pairs that
would share a name are each named with their parameters' words too
(and `any` for the rest of the path); a pair whose name still meets
another's, or has a word that does not start with a letter, prints a
line and is a could question, left out, and so is a rule with `*`
anywhere but as the last segment. A permission implies each one its
pattern covers by the matcher's rule, with its methods including the
other's, and the implications written are the fewest that give
them all. Each role is granted the permissions of its rows. Every
such permission is inferred, with a could question offering to
rename them all.
With `--routes`, extract permissions reads the route table too and
writes its routes as extract router does, under the same code
source, read at the later of the two tables' commits. A route that
checks no permission takes the matching permission that every other
matching one implies; a route two match with neither implying the
other is a must question at its permission naming the narrowest
matches, and so is a route no rule reaches, asking whether it is
closed on purpose. A permission no route reaches prints a line and
is a could question.

Consequences: A system that checks pattern rows is extracted with its roles,
permissions and implications and each route's one permission, and
the questions a reviewer answers are only the ambiguous, closed and
dead ones and the names. A specification with no implies validates,
documents and generates byte for byte as before, the lending desk's
among them. A tree from extract permissions --routes stands in for
extract router on such a system, so the two are not both run on one
route table.

**Insight:** implies is design, not implementation, because the client depends on it: a holder of v1.all calls a read without being told of v1.get, which is the interface boundary's test. Implications rather than one permission per route (decision 1): the matrix stays one a person reads, with few permissions whose names mean something, and a route added under a pattern changes no permission. RBAC's role hierarchy (ANSI INCITS 359) orders roles, not permissions; ordering permissions is the one thing the policy's overlapping rows say, so it is put where they say it. Every check counts implied permissions because a check that counted only the listed ones would pass a role that reaches two separated permissions through one, which is the fail-open the checks exist to refuse. Cycles are refused because a cycle makes two names one permission, which is one thing said two ways. public is refused on either side for the same reason as in separation of duties: everyone holds it, so implying it says nothing, and public implying another would open that one to everyone without anyone writing public on it. The naming rule is fixed so that two runs and two people give the same name, and it keeps the plan's rule unchanged where no names meet; the list and read-one pair every API has (`/v1/items` and `/v1/items/{id}` with GET) would meet under it, so the parameters' words are what tells them apart, which the plan did not settle. The matchers read `*` only as the last segment because both libraries the plan names do, and a rule written another way is a line, not a guess. A pattern covers another by inclusion of the paths each matches, the one relation that is the same whichever matcher wrote either; a rule that reaches only part of a route's paths does not reach it, since the route's caller would be refused for some values. The route's permission is the one every other match implies, so that the most specific rule wins only where the others agree it is narrower; anything else is an ambiguity, and an ambiguity is a question at the operation, never a pick. --routes writes the routes in the permissions tree, rather than a second tree joined by merge, because a question at the operation needs the operation, and the two tables are one surface for such a system: it names no permission in its routes. Compiler test: an ambiguous route, a closed route, a dead rule, a name that cannot be made and a pattern the matchers do not read are each a question, never dropped and never guessed. Acceptance test: a reviewer reads the matrix with the implications marked and sees in one table what each role reaches.

### ADR-105: The words a document is read by are a vocabulary, a data file per language, English shipped; a source names its language, and the small points of the documents reader go with it

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 3 of docs/estate.md, build item 4, and the documents half of
point 10. extract documents found a commitment by English modal
words and read a table of fields only under English headers; the
yes words of a Required column, the sensitivity words, the types and
merge's days were English too, all of it in the code. A document in
another language gave its outline and nothing else, each table a
could line. Two small points went with it: a leading row-number
column made a table unreadable, and a document given to the
customer needed givenOutside written on its source by hand.

Decision: A vocabulary is a YAML file, `<tag>.specarch-vocabulary.yaml`
(docs/vocabularies.md), holding for one language: the commitment
words by priority (must, should), the frequency, time-limit,
pronoun, linking-verb and leading words, the number words with
their values, the units with the ISO 8601 duration each stands for,
the separators of a time of day, the table headers (field, type,
required, sensitivity, description and the row-number header), the
yes words, the sensitivity words of each sensitivity and the type
words of each type the reader writes. SpecArch ships the English
file, embedded in the binary, and reads it when nothing is named;
a project's file lives in its specification repository. Every key
is written, a list may be empty. The file is checked when read: a
key missing or unknown, a number, a duration or a tag in another
form, a word twice in a list, and a word in two lists of one group
(commitments, headers, sensitivities, types) are refused with the
file and the line, exit 1. Words in different groups may meet:
required is both a header and a yes word in English, and means one
thing in each place.
extract documents takes `--language <tag>` (a vocabulary SpecArch
ships) or `--vocabulary <file>`, or both naming one language, and
then prints a line naming the vocabulary and writes `language` on
the source; a tag with no shipped vocabulary and no file is refused
with the keys to write, exit 2. With neither, English is read and
no `language` is written, so the English tree is the one written
before, byte for byte. `language` on a source is a BCP 47 tag: the
language subtag and the subtags after it, by the schema's pattern.
A leading column headed with the row-number word is skipped in
every table, and `--given-outside` writes `givenOutside: true` on
the source.
merge reads a requirement's number of days by the vocabulary of the
language of the source it cites first: English when the source
names none, the shipped one, or one given with `--vocabulary`
(repeated, one per language). A unit counts when its duration is
whole days, so weeks count and hours do not. A language with no
vocabulary is said once per source, and its requirements are not
compared.

Consequences: A document in another language is read as fully as one in English
once its vocabulary exists, and the second-language conformance
case gives the same counts, priorities, fields, sensitivities and
questions as the English handbook. Which languages SpecArch ships
beyond English is decided when a project first supplies one. merge
joins a requirement in another language with a check only where the
check's name holds the subject's words, so in practice where the
code is named in that language. The questions and lines SpecArch
writes stay in English.

**Insight:** The words are data because they are what a project changes: a wrong or missing word is one line in a file, changed without a release, which is the acceptance test. They are a file per language, and the language is on the source, because the language is a fact about the document, so it is design, and a reader of the tree has to know which words were applied to read what was found and what was not. BCP 47 is the tag every platform and the HTTP Content-Language header use; the tag here is a lookup key, so the pattern catches a typo such as english and does not check the registry, which would tie the schema to a list that grows. A word in two lists of one group is refused because it would mean both, and the reader would pick one by the order it happened to check them, which is ambiguity, an error; groups are where a word has to mean one thing, and a whole-file rule would refuse English itself. Types are in the vocabulary though the plan's list did not name them, since a table in another language writes its types in that language, and without them every field would be a could line. Units are in it because merge reads them: a key nothing reads would be a placeholder. A vocabulary is checked by the reader in Go and has no JSON Schema, so that one definition says what a vocabulary is; the validator does not read vocabularies, so the Swift build is untouched beyond the schema's new key. The matchers write a word's edges out rather than use RE2's `\b`, which knows only ASCII letters and so never matches before or after a word such as prüfen. The English run was kept byte-identical by making the English file say exactly what the code said, so a change to English is a change to the file, seen in its diff. Compiler test: a table whose headers no vocabulary matches still prints its could line and keeps the outline; the vocabulary widens what is read and refuses nothing of the document. Only the vocabulary, a tool input, is refused, at its file and line.

### ADR-106: A client is keyed by its software_id with a kind, its client_id is a deployment value, and its version is checked once at the edge against a declared claim, after RFC 7591

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: docs/caller-context.md, the owner's decision 1. A role may hold a
permission only through one application, and an estate wants to
refuse an application whose version is too old. The design as first
proposed named a client by a key of its own and said nothing of its
version. The owner asked for the standard's names: RFC 7591
registers a client with client_id, software_id, software_version
and a software_statement, and a hop that refuses an old version
needs a value to check and a place to check it, since no claim of a
token names the version.

Decision: clients is keyed by the software_id of RFC 7591: the name the
publisher gives the software, the same across its versions, in
kebab-case like every key; through, via and callers name it. The
client_id is issued by the authorisation server per registration and
differs per environment, so it is a deployment value of the
implementation file (deployments.<environment>.clients.<name>.clientId),
never a design key. Each client says its kind, application (where a
person signs in) or service (a program that calls on its own account
or carries a person's call); a kind outside the two is refused
(client). A client may say softwareVersion, the versions it is
admitted at: a lower bound included and an upper bound excluded,
each a Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 version, written ">=1.2.0 <2.0.0";
and softwareStatement true when the version is the publisher's,
asserted in the signed statement of RFC 7591, section 2.3, which the
issuer verified at registration.
The version is checked once, at the edge: the hop that accepts the
client's own request, a person's access token or the client's own
proof. It is read from the claim softwareVersion of that token,
which the issuer fills from the registration; a specification with
a softwareVersion on any client whose edge token declares no such
claim is refused (software_version). No later hop checks it: a
Txn-Token carries no version, and the chain of ADR-111 binds every
later hop to the edge that did. A refusal is 403 with the problem
type the design declares for it, never 426. With softwareStatement
the techspec marks the check as security; without it the version is
self-asserted (RFC 7591, section 5) and the check is marked
compatibility. A native application whose installs run different
versions registers each instance, the per-instance registration RFC
8252, section 8.4, names RFC 7591 for; a browser application has the
version it was deployed at, and its registration is updated when
that changes. Derived red case at the edge, for every client with
softwareVersion: refused with a version outside the admitted range,
with the security event of ADR-109.

Consequences: A client's name in a specification is the one that survives a
re-registration and an environment, and the per-environment
identifier sits with the other deployment values. Which hop checks
the version is written, and a reader of the core's code expects no
version check there. An estate that wants the version trusted
registers its applications with a software statement; one that
does not is told, in the techspec, that the check is for
compatibility.

**Insight:** software_id rather than client_id as the key, because RFC 7591 makes client_id the server's issue per registration, so a design keyed by it would change at every environment and re-registration, and software_id "SHOULD remain the same across multiple updates or versions of the same piece of software": a name that is the software's is the name a grant is written against. The version is checked at the edge and nowhere else because a claim is the only thing a hop can check, no claim of a Txn-Token carries the version, and a check whose input is not on the wire would be pretending; the alternative, every hop checking a version the client reports in a request header, lost because a header the client writes is self-asserted at every hop and could never be the trusted form, where the registration is where the standard puts the version and RFC 7591 itself draws the line the owner drew: a software statement's claims may be trusted, everything else "MUST treat all client metadata as self-asserted". A range of versions rather than a list, because an estate admits "this version and later, before the next major" and a list would be rewritten at every release; Semantic Versioning gives the order RFC 7591's string equality does not. 403 and not 426 because RFC 9110 reserves 426 for a server that "refuses to perform the request using the current protocol", and an application's version is not the protocol; 403 is the server that "understood the request but refuses to fulfill it", with the problem document saying why. Compiler test: a version range that does not parse, a client with a version and no claim to check it against, and a kind outside the two are each an error at the client, and the client stays read with its roles and proof. Acceptance test: the techspec's client table shows each client's admitted versions and whether the check is security or compatibility, one line per client.

**Note:** From RFC 7591, OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Protocol, 2015: software_id SHOULD remain the same across multiple updates or versions of the same piece of software; client_id is issued by the authorization server; apart from a software statement's claims, the server MUST treat all client metadata as self-asserted. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591>

**Note:** From RFC 8252, OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps, 2017: Except when using a mechanism like Dynamic Client Registration to provision per-instance secrets, native apps are classified as public clients. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252>

**Note:** From RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, 2022: 403 Forbidden: the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it. 426 Upgrade Required: the server refuses to perform the request using the current protocol. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110>

**Note:** From Semantic Versioning, 2.0.0: Versions are ordered by major, minor and patch, so a range with a lower and an upper bound is well defined. <https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html>

### ADR-107: Clients, roles and the trust domain live in an identity module the other modules reference, every hop's route has its own permission, and permissions, clients and roles are reference targets

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: docs/caller-context.md, the owner's decision 2, with the estate's
decision 2 (docs/estate.md). A role's grant through one application
names a permission of the service that enforces it, and a call
passes through services in several modules, each with a
specification of its own. The owner's first answer put the clients
and the roles in the umbrella; the umbrella lists and pins the
modules and holds nothing of their design (docs/estate.md, section
2), so they needed a module of their own. The first design also
checked the permission at the last hop only, with the earlier hops
forwarding.

Decision: One module of the estate is the identity module: a specification
like any other, holding trustDomain (the URI that names the trust
domain), clients and roles, and the exchange operation that issues
the estate's tokens. Every other module declares it as a dependency
with specification and version, and names its clients and roles by
reference, identity#/clients/<name> and identity#/roles/<name>, in
through, via and callers; a role's permissions and through name
each permission in the module that enforces it, core#/permissions/<name>.
The reference targets of the estate's decision 2 widen by three:
#/permissions/<name>, #/clients/<name> and #/roles/<name>. The
umbrella still lists and pins, nothing more.
Every hop's route has a permission of its own, so a call through
the front ends' backend, the middleware and the core checks three
permissions, one in each module; a route with none is the schema
error it is today. A module validated alone counts a permission
granted only by a referenced role as an unresolved reference in its
summary line, beside the open questions; the umbrella run resolves
every reference and refuses a permission no role grants and a
through, via or callers naming a client or a role the identity
module does not hold (reference), at the entry.

Consequences: An estate has one place where its clients and roles are written and
one trust domain, and the modules that enforce permissions keep
them. A module alone validates with its grants as gaps, which is
what one team needs; the estate's consistency is checked in the
umbrella run. A route that forwarded a call without a permission of
its own is now an error, which is the fail-closed rule applied at
every hop.

**Insight:** A module rather than the umbrella, because the estate's decision 2 made the umbrella a list of modules with their versions and nothing copied into it, and a clients object in it would be the one exception, with a second place for a thing the modules reference; an identity service is a module of the estate already, with the exchange operation ADR-097 gives it, so its specification is where the clients and the roles belong. A permission per hop rather than one at the last, because a hop with no permission admits every caller that reaches it, which is the fail-open SA-5 refuses, and because the front ends' backend and the middleware are services with routes of their own that the reader extracts like any. The references take the estate's form rather than a copy of the role into each module, because a copy is a second place to say one thing. Compiler test: a reference the validator cannot resolve alone is a counted gap and the module is still read; a reference the umbrella run cannot resolve is an error at the entry. Acceptance test: the identity module's techspec shows the one client table and the one matrix for the estate, and each module's techspec shows which of its permissions each referenced role reaches.

### ADR-108: Inside a trust domain the application is checked at every hop in a Transaction Token's tctx, a call crossing a domain follows identity chaining, and the confused-deputy cases take their Txn-Token forms

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: docs/caller-context.md, the owner's decisions 3 and 6. The design
as first proposed checked the application only where the person's
own token is accepted, because after a token exchange RFC 8693
makes client_id the service that requested the token and no
standard claim carries the application on; later hops were to
trust the first through the chain of act claims. The owner wants
the application checked at every hop, with the Transaction Tokens
draft of the OAuth working group, and the two confused-deputy
cases derived at every operation for people once a service exists.

Decision: Inside a trust domain a call on a person's behalf carries one
Transaction Token (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens, cited as a
draft) from the edge to the last hop. The edge, the hop that
accepted the person's own access token, requests it from the
identity module's exchange operation with the token type
urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:txn_token, and the issuer writes
the application's software_id into tctx under the name
application: tctx is the claim the draft makes immutable through
the call chain, so the value every hop reads is the one the edge
had. A role's through is checked at every hop naming the
permission: against client_id on an access token, against
tctx.application on a Txn-Token. The token's sub is the person,
req_wl the edge workload, txn the transaction's identifier, aud the
trust domain (ADR-109), and scope, which the draft requires, holds
the permission the edge operation checked, in that module's wire
form; each later hop checks that scope is the permission of an edge
operation whose chain, derived by ADR-111, reaches it.
A call that leaves the trust domain follows OAuth identity chaining
(draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining, cited as a draft): the hop at
the boundary obtains a JWT authorisation grant from its own issuer
and presents it to the other domain's issuer for an access token
of that domain, which may carry act as RFC 8693 registers it; a
Txn-Token is never presented outside its domain. act nested inside
a domain is not used.
The confused-deputy cases are derived at every operation for people
once any service is declared, whether or not via is written, each
a security event of ADR-109: refused for a service's own token (a
hop calls on with its own proof or machine token and no
Txn-Token, and the person is lost with their rows, roles and
through); and refused for a person's token requested by a service
with no actor, which on an access token is client_id naming a
service with no act, and on a Txn-Token takes two forms, req_wl
naming a workload that is not an edge, and txn differing from the
one the hop received, since a hop passes the token on unmodified
and never mints a transaction of its own.

Consequences: Every hop checks the application and the person with one token
and no exchange per hop, and the core's techspec says what it
checks the application against. The identity module holds the
transaction token service, and its exchange operation's response
is the Txn-Token. An estate with two trust domains writes the
boundary hop's outbound call as identity chaining and its inbound
token as an access token with act. The draft's claim names are
taken at version 11 and are revisited when it is published.

**Insight:** Every hop rather than the edge only, because the owner's rule is that no hop trusts another for the application, and the first design's reason for stopping at the edge, that no standard claim carries the application on, no longer holds once a Txn-Token's tctx does: the draft exists for "context that remains immutable throughout the Call Chain", which is exactly this fact. The application rides in tctx and not in rctx, because the draft calls only tctx immutable and makes rctx the issuer's environmental context, and under a name the design fixes, application, because the draft defines no member for it and two issuers naming it two ways would be two ways to say one thing. scope holds the edge's permission because the draft requires scope, says it captures the transaction's purpose as narrowly as possible, and the permission the person was admitted for is the narrowest purpose the specification names; a token minted to read invoices is then refused at a delete. Identity chaining at a boundary rather than act nesting, because the draft defers crossing a domain to that draft and says a Txn-Token is accepted only inside the domain its aud names; act nesting inside a domain lost because one Txn-Token per transaction is the draft's design and a chain of exchanges per hop would mint a token per hop with no immutable context. The deputy cases take Txn-Token forms because the first design keyed them on client_id and act, which a Txn-Token lacks; req_wl and txn are what it has, and the draft's rule that a hop passes the token on unmodified is what a differing txn breaks. Compiler test: a Txn-Token declared without tctx.application where a through exists is an error at the token and the token is still read. Acceptance test: "only from the administration application" is one line on the role and holds at every hop, and the call diagram draws one token across the domain.

**Note:** From Transaction Tokens, an Internet-Draft of the IETF OAuth working group (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens-11), 11, 30 July 2026: tctx holds values that remain immutable throughout the Call Chain; aud identifies the Trust Domain and a Txn-Token MUST NOT be accepted outside it; scope, sub, req_wl, txn, iat and exp are REQUIRED; a workload passes the Txn-Token on unmodified; for cross-domain access implementers SHOULD use OAuth Identity and Authorization Chaining Across Domains. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens/>

**Note:** From OAuth Identity and Authorization Chaining Across Domains, an Internet-Draft of the IETF OAuth working group (draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining-17), 17, 19 July 2026: A JWT authorization grant, obtained through an intra-domain OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, facilitates the cross-domain acquisition of an access token; the same protocol is used every time a trust domain boundary is crossed. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining/>

**Note:** From RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, 2020: The act claim provides a means within a JWT to express that delegation has occurred; client_id carries the client identifier of the OAuth 2.0 client that requested the token. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693>

### ADR-109: The audience rule is per token kind, and every refusal of a caller derives a security event with a fixed name and severity, written to a declared append-only store with an alarm channel, after RFC 8417 and ASVS V16

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: docs/caller-context.md, the owner's decision 4. The design as first
proposed required aud with const or enum on every accepted token
and, in the umbrella, refused two modules accepting one aud value.
A Transaction Token's aud names the trust domain, one value for
every hop in it, so that rule would refuse every Txn-Token domain.
The owner also wants every refusal of a caller logged to a separate
append-only store in a standard form, with severities and an alarm
channel, and first asked that the validator refuse a refusal with
no event declared.

Decision: A token accepted without a fixed audience is an error
(token_audience), and what fixed means is per token kind: an
access token declares aud with const or enum naming the service
that accepts it, as RFC 9068, section 4, and RFC 7519, section
4.1.3, require; a Txn-Token (tokenType txn_token, ADR-111)
declares no aud, since its audience is the identity module's
trustDomain by the draft's rule, and aud written on one is refused
as a second way to say it. The estate's check that two modules do
not accept one aud value runs over access tokens only. A Txn-Token
captured at one hop and replayed at another is refused not by its
audience but by the workload identity of the immediate caller,
which via binds to the caller's proof (ADR-111).
Every refusal of a caller derives a security event with the case:
nobody writes one per case, and a refusal with no event cannot
exist. The event has a fixed name per rule, the identifier URI
<trustDomain>/events/<rule>, and a fixed severity:
a token for another audience, high; an immediate caller not listed
in via, high; the confused deputy in each form, high; a caller not
in callers, medium; an application not in through, medium; a
version outside the admitted range, medium with a software
statement and low without; an expired token, low. The identity
module declares securityEvents with store, the dependency that is
the separate append-only store every module writes to, and alarm,
the dependency that is the alarm channel; an estate with a client
and no securityEvents is refused (security_events). An event is a
Security Event Token (RFC 8417): events keyed by the identifier
URI, jti, iat, toe, txn always, and in the event the rule, the
severity, the operation, the client, sub, req_wl, the jti of the
refused token and the SHA-256 of it; never the token. An event
of severity high, or a repeat of any event for one client within
a window, goes to the alarm channel too; the count and the window
are deployment values of the implementation file. The validator
derives the event beside the red case; the techspec lists the
events with their severities under a Security events heading.

Consequences: A Txn-Token domain validates, and the replay the audience check
refuses for access tokens is refused for Txn-Tokens by the caller's
identity, which the design says in so many words. Every refusal
of this design and of ADR-096 and ADR-097 is logged in one form,
with one transaction identifier across the chain, to a store the
specification names, and a reviewer reads the list of events in
the techspec without reading the code. A project logs the token
itself nowhere.

**Insight:** Per token kind rather than one rule, because the draft says a Txn-Token's aud "MUST identify the Trust Domain" and the first design's rule, right for access tokens, would have made every Txn-Token domain an error; the alternative, exempting Txn-Tokens from the audience rule altogether, lost because a token with no audience at all is the replay the rule exists to refuse, and the trust domain is an audience, checked at every hop. Events derived rather than declared, because the first form, "the validator errors when a refusal has no event declared", cannot hold for the derived cases nobody writes, and a case that someone could forget to log is the gap ASVS V16 exists to close: 16.3.2 wants failed authorisation attempts logged, every one. A fixed name per rule and a fixed table of severities, because two projects then log one refusal under one name at one severity, and a severity written per case would be a placeholder nobody fills; the identifier is a URI under the trust domain because RFC 8417 makes each event's member name a URI. The SET format because it is the published form of a security event as a JWT with txn, which the Txn-Token draft takes from the same RFC, so one identifier joins the refusal to the transaction it refused. jti and a hash and never the token, because the draft's security considerations say complete Txn-Tokens must not be logged verbatim and ASVS 16.2.5 allows a session token only hashed or masked. The author declares only the store and the channel because those are what the estate must provide, the interface boundary's test: operators depend on the store existing and on where an alarm arrives; the count and the window are tuning, per deployment. "alarm" is the owner's word. Compiler test: a refusal whose event the project does not write is a derived red case that fails, never a silent gap, and a missing securityEvents is one error at the identity module with every token still read. Acceptance test: the techspec's event table is the list a security reviewer asks for, one line per rule.

**Note:** From Transaction Tokens, an Internet-Draft of the IETF OAuth working group (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens-11), 11, 30 July 2026: aud MUST identify the Trust Domain; complete Txn-Tokens MUST NOT be logged verbatim, log a hash or the payload without the signature. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens/>

**Note:** From RFC 8417, Security Event Token (SET), 2018: A SET is a JWT; the events claim's member names are URIs identifying the event statements; txn is a unique transaction identifier used to correlate related JWTs. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8417>

**Note:** From OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, chapter V16, Security Logging and Error Handling, 5.0.0: 16.3.2: failed authorization attempts are logged. 16.2.1: each log entry includes when, where, who and what. 16.2.5: session tokens are logged only hashed or masked. 16.4.2 and 16.4.3: logs cannot be modified and go to a logically separate system. <https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x25-V16-Security-Logging-and-Error-Handling.md>

**Note:** From RFC 9068, JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens, 2021: The resource server MUST validate that the aud claim contains a resource indicator value corresponding to an identifier the resource server expects for itself, and MUST reject the token otherwise. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068>

### ADR-110: callers is an explicit subset, people is a reserved caller like nobody is a reserved permission, and a service listed with no granting role is an error

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: docs/caller-context.md, the owner's decision 5, and the estate's
question 3. A route both people and a service call, the reporting
service reading the list people read, was left out of meta-model
0.3 (two operations with one handler), and the design as first
proposed recommended callers all, reported in the techspec as every
client with a granting role. ADR-096 has callers clients for a
machine route and nothing for people, who are admitted when it is
left out.

Decision: callers is a list, the explicit subset of who may call: people,
the reserved word for anyone signed in, and clients by name
(identity#/clients/reporting). Left out, it is [people], as
today. Which people is the roles' business, never callers'. The
validator refuses, as callers at the entry, an empty list, a name
that is neither people nor a declared client, a client twice, a
service with no roles (it only carries a person's call and never
calls on its own account), and a client none of whose roles grants
the operation's permission, directly or by implies. ADR-096's
callers clients is written [reporting], naming the clients. There
is no all. A client listed with a granting role is admitted on
its own account, and the derived cases of ADR-096 follow: refused
for a signed-in person where people is absent, refused for every
caller not listed.

Consequences: A route people and one service share is one operation that says
so, and the OpenAPI document keeps one path. A client not listed
is refused whatever its roles grant, and a client listed must hold
a role that grants the permission, so the list and the matrix
agree by construction. A route meant for machines names them.

**Insight:** A subset rather than all, because all would admit a client added later with a granting role without anyone writing it on the operation, the fail-open the estate declined pattern permissions for; the list is as long as the callers and no longer. people reserved rather than a flag beside the list, because nobody is a reserved word on the same scale already (ADR-096) and a flag would be a second way to say who may call. A listed service with no granting role is an error rather than a warning, because a name on an operation that no grant backs is a list and a matrix saying two things, and the fail-closed rule is one rule. Compiler test: a wrong name in callers is an error at the operation and the operation stays read with its permission. Acceptance test: the techspec's matrix row for the service shows the operation beside the roles that reach it, which the policy rows never showed.

### ADR-111: A token says its kind with tokenType, via on each operation names its immediate callers and is required wherever a Txn-Token or an act token is accepted, the validator derives the chain by induction, and every service in a chain proves a workload identity

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: docs/caller-context.md, the owner's decision 7. The design as
first proposed put via on the token as the default, listing whole
chains in call order, with via on an operation to narrow, and
accepted every chain the issuer signed when both were left out. A
Transaction Token records no chain, only req_wl, the workload that
requested it, so the last hop cannot verify a whole chain from the
token; the first design keyed the rule on act, which a Txn-Token
lacks; and the services it named declared no proof, where the
draft says a workload must not authenticate itself with a
Txn-Token.

Decision: A token declares tokenType: access_token, the default when left
out, or txn_token, the suffix of the OAuth token type identifier.
A txn_token has format jwt, is carried in the Txn-Token header and
never in Authorization, which generate openapi writes as an apiKey
scheme in that header for every operation accepting it, and
declares the claims of ADR-108.
via is written on an operation only: the list of the clients that
may be its immediate caller on a person's behalf, each a service.
It is required on every operation whose accepted token is a
txn_token or declares act, and missing there is the error via;
on an operation accepting neither it is refused, and so are an
empty list, a client not declared, an application, a client twice
and a client without a workload-identity proof. There is no
default on the token and no "left out means every chain the
issuer signed". The validator derives the chain by induction
across the estate: for each client in an operation's via, the
operation of that client's module that calls this one (the calls
of its dependency) must either accept a txn_token with a via of
its own or be the edge, accepting an access token; a hop whose
via does not name the caller that calls it, or a caller with no
via where one is required, is a gap, the error via at that hop.
The middleware's delete lists the front ends' backend, the core's
lists the middleware, and the chain is the induction.
Every client a via names declares a proof of a workload-identity
kind: mutualTls (RFC 8705), spiffe (an X.509 or JWT SVID carrying
the SPIFFE ID) or wimse (the Workload Identity Token of the WIMSE
drafts, bound to a key the workload proves it holds); a token
proof there is refused, and a proof of kind token naming a
txn_token is refused anywhere (proof). via binds to that proof:
the hop checks that the immediate caller's workload identity is
the one the implementation file's deployments map for the named
client, and the Txn-Token's req_wl is the edge, not the caller.
Derived red case at every operation with via: refused with a
caller not listed in via, which the test gives as the edge calling
the last hop directly; each refusal is the security event of
ADR-109.

Consequences: Each hop's specification says who may call it and what the caller
proves, and the estate's chain is checked once, in the umbrella
run, from those local facts. A service forgotten in a chain is an
error at the hop that would admit it, not a token the issuer
signed. A specification declares which header a token rides in by
its kind, and the OpenAPI document shows it. The identity module's
exchange operation issues a txn_token for a call inside the
domain and an access token with act for one that leaves it.

**Insight:** The immediate caller rather than a whole chain, because the draft keeps the call chain out of the token (only req_wl names a workload) so the last hop has nothing to verify a chain against, while its immediate caller's workload identity is something it can check; the chain then holds by induction, each hop vouching for the one before, and the validator is where the induction is checked, since it reads every module. On the operation only, not the token, because a token is minted once for the whole domain and accepted at every hop, so a via on it would say one thing for every hop where each hop's caller differs; the first design's token-level default lost with it. No "every chain the issuer signed" default, because an issuer's may_act policy is a second place for the rule and a hop would admit a chain nobody wrote, the fail-open the estate declined pattern permissions for. The rule keys on tokenType and act rather than act alone, because a Txn-Token has no act and via would otherwise not be required at the hops the owner wants it on; tokenType is the token's own word for what it is, taken from the OAuth token type identifiers so that the exchange request and the specification say it one way. The Txn-Token header because the draft says the Authorization header MUST NOT be used, workloads use it for other purposes. Proof is mandatory on a chain's services because the draft says a workload MUST NOT use a Txn-Token to authenticate itself, so a hop with no proof has nothing a via could bind to; the three kinds are the published forms of a workload's identity, and an estate that has none is told so at the client rather than at the first breach. Compiler test: a missing via, a gap in the chain and a service with no proof are each an error at the entry and the operation stays read with its permission. Acceptance test: via is one line per operation that reads as the call is drawn, and the techspec's call diagram draws the chain the induction found with the token on each arrow.

**Note:** From Transaction Tokens, an Internet-Draft of the IETF OAuth working group (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens-11), 11, 30 July 2026: A Txn-Token is carried in the Txn-Token header, one per request; the Authorization header MUST NOT be used; a workload MUST NOT use a transaction token to authenticate itself to another workload; the token type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:txn_token; req_wl identifies the workload that requested the Txn-Token. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens/>

**Note:** From RFC 8705, OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication and Certificate-Bound Access Tokens, 2020: An authorization server binds an access token to the client certificate presented over mutual TLS, so that only the holder of the private key can use it. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8705>

**Note:** From The SPIFFE Standards, the SPIFFE ID and the SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document (SVID) as an X.509 certificate or a JWT: A SPIFFE ID is a structured string, represented as a URI, which serves as the name of an entity; an SVID is a document which carries the SPIFFE ID itself, as an X.509 certificate or a JWT. <https://github.com/spiffe/spiffe/tree/main/standards>

**Note:** From WIMSE Workload Credentials, an Internet-Draft of the IETF WIMSE working group (draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds-02), 02, 2 July 2026: A Workload Identity Token carries the workload identifier as sub and a cnf claim with the workload's public key; the workload must prove possession of the matching private key, so it is not a bearer token. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds/>

### ADR-112: A specification names an element of another through a dependency as <dependency>#/<pointer>, resolved when that specification is given in the same run and counted as unresolved otherwise; and merge asks when two trees disagree on how roles go on the wire

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 2 of docs/estate.md, build item 5, and the owner's decision 2
there: a reference is <dependency>#/<pointer> through dependencies,
in $ref's own URI form. An estate of modules owned by different teams
is specified one module at a time, and a module keeps another's
customer number, picks from another's list and calls another's
operations; $ref reached only the same specification, and calls
named a system, not an element of it. The plan named a dependency's
specification as the key the umbrella lists it under, which is build
item 6, while this item has to resolve two specifications given
together without one. The dispatcher added the open point of
ADR-099: merge took info.roleNames from whichever tree stated it and
asked nothing when another tree read its roles as named.

Decision: info gains name, the specification's name in kebab case. A
dependency gains specification, another specification's info.name,
and version, the info.version its references were written against,
each only with the other. A reference is the dependency's name, #,
and a JSON pointer into that specification; it stands in a field's
$ref (an entity, enum, view or schema), a many-to-one or one-to-one
relation's target and a list page's entity (an entity), and a
picker's source, a list page's source and an entry of calls (an
operation, as #/paths/<path>/<method> with the path's slashes
written ~1). A bare calls entry names the system, as before, and is
not a reference.
validate, gaps, document and generate read every specification they
