are given before checking any. Given the specification alone, the
validator refuses, as reference at the entry, a name that is not a
dependency, a dependency with no specification, a one-to-many or
many-to-many relation to another specification's entity, another
specification's list on a page that is not a list, and a page or
picker whose entity and list are not of one dependency; every other
reference is counted in the summary line as unresolved, listed in
gaps and the questions document with where it stands, and the
specification validates with no error for it. Given the specification
the dependency names in the same run, each reference resolves there:
an element it does not have, a list that does not list the entity it
is read for, a column, filter, shown or filled field the entity does
not have, and a dependency whose version is not the other's
info.version are reference errors at the entry; a reference to an
element a must question blocks there waits on that question, named in
gaps. Two specifications given under one name make every reference to
the name an error.
Generators read one specification. generate sql writes the column a
relation to another specification's entity keeps, typed as its own
via field, with no foreign key and a comment naming the
specification, version and dependency, and a later migration adds or
drops no foreign key for it. A field typed by another specification's
element is refused as reference at the field by every code target
that would write it (sql only for entities and views), and the UI
targets refuse a list page or picker reading another specification's
list; the idiom contract does not ask a row for such a field. The
techspec names each reference with the specification and version.
merge leaves info.roleNames out and asks one must question blocking
roles when two trees whose roles grant permissions differ: one says
upper_snake and another says nothing of it. info.wireNames is taken
as before.

Consequences: A module validates alone, with its references counted and listed,
and is checked against another by naming both. A specification with
no reference validates, documents and generates byte for byte as
before. Until estate generation, a module whose fields are typed by
another's schema gets no OpenAPI document or Go code for them; its
SQL and documents are written.

**Insight:** The name is on the specification, not only in the umbrella, because two modules given to one run have to find each other without an umbrella, and a folder's name is not the module's (a module's specification sits in a folder named spec); the umbrella's key is then checked equal to info.name, so it is one name said once and checked where it is repeated, as version is. The pointer form is JSON Schema's own (a $ref is a URI reference, RFC 3986 section 4.1, whose fragment is a JSON pointer, RFC 6901), which the rule for new keywords asks for, with the dependency's name standing for the document: a dependency already is the other system and carries its time limit, so the reference adds no second registry. An operation is named by its path and method rather than its operationId because a pointer is a path into the document, and an operationId is a name the other team may change without moving the operation. Only to-one relations may cross, because their key is a field this module keeps; a one-to-many relation's via is in the other module's table and a many-to-many's join is in neither, so neither could be checked or generated across two databases. A page of another module's records is a list because a form or view loads and writes one record through this module's own operations. An unresolved reference is a counted gap and not an error by the compiler test: one module alone is readable and validates, and the error comes only where the other specification contradicts it, at the entry. A reference to a blocked element waits on the question rather than resolving, so the answer there is what unblocks it here. Generators refuse at the entry rather than guess: a column typed by a schema this run has not read would be a type made up, and inlining the schema needs the other specification, which arrives with generation over the estate (build item 6). The SQL column needs no foreign key across databases, which is the design the plan asked for. roleNames: a tree whose roles grant permissions was read from where a permission check reads them, so its silence on roleNames says the roles go on the wire as named; two such trees that differ are a disagreement, and a disagreement is a question, never a pick. A tree's silence on wireNames does not say the names go as written, since most readers (the database, documents, a router) never see a body, so it stays as it was. Acceptance test: a module is shown on its own, with its references listed as gaps, and two modules' consistency is checked by giving both in one run, before the umbrella exists.

### ADR-113: An estate is the file specarch-estate.yaml that lists each module's specification by its info.name with its folder and the version held, brings every module into the run, and checks each against its entry as module

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 2 of docs/estate.md, build item 6: an estate of modules owned
by different teams is specified one module at a time (ADR-112), and
its consistency is to be checked where the estate is, in an umbrella
repository that holds the modules as submodules and commits to none
of them. ADR-112 resolves the references between two specifications
named in one run; nothing listed which specifications make up the
estate, pinned the version of each, or checked that the name a
dependency gives is the module's.

Decision: An estate is a file of its own kind, specarch-estate.yaml, with
specarchEstate 0.1, info (title, version, description) and modules:
each keyed by its specification's info.name in kebab case, with its
location, the folder that holds its specarch.yaml relative to the
estate file, and the version the estate holds. It has no stages and
holds nothing of a module.
validate, gaps, document, generate and the other verbs that read
specifications take an estate as a file named or found under a
folder, and read each module whose folder holds a specification as
if it were named, once however often it is reached, so references
between modules resolve as ADR-112 says. The estate is an input of
validate's count. Each module is checked against its entry with the
rule module: a folder that does not exist or holds no specarch.yaml
at its location; a specification with no info.name, or one that is
not the key, at the module; an info.version that is not the version
listed at its version; and a module whose operations' or jobs' calls
come back to it through the modules their dependencies name, at each
module on the cycle, with the shortest such cycle from the smallest
name on it. The estate's problems are printed by validate, by gaps
before the modules' documents, and by document, and make the status
1; an estate has no problems file of its own.
document techspec given an estate also writes estate.md, the module
map, into --out or else docs beside the estate file: the modules with
the version held and a link to each specification, the estate's
problems, and each dependency that names a specification as an edge
of a flowchart and a row of a table, a specification the estate does
not list drawn apart.

Consequences: validate, gaps and document on an umbrella folder read every module
in one run and resolve every reference between them. A module alone
validates as before. A specification with no estate validates,
documents and generates byte for byte as before. Generators still
read one specification at a time, each module of an estate given on
its own; writing another module's schema inline waits.

**Insight:** A file of its own kind, rather than a specification with a modules section, because an estate has no stages, requirements or design of its own, and a specification that held none would be one with every stage empty; the fixed name lets a folder search find it as it finds specarch.yaml. The key is the module's info.name, so the name is said in the module and checked where it is repeated, as ADR-112 does for a dependency's specification; the version listed is checked the same way, so moving a module to a new version is a change to the estate file a reviewer sees. The estate lists and pins and copies nothing, so each team's specification stays the one truth of its module and the estate cannot drift from it. A cycle of calls is an error because each call in it waits on the next, so one slow module makes every module on the cycle give up at its time limit; a cycle through a dependency named but not called, such as one module keeping another's key, is not one. It is reported at every module on it, since any of their owners may break it, with one cycle chosen the same way in both builds. An estate's problems are about its listing, not about any module, so they go in no module's problems file and are printed wherever the estate is read; by the compiler test the estate is still read, every module that is there is checked, and a module that is not found is an error at its entry, never a run refused. The module map goes to docs beside the estate file because the estate has no implementation file to name an output folder (ADR-073), and the umbrella is where the estate's reader looks. Acceptance test: the estate is shown as one map of the modules and their references, made from the specifications as they stand, and a module moved to a new version is checked against the others in one run before the estate's version changes.

### ADR-114: A check skipped for one kind of caller is a gate with bypassedFor client in the permission table and on a permission check's binding, asked as one must question blocking the permission of every operation the check guards, and joined by merge

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 6 of docs/estate.md, build item 7: an estate's role check
skips a machine-to-machine token entirely, so any service token
passes every route the check guards. The permission table's gates
(ADR-050) say only that a setting switches a check off, so a check
switched off by the kind of caller was read as one that holds every
caller to its roles, and nothing asked about it. The owner decided
on 2026-10-14 (decision 3 of docs/estate.md) that a route both
people and clients call is not given a keyword of its own in this
build and that the gate's question is the record. The caller
context designed the same day (docs/caller-context.md, ADR-110)
answers that row of meta-model 0.3 with callers, the explicit list
of who may call an operation, people and clients by name, with no
all; this build keeps decision 3's gate and leaves callers to the
caller context's own items.

Decision: A gate of the permission table names, in place of setting,
bypassedFor: the kind of caller the check lets through whatever its
roles grant. client, meta-model 0.3's word for a caller on its own
account rather than a person's, is the one kind. A gate with both a
setting and a kind, neither, no check or another kind is refused,
naming the gate, and one listed twice is refused as a setting gate
is. extract permissions prints a line for each and asks one must
question per check, decided by the system owner and citing the
table's gate: "The check C is skipped for every client: a client
passes it whatever its roles grant. Is every client meant to reach
each operation the check guards, or which ones are, and should the
check hold the others to their roles' grants?". Given the route
table with --routes, it blocks the permission of each operation the
check guards: each route that names a permission other than public,
and, where the check reads a policy of rules (ADR-100), every route,
since the policy decides each one; a line counts them. Without the
route table, or where the check guards no route, it blocks the
roles.
The implementation file's bindings.http.permissionChecks item takes
bypassedFor: client too, in the implementation schema, so both
validator builds read it. extract go asks the same question, in the
same words, with the check named by its function's name, the
method's alone for Type.Method as a gate on a setting names it,
blocking the permission of each operation that calls the check and
citing the first call. merge asks the question once per check and
kind, blocking every operation any tree says the check guards, with
every tree's citation, and never leaves it out as answered.

Consequences: A permission table without bypassedFor reads as before, and so does
an implementation file without it; the counting line of extract
permissions names a kind of caller beside a setting. The setting
gate still blocks the roles. A printed tree and a parsed one that
disagree on which operations the check guards are joined into their
union; asking about the difference waits for a case that needs it.

**Insight:** A gate of its own form, beside the setting gate, because it is the same fact of the same check, a condition under which the check fails open, and the printer that declares one declares the other; a second list would be a second way to say it. The value is the caller kind rather than a token type or a header, because that is what the answer is about and what meta-model 0.3 names; client alone, because the other kind, people, is what the check is for, and a check skipped for people is a check that does nothing, which is not a gate but a missing check. Asked at every guarded operation rather than once at the roles, because the compiler test puts a problem at the entry it concerns: the operations are where a reviewer sees that a client reaches them unchecked, and the techspec marks each. One question per check, not one per operation, because it is one decision the owners make about one check, and a question per route would be twenty answers to one question. A route the check does not guard (one that names no permission or names public) is not blocked, since a client reaches it as anyone does. In extract go the skip is declared, not found: a test of the caller's kind is a comparison of a header, a claim or a token's prefix, written the project's way, and the setting gate's shape (an early return while a setting is empty) has no counterpart that syntax recognises without guessing. The implementation file already names the project's checks, so the person who names a check says there that it skips clients; it is a fact of the stack, not of the design. merge never leaves the question out as answered because ADR-049's rule (a question whose blocked keys another tree gives is answered) would drop it whenever the other tree gives the permissions, and giving a permission says nothing of who may skip it. The answer, where the owners say a client is meant to reach an operation, is the client named in that operation's callers once the caller context is built (docs/caller-context.md, ADR-110), which the validator refuses unless one of the client's roles grants the permission; where they say it is not, the check is to change. Until then the question is the record, which needs no keyword in a 0.2 tree. Acceptance test: the bypass shows at each operation of the first techspec made from the readers, so an owner looking at a route sees that every client reaches it, and the change asked for is one line, in the callers of that operation or in the check.

### ADR-115: The name of a page's schema file is the ui binding's schemaFile in the implementation file, page.schema.ts when left out, read by extract pages and written by the TypeScript UI generator

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 7 of docs/estate.md, first half of build item 8: an admin
application keeps the schema its component library renders a page
from in _schema.ts beside page.tsx, a private file by the App
Router's rule, where extract pages reads page.schema.ts (ADR-057)
and specarch-gen-ui-typescript writes it (ADR-067). The name is the
project's convention, so a project with another one got pages with
no content from the reader and schemas it does not use from the
generator.

Decision: The ui binding of an implementation file takes schemaFile, the name
of the file beside a page's file that holds its schema. The
implementation schema holds it to a TypeScript or JavaScript file
name with no folder, and not one the App Router serves itself
(page, route, layout, loading, error, not-found, template or
default), so both validator builds report another value at its
entry. extract pages takes --implementation with or without
--facts, prints a line naming the schema file the binding gives,
and reads each page's schema from the file of that name; a name the
reader cannot take prints a line, is asked for in a must question
blocking the pages, and page.schema.ts is read meanwhile.
specarch-gen-ui-typescript writes each page's schema under that
name and imports it from there in the page and its derived tests.
Left out, the name is page.schema.ts, as before.

Consequences: An implementation file without schemaFile reads and generates as
before, byte for byte. The Pages Router and Nuxt readers keep no
schema file of their own.

**Insight:** One key in the implementation file, because the name is a fact of the stack and not of the design, and one key read by both the reader and the generator, so a project that has the one convention gets both halves from it and the two cannot disagree. The ui binding, beside components, because both say how the project's component library is used. The router's own file names are refused because a schema file of that name would be served as a page, a route or a layout, and the reader would read the same file twice. A name the reader cannot take is asked for, not refused, by the compiler test: the router's folder is still read, every page is written, and the question stands at the pages until the name is corrected. Acceptance test: the first techspec made from such an application shows each page's content, read from the file the team keeps it in, and the generator's output lands in the files the team already reviews.

### ADR-116: specarch facts writes the code-facts dumps from the installed binary; the JavaScript reader is inside it on typescript-go copied into third_party at a pinned tag, with a Vue reader of its own, and the Swift and Dart readers are carried by it and built in a per-user cache

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 7 of docs/estate.md, second half of build item 8: the code-facts
dumps of JavaScript, Swift and Dart were made by scripts of a SpecArch
checkout, the JavaScript one by a Node program on the TypeScript
compiler 6.0.3 and @vue/compiler-sfc installed with npm ci, and a team
that installs the binary has no checkout. TypeScript 7 ships its
compiler written in Go, github.com/microsoft/typescript-go
(Apache-2.0); its parser, binder, checker and program are under
internal/, which Go lets no other module import, and it offers no
public Go API, only a JSON-RPC API to its own binary. The JavaScript
reader resolves names with the checker, so it needs the program and
the checker, not the parser alone. The owner decided on 2026-10-14
to copy the needed Go source at a pinned release tag rather than run
the tsgo binary beside specarch, and to write a Go reader of the Vue
parts the facts use, falling back to a Node helper for Vue only if
it could not match the existing dumps.

Decision: specarch facts <language> <folder> <dump> writes the dump the
scripts wrote, with the same checks of a committed folder, the same
file list and the same repository key; tools/code-facts/dump-*.sh
build specarch from the checkout and call it.
javascript runs a reader inside the binary, internal/facts, a port
of the Node reader onto typescript-go: the packages the program and
the checker need (44, with the bundled lib.d.ts files) are copied
into third_party/typescript-go by tools/typescript-go/pull.sh at the
tag typescript/v7.0.2, out of internal/ with their import paths
rewritten and nothing else changed, with upstream's LICENSE,
NOTICE.txt and UPSTREAM naming the tag and its commit. The script is
how a later tag is pulled in, followed by the modules upstream's
go.mod pins, their scan, and every JavaScript dump made again and
compared. Its dumps name TypeScript 7.0.2, which specarch extract
reads. A .vue file is split by the reader's own Vue reader, which
reads a component as Vue 3's compiler-sfc parses it, and the dump
names it as the SpecArch Vue reader, version 1, which extract reads
in place of @vue/compiler-sfc 3.5.43. The Node reader is removed.
swift and dart run readers/swift and readers/dart, which the binary
embeds with Package.resolved or pubspec.lock: they are written once
into the user's cache ($XDG_CACHE_HOME, else the operating system's
cache folder, under specarch/readers/<language>-<hash of the files>)
and built there with swift build or dart pub get --enforce-lockfile.

Consequences: The binary grows from about 19 MB to about 40 MB, most of it the
compiler and the bundled library files. go.mod gains
go-json-experiment/json, zeebo/xxh3 (with klauspost/cpuid), and
x/sync and x/sys at the versions the graph already held. A dump of
JavaScript made before names TypeScript 6.0.3 and is refused until
it is made again. The Swift and Dart readers still need their
toolchains, and their first run builds them.

**Insight:** The compiler's own Go source, because the reader's facts are the checker's answers, and only the checker gives them as TypeScript gives them; a resolver of our own would be a second resolver to keep right. Copied rather than run as a second binary, because one binary is what a team installs and pins, and a subprocess API is one more version to keep in step. Copied whole per package and never edited, so pulling a tag is mechanical and every difference in a dump after it is the compiler's, seen in the dumps' diff. Swift and Dart keep their helpers because no Go parser of either is faithful to SwiftSyntax or the analyzer; they are pinned by their lock files and a cache named by a hash, so a binary never runs another binary's reader. The port was checked against the Node reader before it was removed: every JavaScript, TypeScript and Vue file committed under spec/tests and examples, about 15,000 facts, gave the same dump from both, and the 14 committed JavaScript dumps were made again identical below the parser line. TypeScript 7 answered one thing differently: a name imported from a CommonJS module that exports it as module.exports = { allow } resolves to the shorthand property, where 6.0.3 resolved it to the function; the reader follows such a property to its value's declaration, so the dump keeps the place the value is declared. The Vue reader gave the same facts on every .vue file there, so the Node helper for Vue was not needed. Acceptance test: the first techspec of a module comes from a dump the team makes with the binary it installed, with nothing else to install for JavaScript, and a dump made again after a change is the same as before wherever the source did not change.

### ADR-117: merge keeps a reference where the shape written in place agrees with the named one, leaves the key out where a key both give differs, and asks about properties only one side lists

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: An OpenAPI document names a request body's schema by reference,
`{$ref: '#/schemas/CreateThingRequest'}`, and writes the schema once
under its components; the code's handler decodes the body into a
struct, which the Go reader writes in place, `{type: object,
properties: {...}, required: [...]}`. ADR-045 joins two trees key
by key: a key only one tree gives is kept, and a key both give with
different values is left out with a must question. The two forms
share no key, so both were kept, and the merged tree held `$ref`
beside `type`, which the design schema refuses as two forms of one
field. Each tree validated on its own, and the merged one did not,
in either order; the same held at every position where two schema
mappings meet: a response, a parameter, an array's items, a
property. A reader that asked a question below the position, the
width of an `int64` or the shape of a map, blocked a pointer that
no longer existed once one form was taken.

Decision: A position where exactly one tree gives `$ref` and another gives a
shape in place (a `type`, `properties` or `items`) is not joined key
by key. It is kept as it was first given while the trees are read,
and settled once every tree is in, when the merged entries hold the
reference's target under schemas, entities or enums. The named shape
and each shape written in place are compared on what both say: the
keys that say what a value is (type, format, the widths and bounds,
pattern, enum as a set), `required` as a set, the items, and each
property both list, down through a property that is itself a
reference on one side and a shape on the other. A key only one side
gives says nothing.
Where nothing both say differs, the reference is kept, the one name
for the shape, and a line names the trees that refer and the trees
that write; the element above carries every tree's citation as
before. Where a key both give differs, the key is left out and the
must question of ADR-045 asks which is right, its why naming each
difference (the property, and what each side says). Where nothing
both say differs and the sides list different properties, the
reference is kept and one should question at the position names
the properties each lists and the other does not; nothing is
written into the named shape and nothing is dropped unsaid.
A question a tree asked at the position where the reference is kept
is answered by the trees that refer, since the named shape is the
shape. A question asked below the position follows the reference:
its pointer is written under the named entry, where the rules of
ADR-049 and ADR-050 take it from there, so a width the document's
schema gives answers it and one it does not give stays asked, at
the property it is about. Where the key is left out, a question
below it moves up to the position, the one missing key the must
question blocks. A field of an entity left out so leaves the
entity's required list too, which may only name the fields the
entity has.
An entity's field one tree gives as an object with nothing more and
another as a schema is not such a position: it is the schema kept
as JSON (ADR-077).

Consequences: A merged specification whose trees refer and write in place
validates on its own, and gaps reads it. Two trees that both write a
shape in place, or both refer, merge as before. A key only the
document gives (a maximum length, a pattern) stays with the named
schema, and a key only the code gives at a property both list (a
nullable type where the document states none) is a disagreement,
asked as any other. Where the trees give the same position three
ways, the trees that write in place are each compared with the
named shape.

**Insight:** The reference rather than the shape in place, because the design says a shape once and names it everywhere else (docs/principles.md, one way to say one thing); writing the shape out where the code has it would say the same thing twice and let the two drift. Comparing only what both say, because that is ADR-045's rule for every other key, and a struct cannot state a maximum length or a pattern that a document states; a key only one side gives was never a disagreement. Properties only one side lists as a should question rather than a union or a silence, because writing the code's extra property into the named schema would say every operation that refers to it takes that property, which the merge does not know, and leaving it out would hide a difference between the document and the code, which is what the merge is for; should rather than must, because the shapes do not contradict each other and the reader decides whether the document or the code is to change. Settling the position after every tree is in rather than as the trees are read, because the named entry may come from a tree merged later, or from a section merged after the one that refers to it, and the comparison needs the whole entry. Moving a question below the position to the named entry, because the validator holds every question to a pointer the tree has (BUG-010), and the question is about the property, which now lives under its name; collapsing it to the position where the key is left out, for the same rule. Acceptance test: the first merge of a service's OpenAPI document with its Go source validates with no error, and an owner reading the techspec sees one schema per request body, cited from both, and a question wherever the struct and the schema disagree; the change asked for is one line at the property named, in the document or in the code.

### ADR-118: Workflow definitions in a format of a project's own are read through a workflow table the project's printer writes, read by extract workflows --table into the workflows the BPMN reader writes, with the same questions at the same keys

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 8 of docs/estate.md, build item 9: an estate's workflow
engine keeps its definitions in JSON of its own (a flow per action,
a trigger, a binding and a form schema, in many files), and the
same files sit in two folders of which the seeding script loads
one. Only extract outline took them, so gaps listed the folder as
unread. A documented plug-in reader was asked for, or a neutral
format a project's printer writes. The owner decided on 2026-10-14
(decision 5 of docs/estate.md) that a standard workflow format gets
a reader of its own, as BPMN 2.0 has (ADR-054), and a format of a
project's own gets a table its printer writes.

Decision: SpecArch defines the workflow table, as it does the route table
(ADR-044) and the permission table (ADR-050): a JSON object with
workflowTable 1, the path of the folder the engine loads its
definitions from, the commit that last changed it, repository when
the dump is in another repository (ADR-098), and workflows, each
with name, file (the file it is defined in, or null), description
(or null), trigger (operation, a name or null, and form, a list of
fields each with a name and the engine's type), steps in order, and
emits (the messages it publishes when it ends, channel/Message). A
step has a name and a kind: approval with approvers, deadline,
onDeadline and escalateTo; operation with operation; other with a
description. Every key is written, null where the format allows
it, and no other key is; a table that breaks this, a workflow with
no name or listed twice, and a step or a form field with no name
are refused, naming the workflow and the step.
tools/workflows/dump-workflows.sh runs the project's printer in a
committed folder and wraps what it prints with the version, the
path and the commit, as dump-routes.sh does.
extract workflows --table reads it with the BPMN reader's rules and
questions at the same keys: the workflow named in kebab-case, a step
in camelCase, an approver as a role in kebab-case citing the
workflow's file, the trigger's and each operation step's operation
left out with a must question naming it under names, and the
subject, each approval's permission and each role's grants and
description must questions. A value the subset does not hold prints
a line and is asked for or left out, as the BPMN reader does with
an element; a step of kind other ends the steps there with a must
question on the workflow. The form's fields and the messages
emitted each print a line and are a could question, since the 0.2
workflow holds neither: the form is the request body of the
trigger's operation, which another tree declares, and emits names
messages of channels, which the table does not declare and the
validator checks. The workflow cites its file, or the folder when
the file is null, outside the folder or not in the repository.

Consequences: extract workflows reads a BPMN 2.0 XML file as before; --table is
refused for any other source. A project writes its printer, a
command that loads the definitions as the engine does and prints
the list of workflows. A plug-in reader protocol waits until a
format appears that a printer cannot flatten into the sequential
subset.

**Insight:** A table the project prints rather than a reader of the project's format, because the readers' test keeps extract's rules in one place: a plug-in that writes elements would be a second place for them, and a format of one project is not a standard whose rules SpecArch can learn once. The printer loads the definitions as the engine does, so the two-folders question is answered by construction: the folder the engine does not load is never read, and the commit names what was loaded. The same questions at the same keys as the BPMN reader, because merge leaves out a question another tree asks at the same key, so the two readings of one workflow merge into one workflow with both citations and each question once, and a disagreement between them is a must question at the key, as for any two trees. The keys of a step are the 0.2 workflow step's own (approvers, deadline, onDeadline, escalateTo, operation), one word for one meaning. Every key written and null allowed, as the route table writes a permission null, because a key left out is ambiguous between a printer that cannot say and one that forgot; null says the first, and the reader asks for it. Kind other, rather than refusing a step the subset does not hold, because the compiler test keeps an incomplete definition readable: the steps before it are written, and the rest is a must question at the workflow. The form and the messages are kept as could questions rather than written in a key of the reader's own, because the 0.2 workflow has no key for either and a tree a reader writes validates on its own; a reviewer who reads the question writes the request body or the channel where the specification holds them. Acceptance test: the first techspec of a module whose workflows are in its own format shows each workflow with its steps, approvers and deadlines, merged with the routes' tree, and a change a reviewer asks for in a workflow is a change to its definition, printed again.

### ADR-119: An element says it is internal with audience, document --audience external leaves it out and counts it, and a requirement another stakeholder's component fulfils carries ownedBy and fulfilledBy

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 9 of docs/estate.md, build item 10. An estate's specification
holds what its team writes for itself beside what it promises the
customer: a note from inside the team, a requirement written as a
proposal below the promises. Today an extension key and a rule read
by people keep such an element out of the customer's documents, and
nothing checks it. A promise in the customer's documents that
another component keeps has no form either: written as a
requirement, the validator asks what here satisfies and verifies
it; left out, its trace is lost. The owner decided on 2026-10-14
(decision 7 of docs/estate.md) that such a requirement carries
ownedBy, the word SpecArch already has for what someone else builds
(ADR-046), rather than a status value.

Decision: audience, a SpecArch keyword with the one value internal, may be
written on every element named by a key: an entry of a section of
named elements, the session, release, rollback and sign-off, an
operation, an entity's relation or unique constraint, and a
channel's message; left out, the element is for everyone. An
element inside an internal one is internal with it.
The validator, in both builds, reports the error audience where an
element for everyone names an internal element of the
specification at one of four places: a $ref, a relation's target,
a page's entity and a requirement's needs. Other names an element
gives (the permission an operation requires, a role a workflow
names, a satisfies or verifies entry) are not checked.
specarch document --audience external writes a document for
everyone: every internal element is left out with what is inside
it, and so are the satisfies, verifies and needs entries that name
an internal requirement or need, an implementation file's mappings
of an internal element and its satisfies entries naming an internal
requirement, the open questions whose every pointer is at or under
an internal element, and the errors,
warnings and waiting references at one; the summary says how many
elements it left out in each section. It needs --out, writes no
region of specarch.md, and is refused for the problems target.
Without the flag every document holds every element and marks the
internal ones.
A requirement may carry ownedBy, a stakeholder of the
specification, and beside it fulfilledBy,
<dependency>#/requirements/<id>, the requirement of another
specification that fulfils it. The validator checks ownedBy as it
checks a mapping's, resolves fulfilledBy as any reference into
another specification (ADR-112), and warns neither
requirement_unsatisfied nor requirement_unverified for it; it still
warns acceptance_missing. The traceability document lists such a
requirement under Requirements held elsewhere and out of its gaps.

Consequences: The schema gains audience on 36 element definitions and ownedBy and
fulfilledBy on a requirement, with fulfilledBy requiring ownedBy;
the fragment schemas and the Swift build's embedded schemas follow.
The rule enum gains audience. The origin table of
docs/conventions.md gains audience and fulfilledBy, and ownedBy
names both its uses. An element of another specification is not
checked for its audience; that waits on the caller context
(docs/caller-context.md), which designs who may see what across
specifications.

**Insight:** One key with one value, because left out already says everyone: a second value would be a second way to say it. The four places the check reads are the names that make one element part of another's definition, so the external document could not show the element for everyone without the internal one; a satisfies or verifies entry only traces, and the external document drops the entry with the requirement, so an element for everyone may still satisfy an internal proposal. The compiler test holds: an element that breaks the rule is read and marked at the name, never left unread, and a document for everyone leaves out only what the specification says is internal, counting it, so the reader knows the document is not the whole. --out is required with --audience external because both documents are kept, and the folder the implementation files name is the full one's; writing the external one there would make --check of the full one fail. The problems target is refused because the problems file marks the YAML files themselves, which are the team's. ownedBy rather than a status value, as decision 7 says: status keeps the life cycle of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (proposed, accepted, rejected, retired), and who fulfils a requirement is another fact. acceptance_missing stays, since the other component's promise is still accepted by its criteria. fulfilledBy is a reference so the umbrella checks it when the other specification is given, and gaps counts it while it is not. Acceptance test: the first document a customer reads is written from the same specification as the team's, with the internal part left out and counted, and a change a customer asks for in a promise another component keeps names the stakeholder who keeps it.

### ADR-120: Material questions form a group of their own in gaps and the questions document, a decision names under opens the questions it raised, and the outputs table counts the questions per stage

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 9 of docs/estate.md, build item 11. An estate's specification
read from its sources holds many open questions, and three things
made the list hard to act on. A question of kind material asks a
stakeholder to send a document, a file or a record, yet gaps and
the questions document put it among the decisions, under "Decided
by", and nothing said how many decisions each stakeholder must
take. A decision that answered a question only in part wrote the
open half in prose or as a new question with nothing tying the two,
so a reader of the new question could not see where it came from.
And the outputs table named every question that holds an output
up in one cell, which a specification with dozens of questions
makes unreadable. The fourth part of the build item, the warning
for a citation whose clause falls under none of its source's listed
clauses, shipped in 0.6.2 as source_clause (both builds, the case
validate-source-clause), so it is not added again under another
name.

Decision: gaps and the questions document list the decision questions by
stage as before and the questions of kind material after them, in
a section of their own, Material to provide, in the same order,
each with Needed from in place of Decided by. The summary gains one
sentence: the decisions each stakeholder must take and the material
each must provide, a material question counted only as the second.
A decision may name under opens, a SpecArch keyword, the questions
it raised, by ID. The validator, in both builds, reports
question_opened, an error at the entry, for a question that is
neither open in the specification nor named under answers by any
decision, with the nearest open question suggested, and for one the
decision answers itself. It checks every decision, whatever its
status. A question a decision opened shows Opened by: the decision
with its title and the questions it answered, then for each of
those that a decision opened in turn, that decision, back along the
chain.
The outputs table gives the questions that hold each output up per
stage, in the order of the stages: how many, and the first three by
priority then ID, the rest counted as "and N more".

Consequences: The schema gains opens on a decision; the fragment schemas and the
Swift build's embedded schemas follow, and the rule enum gains
question_opened. Every gaps output and questions document changes
in its outputs table and gains the summary sentence; one with a
material question gains the section. The Open question paragraph
that other documents write at an element, and the html site's mark,
still say Decided by for a material question, and the draft notice
of each document still names every question; both are left as they
are, since point 9 asks for the change in gaps and the questions
document only.

**Insight:** A material question is answered by sending something, not by choosing, and the person who sends it is often not the one who decides; listed among the decisions it asks the wrong thing, and counted with them it overstates what a stakeholder must decide. Its blocks line stays, since what it holds up is what makes it urgent. Leaving it out of the stage sections keeps each question in the document once. opens is the inverse of answers, so the convention of answering in part is kept and made visible without a new meaning: the open half is a question like any other. An opened question that is answered later leaves the specification, so the check accepts an ID a decision answers, as answers itself does, rather than refusing the record of an older decision. A decision that answers and opens the same question says two contrary things at one ID, which is the ambiguity the principles make an error. Every status is checked because a stale ID is stale in a proposal too. Three identifiers per stage keep a cell one line wide; the stage section above lists every question, so nothing is lost, and the first by priority are the ones a reader acts on first. The stage comes first because a stage's questions go to the people who own that stage. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused that was read before, and a wrong opens entry is read and marked at the entry. The acceptance test holds: a change request arriving as a document is a material question its sender sees in a group addressed to them, and a reviewer's partial answer keeps its open half traced.

### ADR-121: A field may say generatedDefault, an entity's mapping lists its table's plain indexes, the database reader writes them into an implementation fragment, and a list served two ways is two operations named after one handler

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 10 of docs/estate.md, build item 12. Three things a database
or a router of an estate says, and the specification could not, were
a could question at every table or route read from the sources. A
column default the database computes, gen_random_uuid() or
CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, is no value, so default could not hold it. A plain
index had no word, and docs/sync-gates.md already put it in the
implementation file as physical design. And the standard list
contract of the estate serves each list by GET on its path and by
POST on that path with a literal segment added, so one handler
served two routes and the router reader named both by method and
path with a could question each. The owner decided (decision 6 of
docs/estate.md) that a reader may write an implementation fragment.

Decision: A field gains generatedDefault, a SpecArch keyword with a closed set
every stack shares: identifier, a new random UUID, on a field of
format uuid, and currentTime, the instant the record is written, on
a field of format date-time. The schema refuses it beside default and
on a field of another format, so both builds refuse it alike. The
type-rendering idiom, version 1.3.0, names each dialect's expression
in its defaults part, which held an unused now and holds currentTime
in its place: gen_random_uuid() and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on PostgreSQL,
NEWID() and SYSDATETIMEOFFSET() on SQL Server, (UUID()) and
CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on MariaDB, SYSTIMESTAMP on Oracle, which has no
identifier. generate sql writes the expression as the column's
default and refuses a dialect that names none at the field; the
snapshot keeps it, and a change of it is refused as a change of
default is. extract database writes generatedDefault where the
catalogue's default is the expression the idiom names for PostgreSQL
on a field of the format it fits; any other expression stays a could
question, which now names the expressions the idiom names.

An entity's mapping in an implementation file lists under indexes
the plain indexes of its table, each its fields in order and, when
the database names it otherwise, its name; the derived name is
ix_<table>_<columns>. The validator refuses, as field in both builds,
a field the entity lacks and indexes under a mapping that is not an
entity's. generate sql writes each as CREATE INDEX after its table,
keeps them in the snapshot only when there are any, and a next
migration drops an index removed or changed and creates one added,
both in the expand file. extract database, given
--implementation-out and a new file's name, writes there an
implementation fragment: a file holding only mappings, every table's
as its target and its plain btree indexes, each citing the
catalogue. Without the option, a plain index is a could question
that names it; an index of an expression, with a condition, an order
or another method, and a unique index without a constraint, stay
could questions.

extract router reads a handler that serves exactly a GET on a path
and a POST on that path with one literal segment added as one list
served two ways: the GET is named after the handler, the POST after
it with Post added, each cites both routes, one must question asks
what the two do, and no could question asks about their names. The
http binding of an implementation file may say under listRoutes,
with postSegment, that every list is served so; generate openapi
then writes the POST twin of each list operation served by GET,
named after it with Post added, its list's parameters in a JSON body
and the same paged answer, and refuses a twin the specification also
declares. The dxlib dialect, which serves every operation as one
POST, refuses listRoutes.

Consequences: The design schema gains generatedDefault, the implementation schema
indexes on a mapping and listRoutes on a binding; the fragment
schemas and the Swift build's embedded schemas and idioms follow.
type-rendering moves to 1.3.0, so every generated migration header
and snapshot names it, and the library lending example's snapshot
is written again with no new migration. extract database gains
--implementation-out. The go, swift, javascript and dart readers
still name a handler that serves two routes by method and path with
a could question; they take the twin when a project that needs it
comes. The database gate, still to be built, compares a generated
default and a plain index exactly.

**Insight:** A generated default is the database's and the stacks share the two that matter, so a closed set names them once and the idiom, which already holds each dialect's literals, says how each writes them; an open expression would be stack-specific text in the design, and the list stays closed as estate.md asks. Oracle's SYS_GUID gives 16 raw bytes that are no version 4 UUID and do not fit the VARCHAR2(36 CHAR) a uuid is on Oracle, so the idiom leaves it out and the generator says so at the field, which is the compiler test: read, never dropped, marked where it is. now was in the defaults part and read by nothing; one word for one meaning keeps currentTime only. Changing a part moves the idiom's version, so every snapshot and every migration header written from now names 1.3.0. An index is physical design, as docs/sync-gates.md says and SQL's own standard agrees by leaving indexes out of ISO SQL, so it goes in the implementation file and not the design; its fields are the design's names, so a rename is caught by the validator. Its name is kept only when it differs from the derived one, so the database gate can compare names exactly. Creating and dropping an index loses no data, so neither needs destructive: true. The fragment holds only mappings because a catalogue does not say the stack's language, which a whole implementation file requires, and writing a guess would invent what the source does not say. It is written to a new file only, so a fragment edited by hand is never written over. The twin keeps HTTP's own model, two operations, and only takes the noise away; the names follow the single-route rule for the GET, so a design that names its list after its handler meets the reader's tree, and the POST's name is what generate openapi derives, so the two meet in merge. The convention is HTTP's, so it is the implementation file's binding, not the design's. The compiler test holds: nothing read before is refused, and what the meta-model still cannot hold is a could question at its entry. The acceptance test holds: an index or a generated key asked for at a review is one line in the implementation file or one keyword on a field, and the questions an owner reads from an estate are fewer and each one real.

### ADR-122: Every tree a command writes passes validate; merge keeps a type where the trees give a field different types and blocks the permissions a role's disputed grants leave ungranted, and derive names a draft from its subject made a valid name

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: ADR-045 leaves out a key the trees give different values and asks
a must question that blocks the key. The validator covers a
required key missing at a pointer a must question blocks, so a
merged tree with such a key left out passes validate, except in
two cases. A field with neither `$ref` nor `type` fails the design
schema's one-of between the two forms of a field, and the error
names `$ref`, which the question on `type` does not block; so two
databases that give one column as `boolean` and as
`[boolean, "null"]`, one a replica of the other, merged into a
field with a default and no type, and validate, gaps and document
refused the merged tree. A role's grants left out as a disputed
list can leave a permission no role grants, which the validator
reports at the permission, where no question blocks it. derive
named a requirement's acceptance drafts from the requirement's ID
as written, lower-cased, and an ID may hold a dot or an
underscore, so a requirement `AB-1.2` gave the folder
`tests/ab-1.2-acceptance-1`, which validate refuses as a test name
that is not kebab-case.

Decision: A field's `type` the trees give differently is kept with one value
rather than left out, under the same must question. Where the
types differ only in whether null is allowed, the union is kept,
the types every tree lists and `"null"`. Otherwise the first
tree's type is kept, and each key of another tree that goes with
its type (a format, a width or a bound, a pattern, the values, a
default or an example, the items, the properties) that the first
tree does not give is left out with that type, and a tree that
gives the kept type keeps its keys. The question's why says what the sources say,
what the merge keeps and why, and names each key left out with a
type; the merge's output names the type kept at the question.
The must question on a role's `permissions` left out blocks, as
well as the list, each permission the lists name that no merged
role grants, itself or through a permission it implies, among the
permissions the merged specification declares, and its why says
so.
Every tree merge writes passes validate with no error: where
leaving a key out would leave an entry the schema cannot read, one
valid form is kept and the question says which; where a key left
out leaves an error elsewhere, the question blocks that place too.
derive makes each subject's name a valid test name before it names
a draft from it: small letters and digits, every run of other
characters one hyphen, none at either end, and the subject key in
front of a name that starts with no letter; the draft keeps the
subject's own name in its keys and `verifies`. Where two subjects
of one key have different names that give the same valid name,
each after the first in document order takes a suffix, `-2`, `-3`,
and derive asks about it on standard error and in the draft's
`why`. The validator suggests the same names, in both builds.
One rule holds for every command that writes a tree, the readers
of extract, merge, derive, and approve: what it writes passes
validate with no error, the problems it found asked as questions
at the nearest element rather than written as an entry validate
refuses. The conformance suite validates the tree of every case of
those commands that exits 0.

Consequences: A merged specification whose trees disagree on a field's type
validates on its own, and gaps and the documents read it with the
type kept until the question is answered. Where the first tree's
type is kept, a format or width only another tree gave is in the
question and not in the tree. Where the types differ only in
null, the tree says the column may be null until the owner says
which service is wrong. A permission a disputed grants list leaves
ungranted is blocked by the question on the list, and the
validator reports it once the list is answered and it is still
granted by nobody. A requirement whose ID holds a dot gets drafts
validate accepts, under a name that is not its ID. A case of
extract, merge, derive or approve whose tree does not validate
fails the suite.

**Insight:** A type kept rather than left out, because a field without one is not a field to the schema, the generators or a reader of the techspec, and SpecArch reads an incomplete definition rather than refusing it (docs/principles.md): the problem is marked at the entry, by the must question that blocks the type, and nothing is dropped. The union where only null differs, because a nullable column and a non-null one agree on the type and differ on one more value, and the union allows what either allows, so no tree is contradicted while the question is open. The first tree's type otherwise, because the order of the trees is the one input the reviewer chooses and can repeat (ADR-045), and the question says in words that it is not a choice between the sources; the keys that go with the other type leave with it, because a format of one type is refused on another, and leaving them out unsaid would hide what that tree says, so the question names them. A field's type alone and not every required key, because every other key left out is covered by the question that blocks it, and keeping a value the design does not need would choose between the sources where the merge has no reason to. The ungranted permissions blocked by the question on the grants, because the grant is what is missing and it is written in the role, not under the permission; the validator holds that a question on the permission itself is the one place that can say the grant is not known (BUG-011), and the merge is where the grant was left out, so it is the merge that says so. A union of the grants would widen a role while the question is open, which ADR-045 refuses for anything that concerns security. A name made valid rather than copied, because a folder name validate refuses makes the whole tree one validate refuses, and the ID is still cited in the draft's keys, so nothing of it is lost; a suffix and a question rather than an error where two names meet, because the subjects differ and both drafts can be written, and the reviewer decides whether the name suits. Every output of a tree-writing command validated in the suite, because the three cases were found by users, each after a release, each a different command writing a tree validate refused, and one check over every case catches the next before it ships. Acceptance test: two database trees that differ on a column's nullability merge into a tree validate accepts with no error, the column read with the union type and one must question on it; an owner reading the techspec sees the column with both citations and the question, and the change asked for is one line in the migration of the service that is wrong.

### ADR-123: specarch-gen-sqlc writes the sqlc queries the design derives, in PostgreSQL, one file per table, against the tables specarch-gen-sql writes, and leaves every other query to be written by hand beside them

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 11 of docs/estate.md, build item 13. A service on sqlc writes
its queries by hand in SQL files, and sqlc derives typed Go from
them; the query is the reviewed input, which is rule 5 of
docs/generators.md. Most of those queries are the same few shapes of
every entity: insert a record, read, replace or amend one by its
key, and a page of a list with its filters, search and sort. The
design already says each of them by keyword (a request body that
names an entity, a path parameter that is the key, listOf with its
whitelists), so they can be written from it, and every other query
stays the project's own. The plan was to check the generator
against a real project's first hand-written query file; none exists
yet, and the owner chose to build it now against a file written by
hand for the lending desk, with the check against a real project's
file still owed (docs/generators.md, Adding a target).

Decision: The target is sqlc, the plug-in specarch-gen-sqlc. It writes
PostgreSQL only: another dialect is an error at the target, naming
the engine sqlc would read it with. It reads the tables and columns
through specarch-gen-sql's own model (gensql.Schema), so a query
never names a column the migrations do not create, and writes one
file per table, named after the table, holding that table's
queries in the order of the paths, each named after its operation
in PascalCase, as sqlc names the Go method. It derives a query by
keyword only:
- a POST whose request body is an entity, on a path with no
  parameter: an insert of every column but the ones the database
  draws (generatedDefault) and the soft-delete flag, the audit
  columns among them, answering the record (:one, RETURNING);
- a GET that answers an entity, a PUT or a PATCH whose request body
  is one, on a path with one parameter, of an entity whose key is
  one field: a read or a change by the key, a softly deleted
  record left out. A change sets every column a caller may set,
  not the key, a readOnly field, a generated one or the creation's
  audit columns, and sets the change's audit columns; a PATCH keeps
  a column the request leaves out (coalesce of a nullable argument);
- an operation with listOf on an entity, on a path with no
  parameter: the page (:many) and its total (<Operation>Total,
  :one), under the same conditions. Each query parameter that names
  a field of the entity, by its name or its wire name, and each
  filterable field is an equality filter, optional unless the
  parameter is required; the searchable fields are matched
  case-insensitively by position() of the lowered text; the
  sortable fields are a pair of CASE terms each, ascending under the
  field's wire name and descending under it after a minus sign,
  then the key, so a page is stable; the page is LIMIT and OFFSET
  from the arguments page_size and page_offset.
A list of a view, a list under a path parameter, a list with a query
parameter that names no field held in one column, a list whose
filter, search or sort field is held in more than one column, and a
read or change of an entity whose key is not one field are warnings
at the operation, and their queries are left to be written by hand.
An entity another stakeholder owns gets no query. A DELETE and every
other operation derive nothing and are not reported: they are the
queries sqlc's rule leaves to the project. A file in the output
folder that the plug-in did not write is refused without --check
and compared with it, after the generators' rule for files built by
hand. tools/sqlc/compile-queries.sh runs sqlc vet, version 1.31.1 at
a pinned digest, on a folder of queries against a folder of
migrations in a disposable container.

Consequences: The implementation file's dialect setting describes the sqlc target;
the schemas and the Swift build's embedded schemas follow. The
library lending example names the sqlc target and checks in its
queries; CI compares them and compiles them under sqlc. The lending
desk's queries, written by hand under sources/code/queries with a
sqlc.yaml, are compared with generate --check, which differs only
where the members table has no phone number column while Q-6 is
open, and compile against the desk's migrations; the desk's route
and permission dumps and its code edition move to the commit that
added them. The byte comparison of a file written by hand is
exact, so a real project's file that lists the columns in another
order differs at that line; the real project's first file decides
whether --check needs a comparison that reads the queries, and the
check against it is still owed. MariaDB, a DELETE, a list under a
path parameter and a read by a key of several fields are not
written yet.

**Insight:** Keywords only, because the rules for a specification say one way to say one thing: a request body that names an entity says the record is written whole, a key of one field in the path says which record, and listOf says the whitelists. A GET answering an array with no listOf, or a POST whose body is a shape of its own, says no more than that the operation exists; guessing its query from the route would put a meaning in the specification nobody wrote, so those stay the project's, as sqlc's rule has it. The model of gensql, because two derivations of a table's columns would drift, and the queries must compile against what the migrations create. sqlc's own conventions decide the rest: the query names are the Go methods, a nullable argument (sqlc.narg) with a cast is how sqlc types an optional filter, and sqlc builds no SQL at run time, so an optional filter is "the argument is null or the column equals it" and a sort is a CASE term per direction, each of one column's type, since a single CASE over columns of different types does not type-check. Text is matched by position() rather than LIKE, so a percent sign or an underscore in what a user types is matched as itself, as the paginated-list idiom's free-text search means. The key after the sorts makes the order total, without which PostgreSQL may give one record on two pages. LIMIT and OFFSET follow the idiom's page from 1 and page size; the caller passes the offset, so the arithmetic is in one place. PostgreSQL only, because sqlc's engines are PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite; MariaDB would be the second, when a project needs it, and SQL Server and Oracle have no engine. A warning rather than an error for a list left to be written by hand, because listOf is expressible, the query is the project's to write, and the rest of the output is ready; the warning keeps it from being silent. sqlc vet rather than compile, because sqlc compile and generate with no gen block exit 0 with a column that does not exist; vet with no rules of its own type-checks every query as generate does. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused that was read before, and every query left to be written by hand is a warning at its operation. The acceptance test holds: a change request that changes a field changes the queries the next run writes, and generate --check against the queries written by hand names the first line that differs.

### ADR-124: specarch check compares a specification with the dumps of its code by the merge's matching, the database through the tables generate sql writes, fails on a difference an allowlist does not name, and lets the allowlist only shrink

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: Point 12 of docs/estate.md, build item 14. docs/sync-gates.md
designs three comparisons a CI job runs on every change: the spec
against the route table, against the database, and the generated
output against the generator. The third is generate --check. The
readers already read the route table, the permission table and the
catalogue, and merge already matches the elements of two trees,
but nothing exits 1 on a difference, and a service that predates
its specification cannot pass on the first day, so the gate needs
an allowlist of the known differences that may only shrink.

Decision: A verb, specarch check <specification> <dump>..., with --allowlist
<file> and --since <revision>. The specification must pass
validate. Each dump is told by the key that names its format
(routeTable, permissionTable, catalogue) and read with the reader
of specarch extract, after the same checks of the commit it names.
It is compared by the merge's matching:
- a route table, an operation by its method and path, and the
  permission each checks; the list twins bindings.http.listRoutes
  names are the specification's routes too, and an operation another
  stakeholder owns is not compared;
- a permission table, a grant by its role and permission, each
  side widened through the specification's implies, the names read
  as the permissions reader reads them; the gates are not compared;
- a catalogue dump, a table by its name and a column by its table
  and name, where the specification's side is the tables generate
  sql writes for PostgreSQL through the implementation file
  (gensql.Schema), not the database reader's entities.
Exact, and an error: an operation, route, grant, table or column
only one side has; a permission that differs; a column's type as
PostgreSQL's format_type spells it, its nullability and whether a
generated default draws it; the primary key; a foreign key, a
unique constraint by its columns, a check constraint by its name;
a plain index the mapping lists. A report, a warning: the text of
a check both name, and an index the mapping does not list.
Every problem is printed in validate's form at its entry, the
specification's or the dump's line, and its id is the rule and the
subject by the matching (POST /loans, members.phone_number,
desk-staff loans.read). The allowlist holds ids, one per line, and
# comments; an allowed difference is counted, not printed. A line
that names no failing difference of a format the run compares, or
repeats one, or names no rule, is allowlist_stale, and a line about
a format the run does not compare is skipped; with --since, a line the allowlist at that
revision did not hold is allowlist_added, and an allowlist the
revision does not hold is the gate turned on. Status 1 on any
error, 2 on what could not be read, 0 otherwise.

Consequences: docs/sync-gates.md names the verb for gates 1 and 2 and for the
grants. The lending desk's CI runs specarch check on its route
table, permission table and catalogue with an allowlist of what it
knows, fifteen lines, each with why it stays open: the renewal Q-4
leaves unbuilt, the phone number of Q-6, the open member route of
Q-7, the loan period's check of Q-1, the books table of Q-8, the
write-off routes and the supervisor's grants the specification does
not hold yet, the roles tables, the CHAR card numbers and the
address check's two names. MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle catalogues,
a view, an enum type, a unique constraint with a condition and a
column default other than a generated one are not compared yet.

**Insight:** The database is compared against gensql.Schema, because the database reader names an entity after its table (Members) and a field after its column, where the specification has Member and a value object held in three columns, and because it reads a CHAR column as a string of that width, which hides the very difference the gate is for. docs/sync-gates.md asks for names derived by the rules the migration emitter uses, so the two sides meet without a mapping table; the emitter's own model is those rules, and its tables are the ones the specification's migrations would create. The readers stay the way a dump is read, so a stale dump or one of an unknown commit is refused exactly as extract refuses it. Types are compared as PostgreSQL's format_type spells them, since the catalogue prints that spelling and the idiom writes the short one; only the spelling is normalised, never a width or a kind. The exact comparisons are the ones an extractor produces exactly, the reports the ones the database rewrites (a check's text) or no mapping holds, after the rule of docs/sync-gates.md that a gate that reports noise is switched off. A unique constraint is matched by its columns, since the database and the emitter name it each their own way, and a check by its name, which is all both keep. The id names the difference and not its place, as validate's ids do (ADR-065): an allowlist that broke when an entry moved to another file would be rewritten, not shrunk. A stale line fails, because a difference settled and still allowed would let the same difference come back unseen; --since makes a line added fail, the rule docs/sync-gates.md states, from what git holds, so no second file keeps the old list. A grant is widened by implies on both sides, because a table that grants the implied permission as well means what the specification means. The gates of a permission table are left out, since what a kind of caller may do is the caller context's (ADR-110). check is a verb on the readers and the generators' model, which are built in Go only; the Swift build exits 2 for it, as for extract. The compiler test holds: check reads what it is given and never refuses a specification for a difference, which is a problem at its entry, and a dump it cannot read is refused naming why. The acceptance test holds: a change request taken into the specification shows in the next run as a difference at the entry changed until the code follows.

### ADR-125: A map is JSON Schema's additionalProperties on an object, a field or a boolean, read from every reader's map shapes and written by every generator, with patternProperties and propertyNames left out

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: The field subset had no way to say a map. validate refused
additionalProperties as a key the object cannot have, extract
openapi left it out, and the Go reader wrote map[string]T as an
object with a should question naming the Go type, so a map of
integers and a map of any value came out alike, an OpenAPI document
read back lost its value types, and no generator could write the
types again. Extracting a service, writing its specification and
generating it again must give the same interface, so the shape is
needed before 0.7.0. A reported shape is a request property of
map[string]any bound from JSON.

Decision: additionalProperties joins the field subset with its JSON Schema
2020-12 and OpenAPI 3.1 meaning: on an object, the members the
object's properties do not name. Its value is a field, the type of
every such member's value; true, members of any value; or false,
none. Left out, the object says nothing of other members. An object
with additionalProperties and no properties is a map, whose keys
are data; with both, the named members are fixed and the rest follow
additionalProperties, and required names properties only. The
keyword goes on a field of type object, nullable or not, and the
schema refuses it elsewhere; any value is written true, and {} is
refused, as a field that has neither a type nor a reference.
patternProperties and propertyNames stay out of the subset. An
entity and a value object do not take it: their members are columns
and named parts, so a map is a field of one, stored as JSON. The
meta-model stays 0.2 (ADR-052).

The readers write a map wherever the code says one:
- Go: map[K]T is an object whose additionalProperties is T's schema,
  whatever K, since encoding/json writes every key as text; a map
  of an interface or any is true, with a should question blocking
  the values; a value type the meta-model has no type for leaves
  the map true, with the question at the values;
- dxlib: DataTypeMapStringString is a map of strings;
- OpenAPI: additionalProperties is kept, {} as true, values with no
  field the meta-model holds as true with a line, and a component
  schema that is a map, naming no properties, is written in place,
  not as an entity or a schema, and one that names properties stays
  one, its additionalProperties a line;
- Swift: [String: T] and a dictionary keyed by an integer, as
  JSONEncoder writes them as objects; another key and Any values
  print a line;
- Dart: Map keyed by String or int, dynamic or Object values or no
  type arguments true with a should question;
- JavaScript and TypeScript: zod's record() keyed by string(), and
  Record<string, T>, any or unknown values true with a should
  question;
- a database's json and jsonb columns stay an object with a should
  question, since such a column holds any JSON value, not only an
  object.

The generators write it as the design has it: the OpenAPI document
as additionalProperties, its keys never wire-named; the dxlib dialect
a map of plain text as map-string-string and any other as
json-passthrough; the go-dxlib handler a map of text through dxlib's
map getter into map[string]string and any other typed map decoded
from JSON into map[string]T, a pointer for a value that may be null;
the documents a map of T, with the limits of its values as each
value's. type-rendering moves to 1.4.0, its Go row naming the map.
merge treats it as any key, keeping the first tree's value type with
a must question where the types differ, and takes a typed map over
one a tree writes open and asks about (ADR-126). diff calls
allowing more members minor and allowing fewer, or changing the
values' type, major, with additionalProperties left out read as
true.

Consequences: A map of integers and a map of any value differ in every tree a
reader writes, the OpenAPI document generated from it and the one
read back, and the dxlib handler's request type. The extract cases
of Go, Swift, Dart and JavaScript write maps where they printed a
line or asked, and new cases cover validate, merge and diff. The
limits of a map's values derive no test cases and are not checked
by the dxlib handler, as a list's items' limits are not. A map keyed
by an enum (zod's record() keyed by an enum, a Swift dictionary
keyed by another type) still prints a line, since a key constraint
is not in the subset.

**Insight:** JSON Schema and OpenAPI 3.1 say a map this way, and every stack's own map type (Go's map[string]T, TypeScript's Record<string, T>, Swift's [String: T], Dart's Map<String, T>) is the same shape, so the standard keyword with its standard meaning is the one way to say it. JSON Schema reads {} and true alike; the subset keeps true only, after one way to say one thing, and {} is refused rather than read, since a field without a type or a reference is refused everywhere else. The keyword constrains an object only, so on any other type it would say nothing, which is ambiguity the validator reports. patternProperties and propertyNames are left out because a key pattern names no member a stack's type holds: a generator could only leave it unchecked, and no reader writes one. They can join when a real system asks, which is the roadmap's rule for the meta-model. An entity's and a value object's members are named because each is a column or a part; a map has no fixed columns, so it is a field kept as JSON. The Go key is left out of the schema because the wire is text whatever the key, and the design says what is on the wire; the Go type that holds a key is the implementation's. A JSON column is not a map because it may hold an array or a scalar as well. Absent additionalProperties is read as true in diff because that is its meaning in JSON Schema, so a change from absent to true is no change to a client. The compiler test holds: a map the meta-model cannot hold whole is still written, open with true, and the question or the line says what is missing at the entry; {} and the keyword on a string are errors at their entry, the rest of the file read. The acceptance test holds: a map's value type is one field to change, and diff says whether the change breaks a client.

### ADR-126: merge takes a typed map over one another tree writes open and asks about, with no dispute, and closes that tree's question

Status: accepted, 2026-10-14.

Context: A reader that meets a map whose values the code does not type, such
as Go's map[string]any or TypeScript's Record<string, unknown>,
writes it open, additionalProperties: true, with a should question
on what the values are (ADR-125). Another tree read from the same
system, a database's or an OpenAPI document's, may give the values'
type. merge compared the two as any key: true against a field is a
disagreement, so the key was left out with a must question, and the
reader's should question was carried as well. The merged map lost
the type one tree did know, and the owner was asked twice about one
thing a source already said.

Decision: Where one tree writes a map open, additionalProperties: true, with
a question of its own blocking that key, and another tree writes the
map with a value type, merge takes the value type and records no
disagreement, whichever tree is given first. The asking tree's
question is left out as answered, with the line merge prints for
every answered question, naming the trees that give the type. This
holds for every priority of the question; the readers ask a should
question. Where several trees write the map open, each must ask, or
the type is a disagreement as before.

Everything else stays a disagreement with a must question: two value
types that differ (the first tree's type kept so the field is read,
ADR-122), true written by a tree that asks nothing about the values,
and false against true or a type.

Consequences: Merging a code tree with an open map and a tree that types its
values writes the map with that type and asks nothing about it, in
either order; the cases merge-map-typed-then-open and
