merge-map-open-then-typed cover it, beside a pair of differing types
that is still a disagreement. merge-map-values keeps a map written
open with no question against a typed one as a disagreement. A type
taken this way cites both trees through the field's entity, as any
merged key does; it is not marked as filled from another tree, so a
wrong type is caught by review or by the user acceptance test, not by
a question.

**Insight:** A tree that writes true and asks what the values are is saying it does not know them; true is the place-holding value ADR-125 gives that case, so the map stays readable, not a claim that any value is allowed. A type from another tree fills that unknown the way an answer would, which is the rule merge already follows for a key one tree does not give and another does (ADR-049): the open map is the same gap, held by a value instead of left out. Asking a must question there would ask the owner to choose between knowing and not knowing. A tree that writes true and asks nothing is different: an OpenAPI document's additionalProperties: true, or {}, says on purpose that the values may be anything, and that competes with a type as much as another type does. JSON Schema reads true as allowing every value, and only the question marks the true as a reader's stand-in, so the question is what tells the two apart. false allows no member, so it is a claim as well. Two types are two claims, and the order the trees are given must not choose between them beyond keeping the field readable. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or left unread; the open map's question is closed only because the merged map holds the answer, and the line says which tree gave it, so a reader of the output sees where the type came from. The acceptance test holds: the merged map has its value type at once, and a type that turns out wrong is one field to change, with diff saying whether the change breaks a client.

### ADR-127: merge adds up a role's grants from trees that declare different permissions, and disputes only a grant a tree declares and withholds

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: A system of several services keeps one permission table per
service, each read into a tree of its own, and one role is in
several of them: a clerk the stock service's table grants
stock.read and the invoice service's grants invoices.read. merge
compared the lists as any key: two lists that differ were a
disagreement, so the role's permissions were left out with a must
question asking which list is right, and the question blocked
every permission the lists name that no other role grants. The
merged specification lost every grant of such a role, though each
tree still held them, and the owner was asked to choose between
two lists that were both right.

Decision: A role's grants are joined grant by grant once every tree is in,
on the permissions the trees declare. A tree's list says nothing
of a permission the tree does not declare in its permissions
section, so the merged list is the first tree's, then what each
later tree adds, with every tree's citation; a line names the
trees whose grants add up. A permission one tree grants that
another tree, which has the role, declares and does not grant is a
disagreement as before: the list is left out, and the must
question names each such permission with the trees that grant it
and the trees that withhold it, beside the list each tree gives.
A role a printed and a parsed tree both give is compared grant by
grant as before: the printed trees' grants are what the check
reads, and a grant only a seed makes is a must question.

Consequences: Merging the permission tables of several services writes each
shared role with the grants of every table and asks nothing on
the grants; merge-role-grants-add-up covers it.
merge-role-grants-withheld covers the disagreement kept: a
permission both tables declare that one grants the role and the
other withholds. A role's grants are no longer compared while the
trees are read in, since whether a grant is disputed depends on
what every tree that has the role declares; they are joined after
the last tree, before the disputed keys are left out, so the
order the trees are given no longer decides whether a list is a
dispute. merge-role-names-disagree, whose two tables declare
different permissions, now joins the role's grants and asks only
how the roles go on the wire. The lending desk's roles, printed
and parsed, are unchanged.

**Insight:** A permission table claims what it declares. A role that holds stock.read in the stock service's table and invoices.read in the invoice service's holds both, since each check reads only its own table, so the two lists are two parts of one claim, not two claims about one key. Asking which is right asks the owner to choose between two true things, and the question blocked every grant of the role until it was answered. SA-45 turns every disagreement between the trees into a must question; two lists that add up are no disagreement, because neither tree says the other's grant is not made. A tree that declares a permission and does not grant it to a role it has is saying something: its table has the place the grant would be in, and the grant is not there. Against another tree that grants it, that is a disagreement, and the rule keeps it one. It is the case of a document against the code: a manual that lists a role's permissions and leaves one out, against a table that grants it, is a difference the owner decides (docs/from-sources.md, Never choose between a document and the code). A rule that joined the lists whenever the trees come from different sources would lose that case, and a rule that joined them only for sources of one kind would need the trees to say what kind they are, while whether a tree declares the permission is in the tree. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or left unread; the merged role holds every grant with the citation of the tree that makes it, and the line says whose grants were added, so a reader of the output sees where each came from. A grant one tree withholds still surfaces, in the problems file and at the entry, as the question that names it. The acceptance test holds: the merged role grants at once what it grants in every service, so the user acceptance test shows the whole role, and a grant that turns out wrong is one item of one list to change, with diff saying what it breaks.

### ADR-128: extract database reads a partition as the table it is a partition of, and check compares that table alone

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: The catalogue query listed a partition among the tables with nothing
to tell it from a table: a partition is a pg_class row of relkind r
or p like any table, and the query read only the relkind. The reader
made an entity of every table, so a partitioned table with three
partitions gave four entities with the same columns, three of them
named after the partitions, each with the primary key and the
indexes the partition takes from its table under the names
PostgreSQL gives them. Every generated default and every index of
the table was a could question once per partition, and check would
have reported each partition as a table the specification does not
hold (BUG-023).

Decision: The catalogue query prints for each table partitionBy, the partition
key of a partitioned table as pg_get_partkeydef prints it,
partitionOf, the schema and name of the table a partition is a
partition of, and partitionBound, its bound as pg_get_expr prints
it; and for each constraint and each index whether it is inherited,
taken by a partition from its table (coninhcount or conparentid for
a constraint, a pg_inherits row for an index).

extract database reads a partition as the table it is a partition
of, following partitionOf to the table that is no partition, so a
partition of a partition is read as that table too. No entity is
made for a partition. The table's entity cites its partitions in
what the catalogue says of the table, and one could question at the
entity lists every partition with its bound, the partition it is a
partition of when that is not the table, and its own partition key
when it is partitioned itself, saying that partitioning is physical
design the meta-model cannot hold and that each partition is read as
the table. What a partition takes from its table, its inherited
constraints and indexes, is read once, at the table. What a partition
has of its own is a could question at the entity citing the
partition's entry, read as the table's: a constraint not inherited,
an index not inherited that backs no constraint, and a column whose
type, nullability, default, identity or generated expression differs
from the table's. A foreign key that references a partition is read
as a relation to that partition's table, with a could question
saying so. A partition whose table the dump does not list is read as
a table of its own, with a could question saying so, and its own
partitions are read as it. A table that inherits from another
through INHERITS is no partition and stays a table of its own. The
counted line says how many of the tables are partitions when any
is, and the wrote line then says one entity per table that is not a
partition.

An index of a partitioned table, which pg_get_indexdef prints with
ON ONLY, is a plain index as any other: the reader and check read
ON ONLY as ON.

check compares the specification's tables with the tables of the
catalogue that are not partitions. A partition is never compared,
neither as a table the specification does not hold nor by its own
constraints and indexes.

A dump made by the earlier catalogue query has none of the keys and
reads as before, every table an entity.

Consequences: The catalogue query prints three more keys per table and inherited
per constraint and index; a project whose database has partitions
makes its dump again to be read this way. The cases
extract-database-partitioned-table and check-skips-a-partition cover
a table partitioned by range with a default partition, a partition
partitioned again by list, a partition's own default, check and
index, and a check and an index on the partitioned table that every
partition carries as inherited. The counted and wrote
lines change only when a partition is in the dump. The mapping may
gain partitioning later, when a project needs generate sql to write
it; the could question goes then.

**Insight:** ISO SQL has no partitioning. It is each database's way of storing a table's rows, physical design like an index (ADR-121), and PostgreSQL says so itself: a query on a partitioned table reaches the rows of every partition, and a partition exists to hold some of the table's rows. The meta-model says what a record is and how it is kept, not where; an entity for a partition would be a second entity for the same records, and every question of the table asked once more for each partition. The table is what the migrations mean, so the partition is read as it. Partitioning is a could question and not a line in the implementation fragment because the mapping has no key for it. Writing one would take generate sql writing PARTITION BY and each partition's bound, the next migration attaching and detaching partitions, and the database gate comparing them: a design of its own, taken when a project needs the generated SQL to partition, as ADR-121 left the twin to the other readers. Until then the question keeps the partitions read and marked at the entity, which is the compiler test, and the answer to it is where the keyword's design starts. A partition's own constraint, index or column setting is a question and not an error, and not read as the table's, because the meta-model says a constraint for every record of the entity and the source says it for the rows of one partition. Reading it as the table's would claim more than the source says; leaving it out silently would lose it; so it is left out with a question citing the partition, where the reviewer sees what the source has. An inherited constraint or index is told from the partition's own by the catalogue, not by its name: PostgreSQL names an inherited index after the partition and the columns, and a user may name an index of their own the same way. A relation points at an entity, and a partition has none; its rows are the table's, so the relation to the table is what the source says, less narrowly, and the question says so rather than leaving the key out as a reference to a table that was never read. pg_get_indexdef prints ON ONLY for a partitioned table's index to say that the statement makes the index on the table alone, each partition having its own attached to it. The index is the table's, the mapping lists the table's indexes, and the partitions' copies are inherited, so ONLY is part of the dialect's spelling and not a difference. check skips a partition because generate sql writes one table per entity and the specification has no place for a partition until partitioning is a keyword; reporting each as not specified would be a difference the owner cannot settle in the specification. The table's columns and keys are compared through the table, and PostgreSQL holds a partition to its table's columns and gives it the table's constraints and indexes, so the comparison of the table covers them. A partition's own index or constraint is not compared, since the specification cannot hold it; extract's question is where it surfaces. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or left unread, a dump of the earlier query reads as before, and every problem is a question at the entity, in the problems file and at the entry. The acceptance test holds: the tree shows one entity for the table at once, and a constraint a reviewer wants for every row is one constraint to add to the entity.

### ADR-129: An environment says who runs it, and one the customer runs is handed over as source, with a handover section and a handover document

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: The deployment stage said what each environment is for and which
one a release goes to next, and the implementation file said where
each is installed and with which setting values. Every environment
was read as one the team that builds the system installs and runs.
A customer that takes the source into a repository of its own,
builds it and runs production itself, as regulated customers such
as banks do, had no place: the deployment guide described hosts
the vendor does not have, and nothing said what the customer
receives to build and run the system, nor what stays whose
responsibility. How a release is built (the pinned toolchain, the
base images, a reproducible build and its software bill of
materials), how a build is put on a host, and what the hosts must
provide had no keys either, so the deployment guide could not say
them for the vendor's own environments.

Decision: An environment carries runBy, a SpecArch keyword with two values:
vendor, the team that builds the system installs and runs it;
customer, the party that takes the system builds, installs and
runs it on hosts of its own, from the handover. An environment
without runBy is run by the vendor, which is the one meaning every
environment had.

A specification with an environment the customer runs holds
handover, one object of the deployment stage, kept in
deployment/handover.yaml: description, the handover in plain
words; to, the stakeholder who receives it, by key; source, how
the source of a release reaches them; and responsibilities, two
lists of sentences, customer and vendor, saying what stays whose.
It holds nothing another section already says: the settings and
their secrets, the migrations, the release and rollback steps, the
checks and the sign-off, the monitors, the libraries with their
licences and the build are read from where they are.

backup and restore are two more procedures, one object each of the
operation stage (operation/backup.yaml, operation/restore.yaml),
with the steps of release and rollback: how the data of the live
system is saved, and how saved data is put back.

An implementation file's deployment gains three keys. build says
how the artifact of a release is made from the source: description;
task, the task of the file that builds it, by key; baseImages, each
image the build starts from, by name and digest, with its purpose;
reproducible, how a build of the same source on another machine is
compared with the vendor's; and sbom, the task that writes the
software bill of materials of the build and scans it, by key. method
says how the build is put on the hosts: tool, files (what the tool
reads, relative to the implementation file) and description.
infrastructure says what the hosts must provide: cpu, memory,
storage, network, ports and services, one sentence each.

The validator, in both builds, reports under the rule handover: an
environment the customer runs while the specification has no
handover, no release or no rollback (errors at runBy); a handover
while no environment is run by the customer (an error at handover);
and, as warnings at runBy, an environment the customer runs with no
commissioning check in it, no monitor in it, or no backup and
restore. A handover whose to names no stakeholder is the error
stakeholder. An open must question that blocks the stage or the
section holds the error or warning about that section. In an
implementation file, a deployment that installs an environment the
customer runs without build, method or infrastructure is an error
at the deployment (handover), and a build whose task or sbom names
no task of the file is the error build_task.

specarch document handover writes handover.md for the customer's
engineers, who know nothing of SpecArch: what they receive, the
responsibilities, how each implementation builds a release and the
licences of its dependencies, what the hosts must provide, every
setting, the migrations in order, how a release is installed and
rolled back, backup and restore, what is watched, the checks to run
after installing, the acceptance tests and the sign-off sheet. A
specification whose implementation files name an output folder for
it but that has no handover is passed over with a warning of rule
handover, as ADR-073 passes over one that names no folder.
--audience external applies to it as to every other document. The
deployment guide and the technical specification show who runs each
environment once any environment says so, each installation's
build, method and infrastructure, backup and restore after
rollback, and the handover; a specification without the new keys
gets the same documents as before.

Consequences: The design and implementation schemas change, and with them the
fragment schemas and the Swift embed; every map of sections in both
builds lists handover, backup and restore. The library-lending
example's production is run by the library's IT staff, with a
handover, backup and restore procedures, and the Go
implementation's build, method and infrastructure; its documents
are regenerated, and CI checks its handover.md. The open questions
document and gaps list the handover document among the outputs only
for a specification that has a handover. A base image cannot be
named without its digest.

**Insight:** ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 names the two parties acquirer and supplier (6.1.1 and 6.1.2), and its transition process (6.4.10) installs the system in its operational environment without saying who does it. SpecArch writes customer and vendor because those are the words the people who read the documents use. The keyword is on the environment because that is where the question arises: a staging the vendor runs and a production the customer runs differ in nothing but who runs them, and one customer may run a staging of its own as well. The handover is a section of its own, and small, because almost all of what the customer receives is what the specification already holds for the vendor's own deployments; a second copy would drift, and one way to say one thing is the Low IQ Tax. What has no home is who receives it, how the source reaches them and what stays whose responsibility, so those are its keys. The receiver is a stakeholder because a handover goes to a role, never to a person, and the validator then checks the name as it checks every other. Backup and restore are procedures of the operation stage because they run on the live system through its life, like a monitor, not once at a release; they serve the vendor's own production as much as the customer's, which is why they are not keys of the handover. How a release is built and what the hosts must provide depend on the stack, so they are implementation: a Go service and a Java one of the same design need different memory and start from different base images. A base image is pinned by its digest because a tag moves, and a customer comparing a build with the vendor's needs the same input. The build names a task rather than carrying a command because the tasks are where the file keeps its commands. A missing handover, release or rollback is an error because the customer builds and installs the system from them, and a specification that marks an environment customer-run without them promises a handover it cannot make. The checks, the monitors, and backup with restore are warnings, as the traceability gaps are: a specification is written in order, and they are its to-do list for that environment. A must question that blocks the section is the one licence for the gap, as everywhere else. The handover document is a document like any other, so that --audience external stays the one way to leave internal elements out and the folder the implementation file names holds the document with every element, as ADR-119 decided. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or left unread, every gap is a problem at the environment's runBy or at the deployment, and a specification without the keys reads and renders as before. The acceptance test holds: the customer's engineers see the handover document early, and a remark on it changes one key of the handover, one step of a procedure or one line of a deployment.

**Note:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4.10: The transition process establishes the capability to provide the service in its operational environment. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

### ADR-130: The Go reader reads what an endpoint declares where it is registered, and an operation whose body or success is not written is a warning

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: A service on dxlib registers each endpoint with one call that is
given, besides its method and URI, the list of parameters it takes
(names, types, whether each must be sent, bounds and enums, nested
children), the content type its body arrives in and the responses
it may answer. dxlib reads and checks those parameters before the
handler runs, and the handler then reads them through dxlib, or
reads its body in a way of its own. extract go read only the names
in a literal list, to check the handler's reads against them, and
wrote each operation with no parameters, no body and no responses
but the refusals its handler answers. The document dxlib emits has
them, but only when the service's own dumper is run, and a service
that registers through the call with no parameters declared emits
an object that names nothing. Either way an operation could end up
with an empty body or no success response, and nothing in the
questions or the validator said so.

Decision: extract go reads the parameter list, the content type and the
response possibilities the registration call is given. Each is
followed when it is a literal, a pointer to one, a name assigned one
literal once, or a call to a function of the module whose one
statement returns one; anything else is a must question naming the
call and why it was not followed. A parameter is recognised by its
keys, a composite literal with NameId and Type, and a response by
StatusCode, whatever package declares their types, so a project's
own helpers are read as long as they return a literal. Each
parameter type is written in JSON Schema by dxlib's own table, as
dxlib's emitter writes it, with the declaration's description,
bounds, pattern, enum, const, default, annotations, children,
items and map values, and the result goes through extract
openapi's field writer: widths, wire names and every gap are
handled as they are for the emitted document, so merging the two
trees agrees. A parameter inside a list that is not read is written
by its name alone, with a must question on it, and the rest of the
list is written.

Where the parameters go follows dxlib's PreProcessRequest: a POST
or PUT with a JSON, form or multipart content type takes them as
its body's fields, one with an octet stream or plain text takes
that body, and with no content type it takes none; their
parameters, which dxlib reads from the X-Var header, print a line,
since the meta-model holds no parameter carried in a header as
JSON. A GET or DELETE takes them as query parameters, a name
that is also a path segment included, since dxlib reads them from
the query and not from the path. dxlib refuses every other method,
PATCH among them, with 422 before the handler runs, so such a
registration writes no parameter and asks a must question on the
operation: writing its parameters in the query would say dxlib
reads them where it reads nothing. A declared response is written
under its status with its description and the object its data
template gives, the problem the handler answers at that status
beside it; its headers print a line. A declared success leaves
only the descriptions not given to ask. A body that declares no
parameter is written as any object, with a must question on its
fields that names the registration and the handler.

The validator, in both builds, warns under request_body_open of a
request body that is an object naming no property and not saying
additionalProperties, and under success_response_missing of
responses that are refusals alone, with no 1xx, 2xx or 3xx response
and no default. A must question that blocks the operation, its body
or its responses holds the warning, as it holds every other.

Consequences: The dxlib endpoint cases of extract go now write request bodies,
query parameters and declared responses; their goldens change, and
a new case covers the declarations. The notice board's two readings
still merge with no key the trees disagree on, and the Go reading's
question on the widths of its int64 fields is the one the document
asks. A service that registers with no parameters declared gets a
question on each body it takes, and every operation with refusals
alone gets a warning until its success is written or asked.

**Insight:** The registration is where a dxlib service says what an endpoint takes; a handler that reads its parameters through dxlib names none of them by itself, so a reader that looks only at the handler sees an endpoint that takes nothing. The emitted document is the better source when it exists (ADR-076), and this reading is what the source gives when it does not, written the same way so that the two meet in the merge rather than disagree. Recognising a declaration by its keys and not by its type's name is what lets a service's own helpers, or a fork of the library, be read without a table of their names; the keys are the library's contract, the package path is not. Following only a literal, a name assigned once and a function that only returns is what syntax can do without running the code; anything longer is a guess, and a guess is never written. A declared GET parameter whose name is also a path segment is a query parameter because that is where dxlib reads it: writing it as the path parameter would write a request the service does not read. JSON Schema reads an object with no properties as any object, which is a valid schema, so the meta-model cannot refuse it; but written by a reader, or by hand, it most often means the fields were not found. additionalProperties: true is the one way to say any object on purpose, as the field subset already says it (ADR-049). An operation with refusals alone is valid OpenAPI too, and the same reasoning holds: a generator and a test need the success. Both are warnings, as the traceability gaps are, because a specification is written in order; the must question a reader asks is the one licence for the gap. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or left unread, a declaration not followed is a question at the operation, a parameter not read is kept by its name, and the empty body and the missing success are problems at the operation. The acceptance test holds: the operation's fields are there to show early, and a remark on one changes one field.

### ADR-131: The steps a request passes before an operation's handler are declared once as middlewares, and each operation lists the ones it runs

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: A web framework runs a chain of functions before an endpoint's
handler: a session check, a permission check, a tenant, a rate
limit, an audit line. They decide whether a caller must sign in and
what a refused request is answered, and many endpoints share one
chain. The specification had no place for them. extract go named an
endpoint's middlewares only in the citation of its registration and
in the question on an endpoint that checks no privilege, read a
setting that switches one off, and, for the routers, read a
permission from a check the implementation file names. The
technical specification and every other document said nothing of
them, so a reader of the specification could not tell which
operations need a session, and an owner could not review the chain.

Decision: The design gains middlewares, a section of named elements of the
design stage, keyed by kebab-case name: each declares what the step
checks or does (description) and the refusals it answers in place of
the handler (refusals), each a status from 400 to 599, the problem
type under errors that it names and the condition, with the usual
origin, cites, why and audience. An operation gains middlewares, the
names of the ones it runs in the order they run; an empty list says
it runs none. Which function of the code each middleware is belongs
to the implementation file, under bindings.http.middlewares, a map
from the middleware's name to its package and function.

The validator, in both builds, reports a name an operation lists
that is not declared (middleware), checks each refusal's problem as
a response's is (problem: declared, of its own status, and named
once the catalogue exists), and, once the specification declares its
middlewares, warns of an operation with no middlewares key
(middleware_missing). A must question that blocks the operation, or
its middlewares key, holds the warning.

extract go declares every middleware an endpoint's chain names, by
its function's name in kebab-case, with its doc comment as its
description and each refusal its body answers through its request,
as a handler's are read, and lists each operation's middlewares in
order. A chain is followed as the parameter list is (ADR-130), and
through a helper whose one statement returns its variadic
parameter. A chain lists a middleware as often as it runs, so one
that runs twice, before and after another, is named twice. What it
cannot read is a question: a chain not followed, or one with an
expression that names no function, on the operation's middlewares,
with no list written, since part of a chain is not the chain; a middleware outside the module or
one a call makes, on its description and refusals; a function with
no doc comment, on its description; a refusal not a literal; two
functions of one name. extract openapi reads x-dxlib-middlewares the
same way, by the last name of the function the runtime gives, none
when the key is absent, and asks what each middleware does, which
the source's tree answers in the merge; an operation without
x-dxlib-endpoint-type in a document whose dxlib operations run
middlewares says nothing of its own, so its middlewares are a must
question. The permission each reader
already reads from a check stays as it was.

The technical specification names each operation's middlewares in
its table of operations, once any operation names them, and in its
runtime view with their refusals, and lists every middleware under
the cross-cutting concepts with what it does, its refusals and the
operations that run it. The HTML page links each name to its
element.

Consequences: The design schema, its fragment schemas and the Swift embed gain
middlewares, and the implementation schema gains
bindings.http.middlewares; every list of sections in both builds and
the documents lists middlewares. The dxlib cases of extract go and
extract openapi write the chain, and new cases cover the reader, the
validator and the technical specification. The notice board's two
readings merge with the source's description answering the
document's question, and no key the trees disagree on. A generator
does not yet write the chain from the design; it reads the binding
when one does.

**Insight:** The owner asked for the chain to be visible in the specification, per operation and in order, with what each step checks and refuses, each declared once and referenced. The split between design and implementation is the owner's choice (2026-10-19): what a step checks and refuses is what a reviewer and a test need and is the same on every stack, while the function that does it, and how a framework chains it, is one stack's binding, as the permission checks are (ADR-081). x-middleware stays a stack-specific extension key: an extension that names a function is the binding, and the design's middlewares names none. The word middleware is kept because it is the one the people who write and read these systems use, in Go, Node and .NET alike, and the alternatives either name something else here (guard is the precondition of a data change) or a single kind of step (check, filter). A middleware is declared once because one chain serves many operations, and one way to say one thing is the Low IQ Tax; the order is the operation's, since one middleware may run before another on one operation and after it on another. The refusals are checked as responses are because a refusal is a response the handler does not write, and a client branches on its problem type the same way. The warning on an operation with no middlewares follows the rule of the problem catalogue: once a specification starts to say it, every operation says it, and [] is the way to say none, so that silence never stands for none. A specification that declares no middleware is read as before. A middleware is named by its function's last name because both the source and the runtime's name give it, so the two readings meet in the merge; a closure has no name of its own, so it is asked. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or left unread, a chain not followed is a question at the operation, a middleware not found is kept by its name with a question, and every gap is a problem at the element. The acceptance test holds: an owner sees each operation's chain early, in the technical specification, and a remark on it changes one list or one middleware.

### ADR-132: merge keeps a schema or a view named like an entity beside it and asks whether they are one element, and the validator holds the one-namespace error while that question is open

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: A service's OpenAPI document declares a component schema that no
operation creates and no path with a parameter answers, so extract
openapi writes it under schemas, a shape with no identity it saw
(ADR-060). The service's database holds a table of the same name,
which extract database writes under entities. Each tree passes
validate on its own. merge joined the trees section by section, so
the merged tree held /schemas/Note beside /entities/Note, and
validate refused it: a schema, an entity and a view are one
namespace, since each becomes a schema of its own in the interface
(value_object). merge asked no question and reported no
disagreement, so the one place that says what is wrong was the
error on a tree the readers wrote, which no one edits by hand, and
the extraction stopped there. The usual case is a document left
from a service template that documents a schema which happens to
share a name with one of the module's tables; whether the shape is
the record is exactly what the merge cannot tell.

Decision: A name one tree gives to a schema and another to an entity or a
view, or one to a view and another to an entity, is kept in both
entries, each as its trees give it, and merge asks one must
question per schema or view so named: whether the name is one
element or two, with an option that makes the schema or the view
the entity it is named like, where what refers to the one refers to
the other, and an option that gives it another name; the why names
the trees that give it each way, and the question cites both
entries and blocks the schema or the view, the entry the validator
reports. A schema named like a view is asked the same way, at the
schema. A line names the question. The validator, in both builds,
covers the value_object or view error that says the two are one
namespace when a must question blocks the schema or the view it is
reported at; this extends the list of ADR-017, and a should
question covers nothing, as before.

Consequences: merge-schema-named-as-entity covers the merge, and
validate-question-covers-namespace both builds of the validator. A
merged tree with such a name validates with the question counted
and no error; gaps lists the question with what it holds up, and
the OpenAPI generator, which writes both entries as components,
waits with every other generator on the open must question. A
specification with no such question is checked as before.

**Insight:** Neither entry is left out, because what refers to the schema, a list that carries it or a response, would then point at nothing, and the entity is the record the code side has: leaving either out drops a definition, which the compiler principle forbids. The schema is not joined into the entity, because the merge does not know that the shape is the record; the owner chose, in ADR-060, that merge never turns a schema into an entity, and a template's schema that happens to share a table's name is the common case. Neither is renamed, because a name the merge makes up is a placeholder, and the next merge of the same sources would make it again. So the merge asks, as it does for every disagreement (ADR-045): the two trees say two things of one name. The validator holds the error while the question is open, because the merged tree must pass validate for gaps and the documents to read it, and the question is the one place that can say the standing of the name is not known, as a question on a permission no role grants is (ADR-017). The collision is a wrong value only once the owner has said the two are two; until then it is a gap, what the name means. With no must question blocking the entry the error is reported as before, so a specification written by hand is held to the one namespace. The question blocks the schema or the view and not the entity, because the entity is what the operations list and the pages show, and a question on it would hold up every one of them while only the schema's or the view's standing is in doubt; and because the error is reported there, so the question sits where the reader of the problems file is sent. The compiler test holds: both definitions are read and written, the problem is in the problems file as the question and marked at the schema or the view, and no entry is refused. The acceptance test holds: the first merge of a document and a database with a shared name validates and the techspec shows both entries with the question beside them, and the owner's answer is one decision, after which the schema is removed or renamed, or made the entity, at the one entry the question names.

### ADR-133: A layout entry says which packages it depends on under dependsOn, CycloneDX's word, which extract go fills from the imports and the component diagram draws

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, gap A. An implementation file's layout lists the
packages of one implementation with the design objects each
implements, and nothing says which package calls which. A
component diagram drawn from it, C4's third level, has one box per
package and no arrow, so a reviewer of the architecture sees the
parts and not the structure, and an editor that draws the diagram
from the specification has nothing to draw the edges from.

Decision: A layout entry gains dependsOn, a list of keys of the same layout:
the packages this one calls, imports or links against. The
validator, in both builds, reports as the rule depends_on at the
entry a name that is no key of the layout and an entry that names
itself; a cycle is not reported. The rule is its own, not layout,
which already means the file tree: one rule name keeps one meaning. An entry without the key says nothing of
its dependencies, and the schema does not require it.

extract go --implementation fills it for each package from the
imports of its files that name another package of the same module,
by that package's layout key, and nothing outside the module. The
other readers fill it when their code-facts dumps carry imports.

The technical specification's chapter 5 draws, per implementation
file, the component diagram between the markers components
<stack>: a flowchart with a node per layout entry, labelled with its
key and the count of design objects it implements, an edge per
dependsOn, and the libraries drawn apart.

Consequences: The implementation schema gains dependsOn on a layout entry; the
rule depends_on is new in both builds, with a case; extract go's
implementation output gains the key with a case; document techspec
gains the components marker; SpecArch's own Go implementation file
is filled by its own reader. The origin table of docs/conventions.md
gains the row when the item is built.

**Insight:** The word is CycloneDX's, taken with its exact meaning: in a software bill of materials each component names under dependsOn the components it depends on, which is this edge. C4 writes the verb of a relationship in prose and the Structurizr DSL has no keyword for it, so there was no word to take there; imports is Go's and Python's word and not Java's or Swift's; uses is UML's usage dependency, close but not the same, and a borrowed word is never redefined. The key is in the implementation file because what a package depends on is one stack's structure, as the layout itself is; a design that said it would say something of a stack it does not know. A cycle is not an error because Go forbids one and Java, Swift and TypeScript allow one, and the file describes the code as it is. The reader fills it from the imports because an import is what the code says and nothing more, which is the readers' test. The compiler test holds: a name not in the layout is an error at the entry and the diagram still draws every other edge, and an implementation file without the key reads, validates and renders as before. The acceptance test holds: the arrows are the first thing a reviewer of an architecture asks for, they are shown the day the reader fills them, and a wrong arrow is one entry's list to change.

### ADR-134: A dependency says what it is with kind and how it is reached with protocol, after AsyncAPI, a channel names the dependencies that carry it under carriedBy, and the technical specification draws the context diagram from them

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, gap C. A dependency is declared once with a
description, a time limit, and the name and version of its
specification when it has one. A context diagram, C4's first
level, would draw every dependency as the same box, with no edge
that says what travels over it, and could not tell a database from
a payment gateway or say where a channel's messages go. The
convention kept the context picture hand-drawn for that reason.

Decision: A dependency gains kind, a SpecArch keyword with the values system,
database, messageBroker, fileStore and identityProvider, system
when left out; and protocol, AsyncAPI's word for the protocol of a
server, a lowercase string in the form of a URI scheme (https,
grpc, amqp, kafka, mqtt, postgresql, sftp, smtp), not an
enumeration. A channel gains carriedBy, SpecArch's own word: the
keys of the dependencies that carry the channel, the broker it
lives on or the system that receives its messages directly. Which
way a message goes is read from emits and from a job's consumes, as
today.

The validator, in both builds, reports as the rule channel at the
entry a carriedBy entry that is no declared dependency, or one whose
kind is database, fileStore or identityProvider; and as the rule
dependency a specification on a dependency whose kind is database,
messageBroker or fileStore. A specification stays allowed on a
system and on an identityProvider.

The technical specification's chapter 3 draws the context diagram
between the markers context: a person per role and one for anyone
when any operation or page is public, the system named by its
title, the dependencies grouped by kind with a shape per kind and
their protocol, an edge per dependency labelled with the operations
and jobs that call it, an edge to each dependency a channel is
carried by for every channel the system emits on and one the other
way for every channel a job consumes from it. A channel carried by
nothing is drawn at the system's boundary with no peer. The hand-drawn context picture of
the convention becomes a generated one.

Consequences: The design schema, the fragment schemas and the Swift embed gain
kind and protocol on a dependency and carriedBy on a channel; the
rule channel is new and dependency grows, in both builds, with
cases; document techspec gains the context marker; the
library-lending example's dependencies and channels are keyed and
its hand-drawn picture replaced; the convention's diagram table and
origin table change when the item is built. The caller-context's
clients join the diagram when they are built (ADR-135).

**Insight:** The rule for new keywords puts AsyncAPI before a word of SpecArch's own, and AsyncAPI has a server's protocol, taken with its meaning. AsyncAPI's channel servers was not taken, although it names the same place, for two reasons. An AsyncAPI server is a host with a protocol, and hosts are what a design file excludes: the design schema's stackSpecificKey sends servers, hosts, ports and deployments to the implementation file, where deployments[].servers already means hosts, so one word would mean hosts on one side of the boundary the conventions keep hard and dependencies on the other. And an AsyncAPI channel with no servers is available on every server, where a SpecArch channel carried by nothing is this system's own; the borrowed word would have been taken with another meaning, which the rule forbids. carriedBy is SpecArch's own, marked so in the schema and in the origin table when built, and the origin table's row for channels keeps saying no servers. AsyncAPI's action (send or receive) was not taken because emits and consumes say it already, and one way to say one thing is the Low IQ Tax. C4's technology lost to protocol: it is a free sentence ("JSON over HTTPS") nothing can check, and the link check of the deployment compares a word. protocol is a string and not an enumeration because AsyncAPI keeps it open and a new protocol should not wait for a release of SpecArch. kind is SpecArch's own because no standard enumerates what a system calls: C4 draws a database by a tag, ArchiMate by system software. The five values are the ones that change the picture or a check; a payment gateway and a tax authority are both systems, told apart by their descriptions, and a longer list of business kinds would age with every project. identityProvider is among them because the caller-context design names the token issuer at every hop, and the context diagram should show where the tokens come from. A specification is allowed on an identityProvider as on a system because an identity provider specified on its own is a system of the estate: the identity module of docs/caller-context.md is the token issuer, and every other module declares it with specification and version so that identity#/clients/bff and identity#/roles/invoice-manager resolve, which the reference rule needs; a database, a broker and a file store have no SpecArch specification, so a specification on one is the error. A dependency is a system someone else runs, so this system's own database and broker are not dependencies; they are servers of its deployment (ADR-136), and the one word database is used in both places so that a reader meets one word for one thing. The keys are in the design because what a system calls, how it talks to it and where its messages go are the same on every stack; the host and port are a deployment's and stay in the implementation file. The compiler test holds: a dependency of no kind, a channel of no servers and a specification with no dependency at all read and render as before; a wrong server is an error at the entry and the diagram still draws the channel at the boundary. The acceptance test holds: the context diagram is the first picture a stakeholder sees, and a remark on it changes one key of one dependency.

### ADR-135: A role carries no kind; the context diagram draws a person per role and a system per client of kind service, which clients and callers already say

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, gap D. The gap proposed kind, person or system,
on a role, so that a context diagram draws people and calling
systems apart, a role without it being a person. A calling service
with a role is a fact the caller-context design already placed: a
client of kind service holds roles of its own, and an operation
that serves one lists it under callers, with people the reserved
word for anyone signed in (ADR-106, ADR-110).

Decision: No keyword is added. The context diagram (ADR-134) draws one person
per role and, once the clients section exists, one system per
client of kind service, labelled with the roles it holds, leaving a
role only clients hold out of the people; an application client is
drawn on the person's edge as the way they reach the system, not as
a node. A role a job acts as, the job's role, is left out of the
people too, whatever else holds it; the job gets no node, since it
is the system's own work, and appears on the edges, where the
operations and jobs that call a dependency, emit on a channel or
consume from one label them. Until the caller-context's first two
build items land, every role no job acts as is drawn as a person,
which is what every specification means today.

Consequences: The context diagram reads clients when the section exists; the
build item for this gap is the caller-context's build items 1 and 2
(docs/caller-context.md, Building), not a new one. The gap's
proposal is recorded here so that it is not raised again.

**Insight:** A role is what its holders may do, a set of grants; who holds it is not the role's business, and clients with callers say it where the fact belongs. A kind on the role would say one fact in two places, which the Low IQ Tax forbids, and would break on the common case of a role both kinds hold: the invoice-reader role the reporting service and an auditor both hold would need two roles, one per kind, with one list of grants kept twice. The alternative that lost, the key as proposed with person as its default, would also have let a specification mark a role as a system while no client holds it, a claim nothing could check. A job's role is left out of the people because it is the grants the system gives its own work, and nobody holds it; a person who needs the same grants holds a role of their own, so a role both a job and a person use is not told apart and is drawn as the job's. The compiler test holds: nothing changes in what is read, and a specification with no clients draws every role as a person. The acceptance test holds: the picture tells a person from a system the day clients are written, and a remark on it ("the reporting service is a system, not a person") is a client entry, which the caller-context design already asks for.

### ADR-136: A server of a deployment has a name, a kind, what of the implementation it runs, or the dependency it is in that environment, and the deployment guide and technical specification draw the deployment diagram from them

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, gap E. An implementation file's deployments say
where each environment runs as a list of servers, each a URL and a
sentence. A deployment diagram, C4's deployment view, drawn from it
shows hosts with nothing on them: nothing says which package or
target runs on which server, that a server is the database, or
that a server is where a dependency is reached in this environment,
and nothing can refer to a server, since it has no name.

Decision: A server gains name, a kebab-case name unique within its
deployment, optional, and what the other keys refer to; kind, with
the values service, database, messageBroker, proxy and fileStore,
service when left out; runs, with packages, keys of layout, and
targets, keys of targets, what of this implementation runs there;
and dependency, the key of a dependency of the design this server
is in this environment. Such a server's kind is the dependency's
own, one of ADR-134's five, system and identityProvider among them,
and it is drawn as that dependency in the dependency's shape; it
runs nothing of ours, and the server's own kind keeps its five
values, since kind or runs written on such a server is the error.

The validator, in both builds, reports as the rule server at the
entry a name used twice in one deployment, a package or target the
file does not have, packages on a server whose kind is not service,
kind or runs on a server that names a dependency, and a dependency
that is not declared.

The deployment guide and the technical specification's chapter 7
draw, per deployment, the deployment diagram between the markers
deployment <deployment>: a node per server with its name, kind,
host and what it runs, in the kind's shape, a server that is a
dependency drawn as that dependency, and the environment named on
the subgraph; with the network keys (ADR-137) the servers sit in
their zones and the edges are the links, and without them the
diagram has no edges and says so under it.

Consequences: The implementation schema's server object gains name, kind, runs
and dependency, with the schema version unchanged since every key
is optional; the rule server is new in both builds, with cases;
document deployment and document techspec gain the deployment
marker; the library-lending example's three deployments are named
and placed, and its hand-drawn deployment picture is replaced; the
convention's hand-drawn deployment row becomes a generated one and
the origin table gains the rows, when the item is built.

**Insight:** The keys are in the implementation file because where one stack's build runs is that implementation's choice, beside build, method and infrastructure, which ADR-129 placed there for the same reason. name is optional so that every file reads as before, and a name chosen by a person rather than derived from the URL's host because two servers can share a host and a host name is not a name. The kinds are the dependency's words (ADR-134) where the thing is the same, so that a reader meets one word for a database whether this system or another runs it; service rather than system because a server of this kind runs part of this system, never another. ArchiMate's node, device and system software lost: they tell physical from logical, which a deployment that names a URL has no need of. C4's deployment node and infrastructure node lost as keywords because C4 tells them apart by whether something of ours runs there, which runs says; C4's container instance lost as a word because it names the thing placed, not the placing. runs holds two lists because the names come from two sections of the file, so one list would need a prefix to tell the sql target from a package of the same name. A target may run on any kind of server, since a proxy serves a ui target's pages as a service does, while packages run only on a service. dependency on a server is how the network's links reach a dependency and how the diagram shows the real host behind one in each environment; the setting that hands the code the address stays what it is, and the validator does not compare the two, because the value the code reads and the host differ legitimately. One diagram per deployment rather than one for all because the environments table already shows the promotion order and three deployments in one picture overrun a page. The compiler test holds: a deployment with no named server reads and renders as before, a wrong name is an error at the entry, and the diagram still draws every other server. The acceptance test holds: a deployment diagram is what an operator and a customer's engineer ask for first, and a remark on it changes one server's runs.

### ADR-137: A server says its zone and what it listens on, a deployment lists its allowed links as firewall rules, the validator checks every declared call has a link, and the documents draw the network diagram from them

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, gap F. A network diagram shows zones, the ports
each host listens on and which host may reach which, and a firewall
check needs the same three facts. The implementation file holds
them as sentences under infrastructure (network, ports, services,
ADR-129), which a reader can follow and nothing can check, and the
convention keeps the picture hand-drawn. The owner may decide it
stays so; this record is the form it takes if not.

Decision: A server gains zone, IEC 62443-3-2's word, the kebab-case name of
the network zone it is in, and listens, a list of what it accepts,
each a port from 1 to 65535 and a protocol in the dependency's form
(ADR-134). A deployment gains links, each from, a named server of
the deployment, to, a named server of the deployment, a
dependency's host among them, port, one the target listens on, and
a description when the reason is not plain. The URL's port does not
count as a listen, and a link in the other direction is another
link.

A package says it runs a job under implements, with the pointer
#/jobs/<name>, so the implementation schema's designRef admits
jobs beside the design objects it names today; the server that
runs the package runs the job.

The validator, in both builds, reports as the rule link at the
entry a from or to that is no named server of the deployment, a
link from a server to itself, and a port the target does not listen
on; and as the warning link_missing at the server, a server that
runs a package implementing an operation or a job that calls a
dependency, or that emits on or consumes from a channel carried by
a dependency, with no link from it to a server that is that
dependency in this deployment, and one that runs a package
implementing an entity or a job that reads or writes one with no
link to the deployment's database server that runs the sql target,
when the deployment has one. A must question that blocks
the deployment or its links holds the warning.

The deployment guide, the handover document and the technical
specification's chapter 7 draw, per deployment with a zone or a
link, the network diagram between the markers network
<deployment>: a subgraph per zone, a node per server, an edge per
link labelled with the port and the target's protocol, and the
deployment's dependencies without a server in it drawn apart as
unreached. The handover document derives its network and ports
paragraphs from the links and listens when a deployment has them
and prints the infrastructure sentences after them; a deployment
with links may leave network and ports out.

Consequences: The implementation schema's server object gains zone and listens,
the deployment object gains links, and designRef admits jobs, so
that implements can name a job and the resolver of implements in
both builds reads it; the rules link and
link_missing are new in both builds, with cases; document
deployment, handover and techspec gain the network marker; the
library-lending example's production gets zones and links; the
convention's table of diagrams gains the network row, a new one
beside the deployment row ADR-136 moves, and the origin table gains
the rows, when the item is built. If the
owner keeps the picture hand-drawn, this record is marked
deprecated and nothing of it is built.

**Insight:** zone is IEC 62443-3-2's word with its meaning, a grouping of assets that share security requirements; its conduit lost because a conduit joins zones and the check needs the host and the port. A link takes the form of a firewall rule from NIST SP 800-41, source, destination and service, because that is what the people who configure a firewall read and what the check compares. listens is SpecArch's own: Compose and Kubernetes each have a word for a published port, neither the same. The URL's port does not count because the check should compare what the file says and not what a URL implies. The missing link is a warning, not an error, because a deployment is written in order and the links are its to-do list, as the handover's checks and monitors are (ADR-129); it is derived from calls and channels because those are the connections the design declares, and nothing else has to have a path. A job is placed through implements, as an operation is, because a job is code that calls, reads and writes like an operation, and a worker server that runs only jobs is the host the check would otherwise not see; a key of its own on the server (jobs beside packages) lost because runs names what of the implementation is on the server, and the job is in a package. The database link is derived from the packages that implement an entity and the jobs that read or write one, because those are the code that reaches the store; a gateway package, one that only emits, or a worker that reaches only a dependency needs no link to the database, and a check that asked for one would make an operator open a path nothing uses, the opposite of what a firewall check is for. The infrastructure sentences stay because the customer's engineers read them and they say what the keys cannot (bandwidth, DNS, the backup store); the documents print the keys first so that the two are not read as rivals. The smallest form was chosen, three keys and one list, over a model of networks, subnets and addresses, because the picture and the check need no more and a deployment that moves a host should change one line. The recommendation to take it rests on the check: it is the one check in this file a reviewer cannot do by reading, and the hand-drawn network picture is the first to drift when a host moves. Taking it later costs nothing, since the server keys of ADR-136 do not change. The compiler test holds: a deployment with no zone, listen or link reads and renders as before; a wrong link is an error at the entry, a missing one a warning at the server, and the diagram still draws every other link. The acceptance test holds: an operator sees the zones and ports the day the deployment is written, and a link the firewall team refuses is one line to remove.

### ADR-138: specarch model prints the merged document with every node's file, line and column, the resolved references and the layout problems as one JSON document in RFC 8785's canonical form, in both builds

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, point G. An editor that shows a specification as
SpecArch reads it needs the merged document, where every node came
from, what refers to what, and the layout problems. With no command
that prints them it would load the files itself, a second loader
in another language that drifts from the first. The Go build keeps
the file of every node and the line and column of every value, the
Swift build keeps the same for its validator, and the references
are resolved by the validator's rules and kept by nothing.

Decision: specarch model <folder>... prints one JSON document on standard
output, in both builds: specarchModel, the shape's version, and
program; specifications, one per root file found, each with its
root, name, version and metaModel, the merged document as plain
values, positions, a map from every node's JSON pointer to its
file, line and column as the problems file reports them,
references, a list of every resolved reference as from, to and
through (the keyword that made it), problems, the layout problems
found while reading in the problems file's form, and
implementations, each with its file, stack, document and positions;
and estates, each with its modules, their locations and versions,
and the specification each resolved to. The bytes are RFC 8785's
canonical form. The command's design is spec/design/commands/model.yaml.
An unreadable folder or one with no specification is exit status 2;
a specification with layout problems is printed with them, status
0.

Consequences: A new command in both builds, with its design under
spec/design/commands and the case model-writes-json; the readers
give up their positions and the validator its resolved references
through one collector in each build; RFC 8785 is implemented in
both. The command list of the technical specification and the
README grow by one when the item is built.

**Insight:** One command in both builds, because the editor's Swift build reads the model through the Swift specarch and the conformance suite compares the two builds byte for byte, which RFC 8785 makes possible: a standard's rule for one byte form needs no rule of SpecArch's own, and an indented form lost because the document is for a program, not a reader; jq is there for a reader. One list of references serves both directions: a usages lookup is the list filtered by its target, one pass in an editor, and a second list would say one fact twice. The validator's errors and warnings are not repeated because the problems file and its SARIF form are their one list (ADR-065), which an editor already reads; a reference that does not resolve is among them, so it is absent here. The layout problems are included because they are found while reading, before any rule runs, and the model is the editor's way to show them. The model carries no rule's result at all: a held entry is the questions rule's finding and is in the problems file with the rest. The compiler test holds: a specification that does not validate is still printed, with every layout problem in it, so the editor shows what SpecArch could read. The acceptance test holds: an editor shows the specification the day the model exists, and what it shows is what validate checks, so a remark made in the editor lands on the entry validate would name.

### ADR-139: generate bpmn writes a lane set with the system's lane and one per approver role, and gives every shape of the SVG the id its BPMN element already has

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/diagrams.md, point H. generate bpmn lays a workflow's steps on
one row and gives the SVG's shapes no identity (ADR-085), so a
viewer cannot map a click to a step, and a reader cannot see which
role approves which step without reading the labels.

Decision: The process gains a lane set: a first lane named after the system,
holding the start event, the service tasks, the gateways and the
end events, and one lane per role that approves, in the order of
the roles' first approval, each holding the approvals that role
makes; an approval with several approvers sits in the lane of its
first-listed role and keeps every role as a potential owner. The
lane set is written for every workflow. The layout stays
deterministic: a row per lane, the steps left to right, the same
workflow the same bytes.

The BPMN XML already gives every element a stable id derived from
the step's name (start, step-<step>, deadline-<step>,
decision-<step>, end-done, end-refused, flow-<n>, and the
interface's operation-<operationId> and message-<name>); no id is
renamed. The SVG, which lacks them, wraps each shape in a group
whose id is that element's id, with data-step naming the step as
the specification spells it and data-role on a lane. The lanes are
the one addition, with a prefix no other element uses: lanes for
the lane set, lane for the system's lane and lane-<role> for a
role's. extract workflows reads the lane set past, from the
potential owners as today, so the round trip holds.

Consequences: specarch-gen-bpmn writes the lane set with its ids, the SVG the
groups with the ids the XML already has; the goldens of generate-bpmn and
extract-workflows-reads-generated-bpmn are regenerated; the
workflow reader is unchanged except that lanes are read past.

**Insight:** A lane is BPMN's own way to say who does a step, and the people who read a process diagram expect it. BPMN puts a flow node in exactly one lane, so an approval of several roles needs a rule; its first role was chosen over a lane per set of roles because a BPMN lane is one participant's. The lane set is written always, and not only when a workflow has several approver roles, because one layout is one thing a viewer learns, and a one-role workflow with the system's lane and the role's lane is still plain. The existing ids are kept because they are already derived from the step names, stable across runs and across the XML and the SVG, so a click in a viewer and an element in a modeller name the same step, and a rename would break every file that cites one. The lane ids take a prefix of their own because BPMN forbids two elements one id, and the system's lane carries no suffix while a role's always does, so no role name can collide with it. The compiler test holds: every workflow is still written, and a step name that cannot be an id is written with a problem at it, as every other mark is. The acceptance test holds: the picture shows who approves what the day it is drawn, and a viewer can open the step a click lands on.

### ADR-140: Where a dxlib registration declares nothing, the Go reader takes the body from the struct the handler decodes and the responses from the maps it answers

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: extract go reads the parameters and the responses a dxlib endpoint
declares where NewEndPoint registers it (ADR-130). Many services on
dxlib pass nil for both on every registration. Their handlers decode
the body themselves, json.Unmarshal(aepr.RequestBodyAsBytes, &req),
check the fields they need with an if that refuses, and answer each
outcome with aepr.WriteResponseAsJSON(status, header,
utils.JSON{...}). For such a service the reader wrote every body as
any object with a must question, and every operation's responses as
the refusals alone, so the specification held no request or
response schema the code gives plainly.

Decision: When the registration's parameter list is read and empty, the
endpoint's body is JSON and the handler decodes the request's
RequestBodyAsBytes, through json.Unmarshal or a json.NewDecoder over
bytes.NewReader or bytes.NewBuffer of it, into a variable it declares
with its type (var x T, x := T{}, x := &T{}, x := new(T)), the body
is written from T by encoding/json's rules with the field writer of
a router's handler body: its json names, its types and widths, a
pointer as nullable, a slice as items, a map as additionalProperties,
a struct of the module in place, a field tagged "-" left out. A field
without omitempty or omitzero is required.

An if of the handler's body itself, not one nested in another
statement, that checks the variable's field and whose block refuses
through the request by a statement of its own, a return of, a call
to, or an assignment or declaration from one of the problem calls
or WriteResponseAsJSON of a literal status from 400, writes what it
checks; so does an else if of its
chain when every branch before it refuses too. Such a check x.F == "" as
required with minLength 1, x.F == nil as required, len(x.F) == 0 as
required with minLength or minItems 1, len(x.F) against a literal as
minLength, maxLength, minItems or maxItems, x.F against a literal
number as minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum or exclusiveMaximum,
x.F != "a" && x.F != "b" as an enum, and a switch of the body on x.F
whose cases are strings and whose default refuses as an enum. Each
part of an || is a check of its own. Any other check that names a
field of the variable and refuses, such as x.A && x.B or x.F != "",
which tests that the field is there and not what it holds, is a
should question at its line on the body's schema, as is a check of
one of these shapes on a field of another type. A refusing check
nested in another statement of the body, under an if, in an else
after a branch that does not refuse, in a case, a loop or a
closure, is a should question at its line that names where it
sits, when it names a field of the variable or sits under a
condition or in a loop over a field that does, such as a parse of
x.F under x.F != "" or a check of each item of a range over x.F. A
block that refuses only inside a statement of its own does not
refuse. A check that names no field of the variable, such as
err != nil, and sits under no condition that does, is not a check
of the body.

A decode the reader cannot write from is the must question on the
body's fields, saying why: a list, which dxlib's own pre-processing
refuses with 422 because it reads a JSON body into an object; a map
that names no field; Request.Body, which dxlib has already read to
its end into RequestBodyAsBytes for a JSON endpoint; a variable of no
type the handler declares. A body decoded twice is a should question.

When the registration's responses are read, each
WriteResponseAsJSON(status, header, body) call on the request is a
response under its status. A literal map (utils.JSON, or a map of
strings to any value) gives an object whose keys are its properties,
each required, since the handler always writes it, and of the type
its value gives: a string, number or boolean literal, a nested
literal map, a list of literal maps that name one set of keys, a
composite literal's type, a name the handler declares with its type,
or a field of such a name. An integer literal is Go's int, whose
width is asked as every int's is. dxlib's own keys, status,
status_code, reason and reason_message, which it adds when the map
lacks them, are not written. A status that is not a literal, a body
that is not a literal map, a key that is not a literal, a value whose
type the handler does not declare, and one status answered with
bodies that name other fields are each a must question at the place
they block; a header prints a line, as a declared one does. Nothing
is written for a response the reader cannot read.

The registration wins. When it declares parameters and the handler
decodes a struct too, the declared body is written, and when the
struct's json names are not the declared names a must question says
the two sources disagree, naming both places. When it declares a
response at a status the handler answers too, the declared response
is written, and a literal map whose keys are not the declared
template's names is a must question of the same kind. A status the
handler answers that the registration does not declare is written
beside the declared ones, as a refusal the handler answers is.
Responses the registration declares in a form not read are asked
about already, and the handler's answers are not added to them.

Consequences: extract-go-dxlib-handler-shapes covers the shapes. The body question
of extract-go-dxlib-declared's POST /loans/import now says that its
handler decodes Request.Body, which dxlib has already read. A service
whose handlers answer literal maps gets success responses, so its
operations' questions ask for the responses' descriptions rather
than for the success itself. Its POST /tasks/assign covers the
checks nested under a presence test and the envelope keys,
POST /tasks/label a refusal kept in err and returned, a check in a
loop over a field and an answer of envelope keys alone, and
POST /tasks/restore a registration and a handler that agree. The router reader's rule for required
is unchanged.

**Insight:** The registration is what dxlib reads and checks, so where it says something it is the stronger source; where it says nothing, the handler is the only place the code says what the endpoint takes and answers, and a decode into a declared struct and a literal map answer are as plain in syntax as a literal parameter list. Required follows omitempty, while a router's body takes required from a validator's tag alone. encoding/json enforces neither when it decodes, and a dxlib handler has no validator: the tag is the one place the author says a field may be left out, and the checks that refuse are what enforces the rest. A field the author wants optional is marked so in the code, and an owner reviewing the extracted body can drop a required name with one change. dxlib's envelope keys are left out because its emitter leaves them out of a data template; writing them would make the Go reading and the emitted document disagree in the merge on every response. The keys left out print a not-held line, so a handler that means one as a field of its own data is asked about, and an answer of envelope keys alone is no body of its own, as a nil body is. Only checks of the decoded variable's fields that refuse are read, because those are the ones that hold the field to a value before the handler goes on; a check that branches without refusing says nothing of what the body may hold. Only the checks of the handler's body itself are rules: a check under another condition holds the field only when that condition holds, and most often that is an optional field checked only when it is there, so writing it as a rule of the whole body would make the field required or bounded where the code is not. Reading a refusal as the block's only when a statement of the block makes it keeps a refusal under an inner condition from turning the outer one into a rule. x.F != "" that refuses is not an enum of "", which no handler means, but a test that the field is there. One that refuses in a shape the reader does not write is asked about rather than passed over, since it holds the body to a rule the schema would otherwise not show. The compiler test holds: nothing is refused or dropped; a decode or an answer the reader cannot write from is a question at the operation, a value it cannot type is kept by its name with a question, and a disagreement keeps the declared form and asks. The acceptance test holds: a dxlib service shows its bodies and its success responses at the first extraction, and a remark on a field changes one field.

### ADR-141: A gateway that forwards by a token claim is a design element of its own under gateways, after RFC 9110's gateway, with the token it verifies, the claim it reads, the dependency each value selects, its own refusals and no permission, and its forwards fix the token's audience

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/gateway.md, ask 1. A service in front of an estate's services
registers routes only for its health and its metrics, and forwards
every other request, whatever its method and path, to the service
the bearer token's audience names, after verifying the token's
