signature against the issuer's keys. The meta-model could not hold
it: an entry under paths is one method on one path with a
permission and a handler, a path parameter holds one segment, and
the readers set a catch-all aside with a line, so the behaviour the
service exists for was missing from its specification, and the
table of services was listed by gaps as a surface not read.

Decision: The design gains gateways, a section keyed by a camelCase name,
each a description; token, the key under tokens of the token the
gateway verifies, with the word and meaning an operation's token
has; claim, the name of a claim that token declares, whose value
selects the service; forwards, a list of rows, each a value, the
claim's value, and a dependency, the key of a dependency of kind
system or identityProvider the request is forwarded to as received;
calls, the dependencies called besides the forwards, the identity
provider whose keys it fetches among them; middlewares, as an
operation's; and refusals, what the gateway answers itself, in a
middleware's form. A gateway names no permission and the schema has
no key for one. It forwards every request no operation under paths
answers; a path it must not forward is an operation that answers
it, closed with nobody when nobody may reach it. A claim whose
value is a list selects a service when exactly one of its values is
a forward's, and is refused when two are.

The validator, in both builds, reports as the rule gateway at the
entry a token not declared, a claim the token does not declare, an
empty forwards, a value twice, a dependency not declared or of kind
database, messageBroker or fileStore, a forward's dependency under
calls, and, when the claim is aud, the token marked default or named
by an operation. token_audience (ADR-109) treats the aud of a token
a gateway forwards by aud as fixed by the forwards and refuses const
or enum on it. ADR-097's one default is counted among the tokens no
gateway forwards by aud: a specification whose every token is
forwarded, as a gateway module with only its health and its metrics
is, declares no default, its operations accept no token, as those of
a specification with no tokens do, and generate openapi writes no
bearer scheme for it; a gateway module whose own operations accept a
token declares and defaults that token as ADR-097 has it.
middleware, middleware_missing, dependency and problem
reach a gateway as they reach an operation; link_missing (ADR-137)
gains the gateway's forwards and calls, and the implementation
schema's designRef admits gateways so a package implements one and
the server that runs the package runs it. In the umbrella run, a
token a gateway forwards by aud is left out of the refusal of two
modules accepting one aud value, and gateway reports a forward
whose value is none of the aud values the module its dependency's
specification names accepts, when that module is given; a module
not given leaves the forward unresolved, no error.

The derived cases, with the gateway a subject of tests: forwarded
to <dependency> per forward; refused with no token, refused with a
bad signature, denied with expired <token>; refused with an unknown
<claim>; refused with a <claim> naming two forwarded services; and
dependency fails <name> and dependency times out <name> for every
dependency forwarded to or called. The technical specification's
chapter 3 draws the gateway's edges in the context diagram, chapter
6 gains a section per gateway with a sequence diagram of one
forwarded request, the test plan lists its cases, and generate
openapi writes nothing for it and prints a line naming it.

Consequences: The design schema, its fragment schema and the Swift embed gain
gateways; the implementation schema's designRef admits gateways;
the rule gateway is new, token_audience and link_missing grow, in
both builds, with cases; derive gains the cases and the rank table
a row; document techspec draws the edges and the section, the test
plan the rows, generate openapi the line; the convention's section
and origin rows are added; the library estate gains a gateway
module. The forward table's reader is ADR-142, the Go reader's
fixes ADR-143.

**Insight:** The word is RFC 9110's, section 3.7: a gateway, also a reverse proxy, is an intermediary that acts as an origin server for the outbound connection and forwards received requests inbound to another server or servers; upstream was not taken because the RFC gives it a direction that changes with the message, backend because it is a product's word, and proxy because ADR-136 gives it to a server in front of a service. claim is RFC 7519's. A section of its own rather than a catch-all operation under paths because OpenAPI has no catch-all, a path parameter holds one segment, and an operation must name a permission the gateway does not check. The table is design because a client must know which audience to ask the issuer for (RFC 8707's resource parameter) and what a wrong one is answered with; where each service is in an environment is a deployment's fact, a server with dependency per deployment (ADR-136), and the setting the code reads is declared as every setting is. The issuer is said by iss with const on the token, RFC 8414's issuer identifier, and the algorithm by the token's signature (ADR-097, RFC 8725 section 3.1), so no issuer or keys key is added; where the keys are, the issuer's jwks_uri, is a deployment's fact. The identity provider is what the gateway calls, so the context diagram and the link check see it with no special case. No permission, and still fail-closed (SA-5): the gateway decides nothing and answers no request of its own, the service it forwards to checks the permission of every path as it would without the gateway, and the gate is a token the issuer signed for a service the table holds; a request without one is refused, and the derived cases make that a test. The caller-context's rule that every hop's route has a permission is about a hop with routes of its own; a gateway has none, and it is no hop of the delegation chain either, since it presents nothing of its own. The forwards fix the audience because RFC 7519, section 4.1.3, is met the way a gateway meets it: the principal processing the token identifies itself with a value in aud, and the gateway identifies itself with every value in its table on the services' behalf, while each service still checks that aud names itself (RFC 9068, section 4). Writing the enum on the claim beside the table would say one list twice and give the validator a disagreement to report, which the Low IQ Tax forbids; const or enum on that aud is refused as aud on a Txn-Token is (ADR-109). The one-default rule leaves the forwarded token out because ADR-097's reason for it, that a service accepts one token nearly everywhere, does not hold for a gateway whose own operations accept none, and a second token declared only to carry default would be a placeholder. The umbrella's one-audience refusal would otherwise refuse every gateway, since its forwards are the audiences of the modules it fronts; leaving its token out and checking that each value is an audience the module accepts turns the false refusal into the check a reader cannot do by eye. The refusals are written and not derived because the statuses are the project's choice, 404 or 403 for an unknown audience. A prefix or a method list is left out because paths already carves the space and no system asked for a partial gateway; the shape admits them. The compiler test holds: a file with no gateways, and a token with no gateway, read and render as before; a wrong row is an error at the row and the section still draws the other forwards. The acceptance test holds: the gateway's section is the first page the services' teams read, and a remark on it changes one row. The element stacks on 0.3's step 4 (tokens) and the diagram keywords' items 2 and 4, so its build item follows them.

### ADR-142: A gateway's table of services is printed by the project in SpecArch's gateway table format and read by extract gateway, as the route, permission and workflow tables are, never from the project's own file, and check compares it

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/gateway.md, ask 2. The gateway loads its table, a value of the
claim to the setting that holds the service's address, from a file
of its own format, so extract outline is all that reads it and gaps
lists it as a surface not read. A reader of the table was asked
for, of the file directly or of a dump the project writes.

Decision: SpecArch defines the gateway table, gatewayTable 1, wrapped by
tools/gateways/dump-gateway.sh around the project's printer with the
folder's path, the commit and, for a submodule, the repository
(ADR-098): the gateway's name, the claim it reads, the environment
the addresses were resolved in or null, and one row per forward
with the claim's value, the project's name for the service or null,
the setting the address is read from or null, and the address as
resolved or null; any other key, or one missing, is refused.

extract gateway reads it into a tree: the gateway, stated, citing
the dump and each row, with its claim and forwards; its description
and its token must questions, the token's blocking it, its refusals
a should question. Each row's dependency is named by the row's name
in camelCase, else by a fixed rule from the value, the host's first
label of a URI and the value itself otherwise, with a could question
to rename it; kind system; protocol from the URL's scheme, or a
should question when there is no URL; description and timeout must
questions; two rows naming one dependency a must question at the
gateway. A row's setting is a setting under configuration, named by
extract go's camelCase rule for an environment variable, secret
false, a string of format uri, described as the forwarded service's
address, with a should question to confirm it is no secret, must
when its name holds secret, token, key or password. With
--implementation-out and an environment, the reader writes an
implementation fragment holding that deployment's servers, one per
row with an address, name, url and dependency (ADR-136); without an
environment the addresses are not written and a line says so.

merge leaves the Go reader's question at a fallback handler
(ADR-143), which blocks gateways once the element exists, out when
a table's gateway answers it, by the rule for a question whose
every blocked key another tree gives, one gateway to one question
over the whole merge, every tree's fallback handler's question
before any tree's catch-all route's, each pass over the trees in
the order given; a question no
gateway is left for stays open. check compares
a specification with its gateway table: forward_not_served at a
forward the table does not hold, forward_not_specified at a table
row the specification does not hold, forward_differs at a forward
whose value the table sends to another dependency (a report when
the row names none, since a name made from the value is a guess),
claim_differs at the gateway,
each an error the allowlist may name.

Consequences: tools/gateways/dump-gateway.sh, the source gateway of specarch
extract with --implementation-out, the reader's paragraph in
spec/design/commands/extract.yaml, merge's answer of the fallback
question, check's three differences, a dump for the library
estate's gateway and a CI step that extracts it twice. Built after
ADR-141, since the tree it writes needs the element.

**Insight:** A reader of the project's own file would put the rules of extract in a second place and read one project's format, which the readers' test forbids and ADR-118 declined for the workflow table; a printer that writes what the gateway loads gives a table that is what runs, which is ADR-044's reason for the route table. The alternative of a second route table version with a catch-all row lost: a route table's row is one operation with one permission, every reader of it would need a second shape for one row, and a forward is not a route. The reader writes what the table says and asks the rest: the table shows a lookup, not a verifier, so the token is a must question (the rule of docs/caller-context.md, The readers); a timeout and a description are not in a table; a name is derived by a fixed rule with the could question the permission table's names carry. The address is a deployment's fact, so it is written only where a deployment can hold it, the fragment of ADR-121 for the environment the printer names, and never into the design. The setting is written because the table names it and the code reads it, as extract go writes an environment variable. The readers' test holds: nothing is written that the table does not say. The compiler test holds: a refused table says why, and a tree with its must questions validates. The acceptance test holds: the owner sees the gateway's forwards the day the dump exists, and check says the day a row drifts.

### ADR-143: extract go reads a package-level string constant as the literal it names and a package-level list assigned once as a literal list, and asks a must question at every fallback handler and catch-all route in place of silence or a line

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: docs/gateway.md, ask 3. Read with the 0.7.0 build, a Go module
whose router registers Match with a package-level var holding a
literal list of net/http method constants and a path from a
package-level const, and a GET with a constant path, gives must
questions for them, "the reader does not read as a literal" and
"not a literal list", where a literal list and path are read; and
gin's NoRoute handler gives nothing, no question, no line, and is
not counted among the registrations. ADR-075 reads a literal or a
known idiom and asks about the rest; it never drops a registration
the table knows.

Decision: A package-level const of a string type is read as the literal it
names, in the same package through any of its files and in another
package of the module through its import, as a handler is found
today, and so is a constant written as literals and constants joined
by +. A package-level var is read as a literal list only when the
syntax shows it never changes: its value is a composite literal of
string literals, string constants or net/http method constants, and
no statement of the module assigns to the name, in its own package
or in another through the import, appends to it or takes its
address, by the test the reader applies to a name a call bound
once. Any other name stays the must question it is, and the
question says what stopped the reader: the second assignment and
its line, or the value that is not a list. The rule holds wherever
a literal path or method list is read: Match, gin's and echo's
method calls, gorilla/mux's Methods, chi's Method, a ServeMux
pattern and a group's prefix.

gin's NoRoute and NoMethod, chi's NotFound and MethodNotAllowed,
gorilla/mux's NotFoundHandler and MethodNotAllowedHandler, echo's
HTTPErrorHandler and a ServeMux pattern of / alone with no method
are each a must question citing the call, or the assignment where the
library's fallback is a field, on a router a name holds or a struct
of the module keeps in a field, asking what the handler answers or
forwards and by which claim, and are counted as registrations; one
in a loop or behind a condition asks the question every
registration there asks. The
question blocks gateways, the section of ADR-141, which the gateway
table answers in the merge (ADR-142), and is written in the design
folder's questions file beside the tree's other design questions,
where question_stage wants a question about that stage. A route whose path ends in a catch-all is
the same must question, naming the prefix and the methods, in place
of a line. gorilla/mux has two catch-alls, and both take the
question: a route variable whose pattern can match a slash
({rest:.*}), which the reader finds by parsing the pattern as Go's
regexp package parses it and reading it for a slash anywhere in it:
a literal holding one, a class whose ranges cover it, or any
character, since a pattern can match a slash only in a string of
its own shape ({file:.+\.png} matches a/b.png and not a/b), so no
one sample string finds them all; each variable is closed at its
matching brace by counting depth, as gorilla/mux reads it, so a
pattern holding braces ({rest:.{1,}}, {id:[0-9]{3}}) stays whole;
and PathPrefix given a handler that is no router. PathPrefix given
a router of the module mounts it under no prefix, as a ServeMux
pattern of / does, since gorilla/mux hands the whole path on, and
Methods or another matcher on that mount is a line, since the
meta-model holds no match on a mount. A gateway table
answers the question in the merge (ADR-142); an answer that the
handler answers a problem document is a decision that closes it
with nothing written.

Consequences: internal/extract resolves constants and lists assigned once and
asks at fallbacks and catch-alls; the walk paragraph of
spec/design/commands/extract.yaml, the Go table of
docs/reading-code.md and step 15 of docs/extraction.md say so; a
test with the fixture listed in BUG-028; BUG-028 and
BUG-029 move to BUG_HISTORY.md with the fixing commit.

**Insight:** Go gives a constant one value at compile time, so the syntax gives it as surely as a literal's, and the reader's own question already calls it a literal it does not read; a handler in another package is found through the import today, so a constant is found the same way. Go has no constant lists, so a method list named by a package-level name is always a var, which the reader may read only when nothing in the module can change it, and syntax can show that for a whole module, every file of it read, where it cannot for a value from outside the module. A name that fails the test stays a question, since a value assigned twice is a guess, and the question names the line so the owner sees why. A fallback handler is where a gateway lives in each library, and where a plain 404 lives too; the reader cannot tell which, and ADR-075 forbids dropping a registration the table knows on a surface it reads, so a must question is the one record, and blocking gateways is right because a handler that takes every unmatched request is the shape of a gateway or of nothing. The catch-all is the other way the same thing is written, so it takes the same question in place of a line that said only that the meta-model does not hold it. These are reader changes and no meta-model change, built first: they need no decision on the element, and a specification with a question at its fallback handler is better than one that does not know it has one. The readers' test holds: a constant and a list assigned once are what the code says; the question writes nothing.

### ADR-144: An operation's handler is followed into the code and recorded under its mapping as steps with their source, drawn as a flowchart, checked against the code and against the operation

Status: accepted, 2026-10-19.

Context: The readers wrote what an endpoint declares and the refusals its
handler answers, and nothing of what the handler does between the
two: which tables it reads and writes, which functions and systems
it calls, where it branches and loops, and what each path ends in.
A reviewer who wanted to know had to open the code, and a
specification read from the code could not say whether the code
did what the registration declared. The owner asked for the
handler's logic in the specification as a flowchart with the source
beside it, cited to the commit, kept in a form SpecArch can validate
and diff, with the code checked against the operation as it is
read, and for every node to carry a stable id and its lines, so
that an editor can open a node's code from the chart.

Decision: The record is implementation, not design: what a handler does on
one stack is one implementation's, as the function it is. It goes
under the operation's mapping in an implementation file, beside
the mapping's target, as handler: the commit the code was read at,
the depth followed, and functions, the handler first and then each
function of the same code its steps reach, once each. A function
holds its name as the code qualifies it, its file and first and
last line, its steps and its source, the lines from the first to
the last with each line's trailing spaces and tabs dropped, and
the first line's indentation dropped from every line, since a
function literal written inside a function begins indented and a
YAML block cannot begin with a tab; the validator drops the same
before it compares. A step
is one kind of thing the code does, in plain words (text), with the
lines it is on: input (a parameter, the body, a header read),
branch (with then and otherwise), choice (with cases), loop (with
body), database (the table and whether it reads or writes, and
whether it is in a transaction), transaction, call (the function
followed, or why the call stopped), external (a call of another
system, with the dependency its host names), response (its status
and the problem a refusal names), return and statement (a defer, a
go statement, a panic, a break, a continue, a goto or a
fallthrough). A break leaves the innermost loop, switch or select,
or the statement its label names, as Go's own rule has it, and the
step says which; a labelled loop or choice carries its label, so
the chart draws the exit to the right statement, and a label on a
block or an if is a goto's target alone, not the inner loop's. A
case that falls through leads into the next case, in the chart and
in the checks, not past the switch. A function literal is a
function of its own, one call deeper, reached by a call step whose
reached key says whether it is called where it is written, passed
to a call or defined for later: its returns are its own, so a
closure passed to a sort or a transaction helper does not end the
handler's chart. A literal defined for later runs nothing where it
is written, so the checks count what it does at the call of the
name it is assigned to, which is a call step of that literal; a
literal passed to a call counts as run by it, since a sort, a
transaction helper or an error group runs it before returning,
and a literal a go statement or a timer runs later is the named
exception, left as it is. It is read with the names of the
function it is written in, since a closure sees them. Steps nest as the
code does rather than naming each other, so the record reads like
the code, a diff of it is a diff of lines, and nobody invents node
ids; each step's id is s and its number in the order written, the
handler's steps first, which the flowchart's node carries.

specarch extract go reads the record for every operation whose
handler is a function literal, a function of the same package or
one of another package of the module, from the handler's body: an
assignment, a declaration, a call statement, a return, an if, a
for, a switch, a select, a defer, a go statement, a break and a
continue each give their steps, a call's arguments before the
call. A call of a function of the module is followed to three
calls deep from the handler and at most forty functions a record;
a call of a method is followed when the receiver's type is known
by syntax, a parameter's, a receiver's, a composite literal's, a
module function's result or a package-level var's declared type.
A call not followed says why on its step: a function value, an
interface's method, a method of a value whose type syntax does not
give, a function outside the module, a fourth call deep. A call
into the standard library is no step, since it is the language and
not the system's logic, and a method of a value of a type outside
the module is none either. A dxlib table's methods are database
steps, their access told by the method's name; database/sql's
calls with a literal statement are too, the table read from the
statement; dxlib's request methods and net/http's, gin's and
echo's request and response calls are input and response steps. The
record is written with --implementation-out, which go now takes as
database does, into the fragment with each operation's mapping;
an operation whose handler was not followed gets its mapping with
the target alone and why.

Given --implementation, the file's handler records are compared
with the ones read: one line counts the handlers unchanged,
changed, not recorded and recorded for an operation the source no
longer registers, and each changed handler lists, per function,
its lines now and before and the step lines added and removed,
marked + and -, by a longest common subsequence of the steps
flattened to kind and text.

The validator, in both builds, warns handler_source when a record
no longer matches the code: the source it holds for a function is
not what the cited file holds at the function's lines, with the
first line that differs, or the lines it has moved to; the file is
not under the folder the code source names under url; or the
record cites no source with a folder. The working tree is read,
from the specification's root through the source's url, since
neither build runs git; the commit the record names says what the
source was taken from.

The technical specification writes, in each operation's runtime
view after its sequence diagram, what the handler does: the
handler, the commit and depth, and per function a Mermaid
flowchart whose nodes are the steps by id, shaped by kind, with yes
and no edges on a branch, an edge per case on a choice, a way back
on a loop and one to the loop's end for a break, then the function's
source in a Go code block, and the calls not followed with why.

While the handler is read, its code is checked against the
operation, and each fault is a should question on the operation
with a new key, certainty: certain when the code as written cannot
work or disagrees with the registration, suspected when a run or a
person must confirm it. The checks: a parameter the registration
declares that no function followed reads; a response declared that
no function followed and no middleware of the chain answers, dxlib's
own 400 and 422 on a declared parameter excepted; a status answered
that the registration does not declare; a path that returns, or
reaches the handler's end, with no response written, where in a
dxlib handler a returned error counts as answered since dxlib's
getters refuse a failed read themselves; a result dropped with the
blank identifier that is an error of a module function (certain) or
the last of several results of any call (suspected), and a call
statement that drops a module function's error; a table written
after the response was written in the same block; a handler that
writes a table and runs no middleware and checks no permission
while other operations do; two writes with no transaction begun;
code after a return or a panic in the same block, and a constant
condition; a handler whose body does nothing, a TODO, FIXME, XXX or
HACK note, a panic that says the code is not built, and a response
of fixed values from a function that reads nothing. A fault in a
function several handlers reach is one question naming every
operation that reaches it. The problems file and the SARIF log
carry the certainty; the questions document and the technical
specification show it in the question's label.

Consequences: The implementation schema gains handler, function and step under a
mapping, and the design schema certainty under a question; the
fragment schemas and the Swift embed are regenerated. extract go
takes --implementation-out and writes the records; given
--implementation it compares them. Both validator builds gain
handler_source and leave a mapping's handler out of the design-key
check. The technical specification draws the charts. Every Go
extraction case gains the questions its stub handlers deserve. A
record is as long as the code it holds, so an implementation file
with many handlers is long; the fragment is written apart so that
an owner puts in what they want. JavaScript and TypeScript can
follow with the same record: the step kinds name nothing of Go.

**Insight:** The owner's request, 2026-10-19, with the note from the editor's diagram design that every node needs a stable id and its lines. The record sits in the implementation file because the owner asked that the existing implementation record be extended, not a parallel structure, and because what a handler does on one stack is not design: the design says what the operation answers, the implementation says how this code gets there. Nested steps were chosen over a node-and-edge graph because they read like the code they came from, which is the Low IQ Tax, and because a diff of nested steps is a diff of lines, which the extraction prints and a reviewer reads without a graph tool. Ids are numbered in document order because steps have no names of their own; the id is stable while the code before it is, and the step's lines say where it is whatever its number. The source is kept in the record because the owner asked for the code beside the chart, so that a reader checks one against the other, and because a record that holds its source can be checked against the code by both validator builds without git: the standard library's parser is in the Go build alone, and git is in neither, so the check compares lines. Trailing spaces and tabs are dropped because YAML cannot write a line that ends in them in a readable block, and formatted Go has none. The faults are questions, not a new kind of problem, because the owner asked that the existing mechanism be extended: a question is the one licence for a specification to be unsure, it blocks the operation it is about, it reaches the problems file, the questions document and the technical specification already, and an owner answers it with a decision. Certainty is a key of its own rather than a word in the text or a priority, since a reader and a tool must tell a fault from a suspicion without reading the sentence, and priority already says what the answer unblocks. The checks are the ones syntax decides from what the reader already holds; a nil or empty value used without a check needs types, which the reader does not have, and is left out rather than guessed. The compiler test holds: a handler not followed gets its mapping with why, a call not followed is a step that says why, nothing is refused, and every fault is a question at the operation with its certainty. The acceptance test holds: an owner sees each handler's chart and its faults in the technical specification as soon as the code is read, and a change to the code shows as a short diff of steps at the next extraction and as one warning in validate until the record is renewed.

### ADR-145: A handshake is declared once with its key agreement, signature, cipher, establishing operation, lifetime and uses, and an operation names the one whose envelope its request and response travel in

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: Services on dxlib register most endpoints with an end-to-end
encryption type: a client first calls a pre-key operation with its
Ed25519 and two X25519 public keys, receives the service's and an
index, derives two shared secrets, and from then on sends each
request as one JSON member holding the index and one holding a hex
envelope, an AES-256-CBC encryption of the length-prefixed header
and body signed with its Ed25519 key, and reads each answer from
the same kind of envelope under the second secret and the service's
key. A browser or a mobile app does exactly that before it may call
anything. The specification had no word for it: an operation read
from such a service showed a JSON body and JSON responses, so a
client built from it would have sent plain JSON to an endpoint that
refuses it, the technical specification showed a field table where
an envelope travels, and docs/dxlib-lessons.md had set the session
key mechanism aside as implementation. What a client must do to
call an operation is the interface, which is design; which bytes
the envelope is made of belongs to the stack.

Decision: handshakes is a section of the design keyed by camelCase name. Each
declares the key agreement both sides run (keyAgreement, x25519 or
x448, RFC 7748), the signature each puts on what it sends
(signature, ed25519 or ed448, RFC 8032), the cipher the envelope is
encrypted with (cipher, by its OpenSSL name: aes-256-cbc,
aes-256-gcm or chacha20-poly1305), the operation a client calls to
perform the exchange (establishedBy, an operationId), how long one
is accepted (lifetime, a duration; left out, it does not expire by
time) and how many envelopes one carries (uses; left out, any
number within its lifetime). An operation names under handshake the
handshake whose envelope its request travels in; its response
travels in the same envelope unless the operation streams a
download (ADR-146), which leaves the envelope and answers the bytes
plain. The establishing operation travels in no envelope: it is
called before one exists. An upload stream cannot name a handshake:
its request body is the file, and the envelope carries a JSON body.

The validator refuses, as handshake, an operation naming a
handshake that is not declared, an establishedBy that names no
operation or one that itself names a handshake, and a handshake on
an upload stream. Every operation that names a handshake derives
the red case expired handshake <name>, as an operation accepting a
token derives its expired case: a caller whose handshake has
expired, or has carried its uses envelopes, is refused and
establishes a new one. The technical specification lists each
handshake with what a client does, in order, and says of each
operation which handshake it travels in.

The bytes on the wire are the stack's. For dxlib they are fixed by
the library: an endpoint whose type is EndPointTypeHTTPEndToEndEncryptionV2
carries the pre-key envelope, a request of {i, d} and a response of
{d}, the envelope dxlib's datablock packs; the exchange is
dxlib_module's pre-login, a request of a0, a1 and a2 answered with
i, b0, b1 and b2. extract go writes such an endpoint under a
handshake named preKey with keyAgreement x25519, signature ed25519
and cipher aes-256-cbc, inferred from the type, and asks as a must
question which operation establishes it unless a registration of
the module declares exactly the parameters a0, a1 and a2, which it
then names; the lifetime is the service's configuration, so it is
left out with a should question. EndPointTypeHTTPDownloadStreamV2
is the same handshake on a download stream. The V1 type dxlib
itself refuses as not implemented, so it is a line and a could
question; the V3 and V4 types are envelopes whose exchange, cipher
and session store the host supplies and dxlib does not read, so
each is a must question on the operation's handshake, as is a type
the reader cannot read. generate openapi in the dxlib dialect
writes the V2 type for a handshake of those three primitives, the
DownloadStreamV2 type when the operation also streams a download,
and an error at the operation for any other primitives, since no
dxlib type carries them. generate go-dxlib writes the exchange's
handler for the establishing operation, whose body must declare
a0, a1 and a2 and whose success must declare i, b0, b1 and b2, the
hooks dxlib calls to open and seal an envelope over a store of
handshakes the service supplies (an in-memory store is written
beside it), and a client that performs the exchange and the
encrypted call, so a generated client and a generated server agree
by construction. The other generators refuse an operation that
names a handshake rather than write a plain call: the tests target
says so in the test and leaves the call to the harness, the
TypeScript screens seal dxlib's envelope in the browser (ADR-161) and
the other ui targets report an error at the page, and the plain
openapi target writes x-specarch-handshake.

Consequences: A client built from the specification knows which operations it may
call plain, which only through an envelope and which operation gives
it the envelope; a reviewer sees the same in the technical
specification; and a service read from dxlib keeps its encryption in
its specification instead of losing it to a JSON body. A handshake
is a fact of the interface boundary like a token, so a service that
moves from dxlib to another stack keeps the same declaration and
changes only how the stack makes the bytes. The TypeScript screens
perform dxlib's handshake in the browser (ADR-161); the plain
JavaScript and SwiftUI screens do not, and a page of theirs that
calls an encrypted operation is an error at the page.

**Insight:** The primitives are named by the standards that define them, RFC 7748 for the curves and RFC 8032 for the signatures, and by OpenSSL's names for the ciphers, which every library spells the same, so that a client on any stack reads the declaration without a dictionary. The declaration stops at what a client must do and leaves the byte layout to the stack, because the layout is dxlib's datablock today and would be another library's tomorrow, while the exchange, the keys and the cipher are what both ends must agree on; writing the layout in the design would be the stack-specific key the design refuses. A handshake is declared once and named by operations, as middlewares are, because a service encrypts nearly everything the same way and the exceptions are what is worth writing. The establishing operation is an operation like any other, with its body and responses, so that a client sees its parameters where it sees every other, and the generator checks them against the exchange it writes rather than inventing a second declaration. uses is declared rather than assumed single, because dxlib's own code lets a pre-key serve until its time runs out while a consumer may delete it after one envelope, and the client must know which. The reader infers the primitives from the endpoint type because dxlib fixes them for that type, as it fixes a parameter type's JSON schema, and asks for what the type does not fix.

**Note:** From RFC 7748, Elliptic Curves for Security, 2016: X25519 and X448 are Diffie-Hellman functions over Curve25519 and Curve448: each party sends its public key and both compute the same shared secret. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7748>

**Note:** From RFC 8032, Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA), 2017: Ed25519 and Ed448 are EdDSA signature schemes; a signature is verified with the signer's public key. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032>

### ADR-146: An operation that carries a file says so with stream and its direction, the media type and the binary string stay where OpenAPI puts them, and the largest download is a limit

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: dxlib serves very large files: an upload endpoint hands the handler
the request body as it arrives, from the first byte to the last, and
a download endpoint writes the response body the same way, with the
file's media type, length and name in the headers, and neither is
ever held whole in memory. The reader wrote an upload's body as a
binary string from its content type and a download as a JSON
response, so nothing told a client, a generator or a reader of the
technical specification that the body is a file streamed through,
how large it may be, or that the download answers no JSON at all.
OpenAPI describes a binary body as a string of format binary under
its media type and has no word for streaming, since to the document
a body is a body however it is read.

Decision: stream is an operation keyword with one key, direction: upload says
the request body is the file, download says the success response's
body is. OpenAPI's own words keep saying what the body is: an
upload's requestBody has one media type whose schema is a string of
format binary, and a download's every 2xx response has one such
media type; stream adds that the body is passed through as it
arrives and bounded as a file. The largest upload is
limits.maxRequestBytes, as for any body; the largest download is
limits.maxResponseBytes, a limit added for it, the largest answer a
client must be ready for, allowed only beside a download stream.

The validator refuses, as stream, an upload on a method other than
post or put, an upload without that request body or with another, a
download without a success response or whose success response
carries another body, and maxResponseBytes beside no download. The
technical specification says of such an operation that it streams
the file in or out, with its media type and bound, in place of a
field table and JSON responses.

For dxlib, extract go writes EndPointTypeHTTPUploadStream as an
upload stream, EndPointTypeHTTPDownloadStream as a download stream,
and EndPointTypeHTTPDownloadStreamV2 as a download stream under the
pre-key handshake (ADR-145); a download's success response is
written as application/octet-stream, the type dxlib's own sender
sets, with a schema of a binary string, in place of what the
registration's data template or the handler's JSON answer declares,
which is left unread and is a should question when either declares
one. generate openapi in the
dxlib dialect writes the upload type with a requestBody of the
binary string as application/octet-stream, the one type dxlib
streams an upload as, with a warning at the operation when the
design names another, and the download type with its success
response described but carrying no content, since dxlib's reader
takes a response's content only as a JSON object. generate go-dxlib
writes
an upload helper that hands the body to the service's own code as a
reader held to maxRequestBytes, since dxlib caps a streamed upload
only by the declared Content-Length and a chunked upload declares
none, and a download helper that writes the headers, the status the
design gives the file and the bytes from a reader as dxlib's own
sender does, refusing a file
above maxResponseBytes before a byte is sent and abandoning the
response on a failed copy so a client never keeps a short file as a
whole one; the client it writes uploads from a stream with the
media type the design gives the file, and downloads to a stream. The
tests target leaves a stream's call to the harness, the
ui targets report an error at a page that submits to or loads from
a stream, and the plain openapi target writes x-specarch-stream.

Consequences: A reader of the specification tells a file endpoint from a JSON one
without opening the code, a client knows which bodies to stream and
how large they may be, and a generated service streams a file
larger than memory in both directions, which the round trip's test
exercises with a generated client against a generated server. A
body of format binary without stream is still allowed: a small
image read whole is one, and the two differ in how the body is
handled, which is what stream says.

**Insight:** OpenAPI's media type and binary string already say what the body is, so stream says only what they cannot: the direction and that the body is passed through, bounded as a file. Repeating the media type under stream would be a second way to say it, which the one way rule refuses; so the validator checks stream against the body rather than letting stream carry its own. The bound of a download goes under limits beside the bound of a request because both are sizes a client plans for, and a new key beside stream for one of them would split one idea in two places. The reader writes the download's media type as octet-stream from dxlib's own sender rather than asking, because the registration's data template is a JSON object dxlib never sends on a stream, and a stream is bytes unless the handler names another type; when the registration declares a template anyway the two sources disagree, which is a question.

**Note:** From RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, 2022: A representation's media type is given by Content-Type and its size by Content-Length; a message body may be of any length, transferred as it is produced. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110>

### ADR-147: The SwiftUI generator writes the same pages as data, each a Swift literal typed by its component's schema type in a package the project writes, found by the target's framework, with the pages read through the one analysis the TypeScript generator reads them through

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: Roadmap target 4 names SwiftUI the default for the iPhone and had
no generator for it. The Next.js and Carbon generator (ADR-067 to
ADR-074, ADR-079, ADR-093) writes each page as a schema of data a
component reads, the components once, the strings once, and the
theme through the design-tokens idiom, and reads the design through
the ui-components idiom's names so a project renders through its
own library by an override. The owner asked for the SwiftUI target
as the same pages, lists, forms, views, navigation, strings and
theme, as a plug-in named specarch-gen-ui-swiftui, an idiom a
project overrides as for Carbon. specarch generate found a plug-in
by the implementation file's language only, so a Swift file would
find specarch-gen-ui-swift, and the TypeScript generator's analysis
of the pages, three thousand lines of what a page holds and what is
refused, was written into that generator.

Decision: The analysis of the pages moves to internal/genscreens: the task,
list, form and view pages as members keyed by the ui-components
idiom's names for the generator's framework, with the routes their
events lead to, their hooks and permission; the session, the menu,
the translations, the theme's colours, the marks and the refusal of
a file built by hand. A generator gives a profile (its name,
platform, framework, language, where its rules run, whether its
screens compare decimals exactly, and how a server of its own pages
a list) and writes the members in its stack; the TypeScript output
is unchanged. specarch generate looks a plug-in up by the target's
framework first, specarch-gen-<target>-<framework>, the framework
given under the target or the platform's default, then by the
language, then the plain name; a framework is a stack of the file
as a dialect is (ADR-023), so the owner's name holds and a language
may have a plug-in per framework. specarch-gen-ui-swiftui writes,
for a ui target of platform iphone and framework swiftui in a Swift
implementation file, into a Swift package the project writes the
Package.swift of, under the module the target's settings.module
names (Screens when none): per page Pages/<Page>Schema.swift, one
literal of the part's schema type whose labels are the idiom's
names, nested values as .init, dictionaries as Swift dictionaries
and rules as Rule literals, and Pages/<Page>View.swift, a view that
hands the schema and its texts to the component behind the guard
with the routes its events lead to; once per package the components
under Screens/ on SwiftUI and Foundation alone, Routes.swift with
one Route enum of every page written and the view each case opens,
Application.swift with the service, the session and the menu,
Strings.swift with every text in every language, Theme.swift
through the design-tokens idiom's swiftui rendering, and a derived
test per guarded page and for the menu under Tests/<module>Tests in
Swift Testing. The page sign-in was asked for from is kept by the
router, not a query, so returnTo is a route; a message crosses a
navigation in the router too. A form's hooks are read from
<Page>Hooks, a type the project writes beside the page, one static
member per field named as the field, so a missing hook fails the
build. The language chosen is kept under a key in
the app's defaults. The server routes of settings.server are refused
for swiftui, since an app calls the service directly, and a schema
built by hand is compared byte for byte, the object-literal
comparison being TypeScript's; both are said in docs/ui-swiftui.md.
Both idioms render swiftui: ui-components names the SwiftUI
components and the same keys, and design-tokens names a Color per
part. The example's sign-in and second-factor screens are written by
hand in a Swift package first, committed alone, and the generator
reproduces them but for the header; CI builds and tests the package
on the macOS job, with no simulator.

Consequences: One specification drives three front ends, plain JavaScript,
Next.js and SwiftUI, with the same pages read once; a rule the
analysis gains reaches both generators that read pages as data, and
a message names the generator that reports it. The TypeScript
generator's goldens hold byte for byte. A Swift project renders
through its own components by overriding the idiom's swiftui parts,
as a TypeScript project overrides nextjs-carbon's. The app wrapper
around the generated package (the App, its navigation stack, its
tint and where it sets the service's URL) stays the project's, as
the Next.js layout does.

**Insight:** The owner named the plug-in for the framework, and a framework is what decides the components (ADR-023, Q1 of docs/ui-nextjs-carbon.md); a lookup by the language alone would have forced specarch-gen-ui-swift and bound every Swift front end to one framework. Reading the pages once keeps the two generators from drifting apart in what they accept and refuse, which three thousand duplicated lines would have done on the first change. A typed Swift literal is Swift's satisfies: the compiler checks the data against the component's type, and .init in a nested value lets the literal stay data with no type name a project's override would have to supply. A router that keeps the page sign-in was asked for from needs no open-redirect check, since an app's routes are an enum. A package with no dependency needs no scan, builds on a Mac without a simulator, and is what a SwiftUI project adds as a local package.

### ADR-152: The plain JavaScript screens address a page as its file with its route's parameters in the query, carry a message to the page they open for one load, and hold a view's sections in its HTML

Status: proposed, 2026-10-20.

Context: specarch-gen-ui wrote list pages only (ADR-040): an action that
opens a page, a selected row, a menu and a view were reported and
left out, and an action whose operation takes the reason its
confirmation asks for was left out too. The plain JavaScript stack
has no router and no build step: the screens are files a static
server hands out, so nothing reads a path such as
/members/{memberId} and finds its page. Pages talk through the
event bus, which lives in one page's module and ends when another
page loads. The html document shows each screen's HTML without
its scripts, to show at the user acceptance test what a page holds
before any service answers. The browser's own confirm cannot take
a reason.

Decision: A page is the file name.html, and its route's parameters travel in
the query by their names: /members/{memberId} is
member-view.html?memberId=... pages.js declares every page the
screens write, and every page another stakeholder owns, once, with
its file and parameters, as events.js declares the events, and
offers href, which writes a page's address, go, which opens it with
a message, and arrived, which a page reads once when it opens. The
message travels in the browser's session storage for that one
load; where storage is off the page opens without it. A link's
parameters come from the fields its with names, then the record's
field of that name, then, on a view, its own route's parameter. A
list's action that opens a page whose route takes no parameter is
one link above the table; one that gives a row's fields is a link
on each row, and onSelect makes the first column a link. Every page
carries the menu from menus. A view's sections, labels and the
places of its values are in its HTML, a value's parts and a list's
item template inside its place, and view.js fills them from the
record its source reads by the route's parameters. Every
confirmation is one dialog, ask.js, which asks for the reason when
the action sends one. A when, a hiddenWhen and later a check are
written as JavaScript functions of the record, of the operators
whose meaning the browser shares: comparisons, &&, ||, ! and size;
a field compared with null counts as null when the record leaves
it out. A link to a page not written is reported where it stands
and left out, as is a menu entry for one; anything the screens
cannot do, an expression they cannot evaluate, a parameter nothing
gives, is an error at its entry, and the rest of the page is still
written, marked.

Consequences: A plain JavaScript project serves the folder as it is, with no
rewrite rule, and a page's address is still one a person can
bookmark and share. A permission is not checked by the screens: a
page or an action the caller may not use is refused by the service,
and the page shows that refusal as its failed state, as the lists
already did. The menu comes in the order of the menus' and entries'
names, since a plug-in receives every object with its keys sorted;
the hand-built reference keeps the order it was written in, and
the check against it leaves the menu out. The lists now ask every
confirmation through ask.js rather than the browser's confirm, and
show the message a page that opened them left. An action whose
when the browser cannot evaluate is left out, not offered on every
row.

**Insight:** The query keeps the stack's rule of no server and no build step, and names each parameter as the route does, so a link reads as the design wrote it. One declaration of the pages, as of the events, keeps a page's name and parameters in one place a reader can check. Session storage, not the query, carries the message, so a reload or a shared address does not repeat "The member is registered.". The sections in the HTML keep the screens readable without their scripts, which is what the html document shows a reviewer before any service exists (docs/acceptance.md), and keep the module to the behaviour. Expressions as functions keep the generated code free of an evaluator, and the operators allowed are the ones whose result is the same in the browser and in the specification's language.

### ADR-153: The plain JavaScript forms hold their fields as native controls in the HTML, checked by the browser, and one form.js adds what HTML cannot say

Status: proposed, 2026-10-20.

Context: Forms and task pages were reported and left out by specarch-gen-ui.
The Next.js target draws its forms through a component library a
project overrides (ADR-069), which plain JavaScript has none of. The
browser checks required, lengths, ranges and types itself and shows
its own message, but it cannot check a rule across fields, compare
two entries, read a JSON Schema pattern as JSON Schema does (HTML
anchors a pattern and reads it with the v flag), ask for a part of a
value only once the value is given, or fill a list from the service.

Decision: A form's fields are native controls in its HTML, each with the
attributes the browser checks from the property's keywords and the
request body's required; a pattern is written as data-pattern and
checked with the u flag, unanchored. A value of a schema is a
fieldset of its parts, in the order of their names, whose required
parts are asked for once any part is given when the value itself may
be left out; a list of values and a form's child rows are rows a
person adds from a template and removes, up to their maximum. The
module hands form.js, written once, what it sends, the checks and
conditions as functions of the record (ADR-152), the pickers, the
record a form loads and the child rows loaded with it, what follows
each success and each refusal. A check's or a refusal's message is
the field's own validity message, so the browser shows it beside the
field and the form is not sent while one stands; each control's
message is the first of its pattern, its second entry and its checks
that it breaks. A hidden field is disabled, so it is neither checked
nor sent: the record is read again once the conditions are applied,
and a field entered twice is hidden and disabled with its second
entry; a second entry is not asked for while the record locks its
field.
A picker keeps the value a loaded record gives it, as an option of
its own while its list is not read or does not hold it, so the order
of the two reads does not lose it. An empty field is null
in the record the rules read and is left out of what is sent. A
form's onSubmitted follows every success its operation answers,
a workflow trigger's 202 among them; a task's are by status. A
success's page takes its route's parameters from the answer, then
the fields sent, the record loaded, and the page's own address. A
picker reads one page of its list at the list's largest page size,
and through the service's search when the list searches; otherwise
it offers that page, with a warning at the picker.

Consequences: The forms read and work without a script for what HTML checks, and
the html document shows each form with all its fields. A message
the browser writes, for a field left empty or too long, is in the
browser's language, not the page's; the generator's own words, for
a pattern and a second entry, are in English. A list's minimum
count of rows is the service's to refuse. A check that names no
field has nowhere to show its message, so it is refused; the
validator does not ask for one, since the Next.js target shows it
above the form. A check, a refusal's field or a picker's fill that
names a field the page does not draw as one control (a field left
out, or one that holds a value) has no control to show its message
or take its value, so it is an error at that name and left out; a
refusal's message is still shown with the page's. A field drawn as a
list, a long text, a box or read-only is not entered twice, and a
field the request body requires is not shown read-only, since it
would not be sent; each is an error at the field, and the field is
drawn once. The settings of the Next.js target, hooks and
layouts, have no counterpart here: a form's sections sit as one
page.

**Insight:** Native controls are what the stack's rule of no package asks for, and they carry the browser's own accessibility: the label, the focus order of the sections, the message beside the field. One form.js keeps each page's module to data, as view.js does for views and events.js for events, so a reader checks one engine once. Reading a pattern as JSON Schema does keeps the browser and the service in agreement on what passes, which the HTML attribute would not.

### ADR-154: extract go asks for the callers of a route a client check or a signature check guards, each named under the implementation file's http binding, and lists the claims where golang-jwt mints a token; it writes no callers, client or token of its own

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: Step 5 of docs/meta-model-0.3.md, the readers. Steps 3 and 4 give
a route's callers, the clients with their proof and the tokens
(ADR-096, ADR-097, ADR-110). callers is the explicit list of who
may call, people and clients by name, with no word for every
client, so a reader cannot write callers clients where a client
check guards a route. A check that admits
only a client, a check that verifies a signature and a call that
mints a token are each written the project's own way: syntax finds
the call and not the client names, the algorithm, the parts signed
or the token's lifetime and checks.

Decision: The implementation file's http binding names the project's gates
that read no permission, beside permissionChecks: clientChecks, a
check that admits only a client, and signatureChecks, a check that
verifies a request's signature, each by package and function and
with no argument. extract go finds them where it finds a permission
check (wrapping a handler, among a route's or a group's middleware,
applied with Use or With, or called in the handler) and also as
middleware named without a call. Each check prints a line counting
the operations it guards and is one must question, decided by the
system owner and citing its first call, blocking the callers of each
of them: for a client check, which clients call them and whether
people do; for a signature check, which client signs, with which
algorithm and over which parts of the request. The reader writes no
callers, so the operation reads as people's until the question is
answered, and declares no client. A call of golang-jwt's
NewWithClaims is a must question blocking the tokens that lists the
keys of the MapClaims literal it is given, or the one the same
function assigns to the name it is given; claims of any other shape
are named as not read.

Consequences: An implementation file without the two keys reads as before. A
route a gate guards keeps the permission its permission check
reads, so the permissions matrix is unchanged, and the gate's
question holds the operation's derived tests until the owner names
its callers. extract router reads a route table that carries no
middleware, and the seeds reader reads dxlib_module's tables, which
hold no client; neither has a gate or a client to find, so both
stay as they are. The checks of the application, the immediate
caller and the audience, the event writers, and an argument on
clientChecks that names the clients, are ADR-159's.

**Insight:** A question rather than callers written from the code, because the compiler principle never guesses: a client list the code does not hold would be a callers line saying more than the source, and callers has no word for every client, which would fail open for a client added later (ADR-110). One question per check rather than per operation, as for a bypassed check (ADR-114): it is one decision about one check, and blocking each operation's callers puts the mark at each entry. A binding rather than recognising an API key or a signature header by name, because the test is a comparison written the project's way; the person who names the permission check names these beside it, as a fact of the stack. golang-jwt alone, because it is the library a Go service mints with by default and its MapClaims literal names the claims by syntax; a struct of claims would need the reader to follow the type's tags, which waits for a source that needs it. Compiler test: a gate named in part, or a function named as two kinds of check, is a must question at the paths and the routes are read with their permissions; every gate found is a problem at each operation it guards. Acceptance test: a reviewer of the first techspec sees, at the route, that a client reaches it and which question names the clients, and the change asked for is the callers line.

### ADR-155: specarch decide writes the decision as a file of its own under the next ID, takes the question out of its file as text, prints the entries to write rather than writing them, and asks for a source when the specification tracks origin

Status: proposed, 2026-10-20.

Context: Answering an open question was two edits by hand: a decision record
under the next free number, with the question's ID under answers,
and the question taken out of whichever file holds it, since the
validator refuses an accepted decision that answers a question still
present. The design of refinement planned a command for it that
prints the elements the question blocked so the agent edits them.
Four things had to be settled: where the record goes, how the
question leaves its file, what the command writes into the blocked
entries, and what origin the record carries in a specification that
tracks origin.

Decision: The record is always a file of its own, design/decisions/<ID>.yaml,
which the loader reads as any fragment of the design stage; the
command refuses a specification whose stages do not list design,
saying to list it, rather than editing the root file's stages. The
ID is ADR- and the largest number any decision carries plus one, at
least three digits. The title is the question's text, the context
the question with its options, what it blocked and its Insight, the
decision the answer, the consequences the entries that are to be
written from it, so that a reader of the decisions sees what was
asked and what was settled without the question, which is gone.

The question's entry leaves its file by an edit of the text, as the
marks are written: from the problem marks above its key to the last
line of its value, found by indentation, and the questions key with
it when the entry was the only one; a file left with only blank and
comment lines is removed. An entry whose key does not start its line
is refused with the line. The edited text is parsed again and the
file is written only when it holds every other entry it held.

The command writes nothing into the entries the question blocked.
It prints each with the file and line of the deepest entry that
exists, the pointer and the keys missing there, and what the entry
is to carry: origin decided and decidedIn the new ID. From that run
on, the keys a must question covered are errors at their entries
until they are written.

With --source the record is stated and cites that source with the
answer as what it says; the source must be declared in the root
file. When the specification tracks origin, --source is required,
since every element of such a specification says where it came
from and the record would otherwise be the one without.

Consequences: An agent or a dispatcher answers a question with one command and
gets back the list of what to write; the record and the question
never disagree, and the number is never taken. A specification's
hand-written questions files keep their formatting and comments. A
decision written by the command reads as any other decision and is
edited like one: a better title, a fuller context. A specification
that keeps its decisions in one file gets its first command-written
decision in a file beside it, which the loader merges as it merges
any fragment.

**Insight:** A file of its own is the one layout that needs no knowledge of how the specification keeps its decisions: appending to the file that holds the last one would have to find the end of its decisions mapping in text, which a mapping that is not last in its file, or one written in flow style, defeats. Text editing is chosen over re-encoding the questions file for the reason the marks are: a file written out again by a YAML encoder loses the author's comments, quoting and line breaks, and the refinement is done on files people edit. The command does not write the blocked entries because the answer is prose and the entry is data: what a loan period of 21 days becomes in the entity is the agent's reading of the answer, which the validator then checks; the command would have to guess, and a guess in the specification is a placeholder. The origin rule follows the design: an answer given in words is a source of kind interview with its date, and a decision in a specification that tracks origin without one would be a warning the command itself caused.

**Note:** From Documenting architecture decisions, 2011: A decision record states the context, the decision and the consequences. <https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions>

### ADR-156: problems.sarif is the agent queue's interface to the open questions, and its property keys are stable

Status: proposed, 2026-10-20.

Context: The design of refinement has a dispatcher read the open questions of
a specification, put each to the person who decides it, with the
options, and feed the answer back. The machine form it reads is
problems.sarif (ADR-065), which carried a question's priority, kind,
certainty, decider, options and blocked entries as properties of
its result, but the question's own text only inside the message,
with the priority, the decider and the way to answer around it, and
nothing named the folder the specification is in, which specarch
decide needs. A dispatcher that parses a message, or opens the
specification to find its folder, is one that reads the text, and
one that reads a key a later release renames breaks without a word.

Decision: A question's result carries, under properties, the question as one
paragraph (question), its priority, kind (questionKind), certainty,
decider (decidedBy), options, blocked entries (blocks) and its
Insight (why); the run carries, under properties, the
specification's folder relative to the log (specification), its
title and its version. The result's message, locations, related
locations and the partial fingerprint specarchId/v1 stay as they
were. These keys are the interface: a later release adds a key and
never renames or takes one away, and the fingerprint is how a
question is known again between runs. docs/refinement.md writes
the interface down, with what the agent queue's side reads and
runs.

Consequences: A dispatcher reads the log, takes every result of kind open, puts
question and options to decidedBy, and runs specarch decide with
the fingerprint as the question's ID, decidedBy, the answer and
the folder from the run's properties, all from the log alone. Every
committed problems.sarif gains the new keys.

**Insight:** SARIF's property bag is the standard's own place for what a tool knows beyond the result, so the fields go there rather than into a second file of SpecArch's own, which ADR-065 refused; the folder goes on the run, since it is one fact about every result, and is relative to the log for the reason the locations are, that an absolute path differs between machines and breaks byte-identical runs. The keys are promised stable because the dispatcher is another program, released on its own, and a key it reads is a contract.

**Note:** From Static Analysis Results Interchange Format (SARIF) Version 2.1.0, 2020: A property bag holds properties a tool wants to convey beyond those the standard defines, and a run may carry one as a result may. <https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html>

### ADR-157: The comparison of the old documents with the refined specification is derived from origin, citations and decisions, tells added from corrected by whether the element cites a source, and is a refinement document like the questions and the problems

Status: proposed, 2026-10-20.

Context: Before approving, a reviewer wants to see what the refinement
changed against the old documents: what was kept, clarified, added
or corrected, and what of the old documents was dropped. The design
of refinement planned a document target for it with four groups
and no format of its own, since origin, the citations and the
decisions already hold the facts, and the outline a source lists as
its clauses already lets gaps show which clauses produced nothing.
Three things had to be settled: how an added element is told from a
corrected one, which elements the document compares, and whether
it is a draft while questions are open.

Decision: The document target comparison writes comparison.md with four
numbered groups. Kept: every element with origin stated, under each
source it cites, with the clause and what the source says. Clarified:
every element with origin inferred, with its why. Added or
corrected: every element with origin decided, with its decision and
the decision's why; it is corrected when it cites a source other
than an interview, since that source said something at that place,
and added otherwise. Dropped: for every source that lists its
clauses, the clauses that no element cites; a clause only a
question cites is named as asked about, not dropped, and a
decision's citation makes no clause produced, since the decisions
are not compared. A stated element whose citation names no source
is listed under Kept under a heading of its own, with the
validator's error at it. Elements without an origin are listed
after the four groups. The elements
compared are the named elements of every section but decisions and
questions, which are the refinement's own record. Problems are
marked at the element's row, as in every document; an element
that is in two tables of Kept, citing two sources or a named and
a nameless one, is marked once, under the first.

The comparison is a refinement document, like the questions
document and the problems files: it is read while questions are
open, so it is never a draft, it is not a row of the outputs table,
and it is not among the documents an approval is of.

Consequences: A reviewer reads one document to see what changed and what was left
behind, and a clause of the manual nobody read shows up before
approval rather than after. A decided element that cites the old
document shows as a correction of it; one that cites only the
interview, or nothing, as an addition. A specification that lists
no outline gets a Dropped section that says to list one. The
coverage section of the questions document keeps showing which
elements each clause produced; the comparison shows the clauses
that produced nothing, which is what a reviewer looks for.

**Insight:** Whether a decided element corrects the old document or adds to it cannot be read from the decision's prose without reading it, so the rule rests on a fact the specification holds: a citation of the old document at that element means the document said something there. The interview is set apart because an answer given in words is the decision's own ground, not an old document. The decisions and the questions are left out because the document compares the system's elements with the sources, and a decision stated by an interview would otherwise read as kept from the interview. The comparison is never a draft because a draft notice says the document is not what will be approved, and this document is never approved: it is the account of the refinement, read while it is going on, and listing it among the outputs would put it beside the documents that are.

**Note:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.3.3.6: Requirements validation is subject to approval by the project authority and the key stakeholders. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

### ADR-158: specarch-gen-scripts writes one guarded psql script per guarded entry whose change the design says, checks the precondition and the exact count inside the change, rolls back unless told to apply, and leaves every other change to be written by hand

Status: proposed, 2026-10-20.

Context: Target 8 of the roadmap. A data change run by hand against a live
system (a correction, a backfill, a record moved on by an operator)
is safer emitted than typed: the emitted script refuses when the
system is not in the state it expects, shows what it would do before
it does it, checks that it changed exactly as many records as it
should, and changes nothing when it is run a second time. The guard
on an operation or a command says the entity, the precondition that
must hold on each record at the moment of the change, and the exact
number of records changed. It does not say what the change writes:
that is said elsewhere in the design, or nowhere.

Decision: The target is scripts, the plug-in specarch-gen-scripts. It writes
one script per operation or command that has a guard, named after
the operationId or the command's words in kebab case, as a psql
script for PostgreSQL, or for MariaDB as ADR-167 says; another
dialect is an error at the target.
It reads the tables and columns through specarch-gen-sql's model
(gensql.Schema) and writes the precondition as specarch-gen-sql
writes a check constraint, so the script names only columns the
migrations create. The change is derived by keyword, or said by the
guard's writes (ADR-168) when no keyword says it:
- the guard's entity has transitions whose trigger is the entry: the
  change sets the stateField to their to, on the records in one of
  their from states; every transition with that trigger must have
  one to, and it must not be one of the from states, since a record
  moved to the state it was in cannot be told from one not yet
  moved and a second run would move it again;
- a PUT whose request body is the guard's entity, on a path with one
  parameter: the change sets every column a caller may set, by the
  key;
- a DELETE on a path with one parameter: the change deletes the
  record by the key, or sets its soft-delete flag when the entity
  is deleted softly.
A path with one parameter means the record is the one with the key
the operator gives; the entity's key must be one field, and
recordsChanged must be 1. A transition triggered by a command, or
by an operation on a path with no parameter, changes every record
in a from state for which the precondition holds, and their number
must be recordsChanged. Every other guarded entry (a POST, a PATCH
or a command no transition names whose guard has no writes, a
transition back to the state it leaves, a PUT that sets a field stored encrypted or sets no column
a caller may set) is a warning at its guard, and its
script is left to be written by hand. An entity another stakeholder
owns gets no script.

Each value the script needs is a psql variable named after its
column (-v id=...), passed into the change with set_config and read
back with current_setting, since psql does not substitute a
variable inside the dollar-quoted body of a DO block; a variable
that is not set is refused by name before anything is read, except
the variable of a column that may be null, which left out sets the
column to NULL and is shown in brackets in the script's usage
line. A
change's audit columns are set too: a timestamp to now(), any other
from its variable. The script runs in one transaction:
1. already applied: when the record by the key already holds what
   the change writes (the to state, the values put, the soft-delete
   flag), it says so and changes nothing;
2. precondition: it counts, locking them, the records the change
   would write (the key, the from states, the precondition, and not
   softly deleted) and refuses unless their number is
   recordsChanged;
3. the change, with the same conditions in its WHERE, so a record
   another writer moved between the count and the change is not
   written;
4. postcondition: the number of records the change wrote is
   recordsChanged exactly, and a record changed by the key holds
   what was written, or it refuses;
5. it commits only when the variable apply is true; otherwise it
   says how many records would change and rolls back.
A refusal raises an exception that names the entry, the entity, the
condition and both counts; psql stops on it and the transaction
is rolled back.

Consequences: The scripts target in an implementation file takes the dialect
setting as the sql target does. No example carries a guard yet, so
the conformance cases are the scripts' only fixtures, and the
scripts are run against a real PostgreSQL only by hand; a project
with guards on its live data changes decides whether CI runs them in
a disposable database. A change the design does not say stays a
warning at its guard; the guard's writes says one (ADR-168).

**Insight:** Keywords only, as for the sqlc queries (ADR-123): a transition says which state a trigger moves a record to, a PUT with an entity body and a key says the record is replaced, and a DELETE with a key says it goes. A POST or a PATCH says no more than that a record is made or partly changed with values the caller sends, and a command no transition names says nothing of what it writes, so guessing would put a meaning in the specification nobody wrote; the warning at the guard keeps that visible and the script the project's. A placeholder in a generated file would be edited by hand and break generate --check, so there is none.
