The precondition and the count are checked inside the change, not only before it, because the guard's promise is that the checks run with the change: under PostgreSQL's read committed isolation an UPDATE or DELETE re-evaluates its WHERE on a row another writer changed, so a record that no longer holds the precondition is skipped and the count comes out short, which the postcondition refuses. The count before the change locks the records (FOR UPDATE) so the refusal names the state found rather than a short count. Dry run by default because the safe mistake is forgetting to apply: the dry run runs every check against the live data and rolls back, so it shows exactly what an applied run would do. A second run finds the record by the key already changed and says so. A hard delete leaves no record to find, and a key whose record was deleted cannot be told from a key that never named one, so its second run is refused by the count (none found, one expected) and exits non-zero, as a change of many records is when it finds none left in a from state; either way nothing changes. psql rather than a program because a database administrator can read every statement the script runs before running it, and psql is what is at hand on a host that runs PostgreSQL. The variables are named after columns because the script is about the table, which the operator reads.

### ADR-159: extract go reads the checks of the clients, the application, the immediate caller and the audience, and the event writers, each named under the implementation file's http binding with the argument that carries the names; literal clients and services are written as callers and via, and everything else is asked; extract permissions reads a grant's client and through

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: Item 5 of docs/caller-context.md, the readers. A service written the
estate's way checks the application the person signed in through,
the immediate caller's workload identity and a token's aud in
middleware of its own, writes a security event when it refuses, and
a policy library's rows name a client as a grant's subject or as
the one client a grant holds through. ADR-154 named clientChecks a
check that admits only a client, asked as callers. The design named
the application check clientChecks too, which a literal "admin-web"
in the code cannot tell apart: whether that name is an application
or a service is the client's kind, which the identity module holds
and the code does not.

Decision: The http binding names applicationChecks, callerChecks and
audienceChecks, each item a package, a function and the argument
that carries the names (applicationArgument, callerArgument,
audienceArgument), eventWriters, and an optional clientArgument on
clientChecks. An argument gives the names as a string or a list of
strings; anything else is read as where the code reads them, such
as a setting, and named. String literals the call passes after that
argument are one must question at the blocks of the operations it
guards, asking whether they are names too or something else, such
as a reason; they are written nowhere. extract go
finds each where it finds a permission check. A client check whose
argument gives literals writes them as the callers of each
operation it guards, a caller check as its via, each with one must
question per check asking for the clients' declarations, which
holds the errors of the names not yet declared; given otherwise,
each is one must question naming where the code reads them. Two or
more literal checks of one kind on a route run in turn, so the
operation's callers or via are the names every one lists; where
their lists differ, that set is written, or none when it is empty,
with a must question at callers or via naming each check's list. An
application check is one must question for the through of every
role granting the operations' permission, naming any operation that
checks the same permission without it, since the reader writes no
role. An audience check is one must question at the tokens, with
the literal as the const to write or the setting whose value per
environment the deployments give, since the reader writes no
token. An event writer is named and nothing is written. A handler
reading the Txn-Token header is a must question for the
operation's transaction token and its via. extract permissions
reads a grant's client as a role named after the client, held by
the client declared as a service, with a must question for its
proof and a could question to rename the role; where a role of the
table has the client's name, the client's role takes the name with
-client added, so neither holds the other's grants, with a must
question at that role and the client's roles asking whether the
client was meant to hold the table's role; and a grant's
through as the role's through, the client declared as an
application; two rows that disagree on the narrowing, a name used
as subject and as through, what each client is and which token
carries the application are must questions.

Consequences: An implementation file without the new keys reads as before, and
so does a client check without clientArgument. The swift,
javascript and dart readers read permissionChecks only, as they do
for ADR-154's gates; the new checks join that gap and are left to
build. A pattern row of the rules with through is left to build:
the rows that carry it are named grants. The lending desk's sources
are unchanged; the cases extract-go-caller-checks and
extract-permissions-client-through hold the new readings.

**Insight:** applicationChecks beside clientChecks rather than one key, because one word must mean one thing and the two checks write different keys, through on a role and callers on an operation; ADR-154's meaning of clientChecks is kept, and the argument is added to it, as its consequences said. Literals written where the reader writes the element they belong to, callers and via on the operation, and asked where it writes none, roles and tokens, because a reader writes nothing the code does not say and never invents an element to hang a literal on. The questions hold the errors of the names written before they are declared, because the compiler principle keeps the tree readable with every gap marked once at its entry. Two gates in sequence written as their common names, and strings after the names asked rather than read, because a list silently replaced by another drops a definition and a reason read as a name admits a caller nobody wrote. A client kept apart from a role of its name, because read as one the client would hold every grant of the role, a grant the table never gives it. Compiler test: a check named in part or twice is a must question at the paths, and every name read is written or asked at its entry. Acceptance test: the first techspec shows who may call each route and which question names the clients still to declare.

### ADR-160: The user manual is written from the flows, menus, pages, roles and errors, and the operations guide from the endpoints, jobs, channels, dependencies, monitors, procedures and deployments; a problem type gains remedy and a monitor gains response

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: ADR-016 left the manual and the operations guide unbuilt until the
specification could say what they need. It can now say most of it.
A flow is a task: who does it and each page on the way with what
the person does there. A menu says how a page is reached, a page
what it shows, which fields a person fills in, the actions offered
and the message shown for each problem, and the roles who may open
it. The operations side has the endpoints with their permissions,
the jobs with their schedules and retries, the channels with what
carries them, the dependencies with their protocol and time limit,
the monitors with their objectives, the backup, restore, release
and rollback procedures, the settings, and in the implementation
files the hosts of each environment. Two sentences have no home:
what a person does after the system refuses them, and what the
operator does when a monitor's objective is missed.

Decision: A problem type gains remedy, what the person who meets the problem
does next, in their words; a monitor gains response, the steps the
operator takes when the objective is missed, in the shape of a
procedure's steps. Both are optional plain text with no reference
in them.
specarch document manual writes manual.md: who uses the system,
the roles holding a permission some page needs, each with the pages
it opens; the menus as the way to every page; a section per flow
with its steps as numbered instructions written from the page, the
event and the action; and a section per page with what it is for,
who opens it, the fields to fill in or the columns shown, the
actions with their confirmation, and for each problem the page
names its message, the problem's condition and its remedy, with a
default message given as the answer to any other problem. A role a
job acts as or a client holds is a program, not a person, and is
left out of who uses the system, unless a flow names it as its
actor.
specarch document operations writes operations.md: the
environments and the hosts each implementation file deploys there;
a checklist of what to look at on the live system, one row per
monitor, job and dependency; the monitors with their responses;
the jobs with their triggers, roles, retries and what becomes of
an item after the last try; the channels with what carries them,
which operations, jobs and workflows publish each message and which
jobs consume it; the dependencies with
what calls them; the endpoints with their permissions; the
settings; and the backup, restore and rollback steps.
Both are written for every specification whose implementation file
names an output folder for them, and a section the specification
has nothing for is one sentence saying so, naming the key that
fills it.

Consequences: An existing specification reads as before: the new keys are
optional and no rule refuses their absence. Every document target
of the design is built, the manual and the operations guide among
them. What a person does with an item a job keeps apart is in the
operations guide through ADR-166. A command-line tool's commands are
in the manual through ADR-165. The
sections that make the manual or the guide a draft, and whose
problems they carry, are the ones each shows: the manual reads jobs
and clients only to tell a program's role from a person's, and the
guide reads workflows only to name a message's publisher, so a
question or a problem on a job, a client or a workflow neither
makes them a draft nor is marked in them; it is marked in the
technical specification. The library
lending example gains remedies, a monitor's response and both
documents, kept current by CI.

**Insight:** remedy and response as plain text rather than a structure, because both are advice to a person and nothing checks or generates from them; a key with references would need a rule in both validators for no gain in either document. Optional rather than required with a warning, because a condition often already says what to do, and a warning on every problem type and monitor of every specification would bury the problems that matter. Written always rather than passed over with a warning as the handover is, because the target is asked for by name under targets, a missing section said in a sentence is the early result an owner looks at and asks to change, and a handover is passed over only because a vendor-run system has no customer to receive one. Programs left out of who uses the system, because a manual addresses people, and jobs and clients are in the operations guide and the technical specification. Compiler test: an incomplete specification gets both documents, with each gap named at its section, and the errors marked as in every document. Acceptance test: a page reviewer reads the manual before any screen is built, and a remark on a step or a message names the page and the key to change.

**Note:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4.12: The operation process uses the system in its intended environment and supports its users. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

### ADR-161: The TypeScript screens call a service in the dxlib dialect as it serves it and perform its pre-key handshake in the browser through the Web Crypto API

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: ADR-145 lets an operation travel in a handshake's envelope and fixes
the bytes per stack; the one stack that makes them is dxlib, whose
services serve every operation as a POST at /<operationId> with its
parameters in one JSON body (the dxlib dialect, ADR-031). The
TypeScript screens called the standard dialect only, the operation's
method and path, and refused a page that called an encrypted
operation, so a web front end of a dxlib service could not be
generated at all: its encrypted operations needed the envelope, and
its plain ones answered at another URL. The plug-in could not even
tell the dialect, since specarch handed it only the implementation
files that name the ui target, and the dialect is the service's
file's.

Decision: specarch generate tells every plug-in the dialect the API is served
in: apiDialect in its request is dxlib when an implementation
file's openapi target names that dialect, and left out otherwise.
specarch-gen-ui-typescript then calls every operation as the
dialect serves it. In the standard dialect a call is the
operation's method at its path, as before. In the dxlib dialect it
is a POST at /<operationId> whose JSON body holds the path's
parameters, under the snake-case name the dialect gives them, the
query and the body; a list reads the paginated-list idiom's dxlib
names, its page counted from 0, its sort a list of a field and a
direction, a filter a member of the filter object and its records
under a dotted name such as list.rows.

A call to an operation that names a handshake travels in dxlib's
pre-key envelope. The screens' transport module establishes the
handshake through its establishedBy operation on the first such
call, an Ed25519 and two X25519 key pairs made by the Web Crypto
API with a0, a1 and a2 sent and b0, b1, b2 and i read back, seals
each request as dxlib's datablock under the first shared key with
AES-256-CBC and the client's signature, opens the answer under the
second and the service's signature, and hands the page a Response
of the status and body inside the envelope, so a page reads an
encrypted answer as it reads a plain one. When dxlib answers plain
with REFRESH_PREKEY, because the handshake is missing, expired or
used up, the module establishes a new one and sends the request
once more. The module imports nothing, so its tests run on Node.

The screens stream a file where a page takes one (ADR-146). A task
page whose submit streams an upload shows a file picker and sends
the file picked as the request's body, a Blob the browser reads as
it sends it, of the media type the design gives the body, refusing a
file above maxRequestBytes before it is sent; since the file is what
such a page takes, the validator lets that task show no field. An
action, on a list's row or on a view, whose operation streams a
download saves the file it answers under the name its
Content-Disposition gives; asked for in an envelope, the request is
sealed and the bytes come back plain. A page that loads from, reads
or submits a stream anywhere else is an error at the page.

The generator reports as an error at the page a call in a
handshake's envelope when no implementation file serves the dxlib
dialect, or when the handshake's primitives are not dxlib's three,
since the module makes dxlib's bytes only; and a server route that
pages a list the service answers whole, under the dxlib dialect,
since that route reads the standard names. The SwiftUI generator
calls the standard dialect only, so a service in the dxlib dialect
is an error at the root for it; the plain JavaScript screens call
both (ADR-164).

Consequences: A dxlib service gets a web front end from the same specification as
its server and its Go client, and the three agree on the envelope by
construction; the round trip in internal/gendxlib drives the
module, as the generator writes it, against a generated dxlib
service on Node. A page in the browser holds its private keys in
memory only, as non-exported CryptoKeys for the agreement and the
signature, and loses the handshake on a reload, when the next
encrypted call establishes a new one. The session is still read at
its path as a plain GET, which a dxlib service may not serve; that
is the session operation's own matter, read by settings.session.
A download is gathered in the browser before it is saved, since no
portable way streams a fetch to a file on disk, so it is held up to
the operation's maxResponseBytes; the transport's download answers
the bytes as a stream, for a page that writes them elsewhere.

**Insight:** The dialect is a fact of the service, declared once on its openapi target; reading it from there through the request keeps one place to say it, where a ui setting would be a second that could disagree. The Web Crypto API carries X25519, Ed25519 and AES-CBC in every current browser and in Node, so the browser needs no cryptographic library, which would be a dependency to scan, pin and keep for code the platform already ships. The transport answers a Response rather than a value of its own so that every page kind keeps reading the status and the body the way it read them before, and an encrypted call changes no page's code. Renewing once on REFRESH_PREKEY, and not more, follows dxlib's own word for the case: the client is told to establish a new handshake, and a second refusal right after one is a fault worth showing rather than a loop.

**Note:** From RFC 7748, Elliptic Curves for Security, 2016: X25519 and X448 are Diffie-Hellman functions over Curve25519 and Curve448: each party sends its public key and both compute the same shared secret. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7748>

**Note:** From RFC 8032, Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA), 2017: Ed25519 and Ed448 are EdDSA signature schemes; a signature is verified with the signer's public key. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032>

### ADR-162: An upload's parameters travel beside the file as one JSON object in a header the stack names, declared under stream as parameters

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: An upload stream's body is the file (ADR-146), so the values that
say what the file is, such as the record it belongs to, its name or
its tags, cannot travel in it. dxlib reads them from the request's
X-Var header, one JSON object beside the streamed body, and checks
each against the type the endpoint declares, of any of its types: a
list, an object, a JSON value, a nullable number. The meta-model had
no word for a parameter carried that way, so extract go left such
parameters out with a note, the dxlib dialect and the go-dxlib
target refused an upload that declared any, and a client could not
send them.

Decision: stream takes a second key, parameters, beside direction upload only:
a schema of type object with its properties, or a $ref to a schema
or an entity, as a request body's is. Its properties are the
upload's parameters, sent together as one JSON object in one header
of the request beside the file. The design names no header: which
one is the stack's, as the bytes of an envelope are (ADR-145). For
dxlib it is X-Var.

The validator refuses parameters beside a download, a schema that
is not an object, and a property that shares a name with a path or
query parameter of the operation. A task page that submits to such
an upload shows the parameters as its fields and the file beside
them; the fields a page may show and must show are the parameters'.

In the dxlib dialect an upload's parameters are written as
x-dxlib-parameters, the object dxlib's own document gives the
parameters of a raw body, with the operation's path and query
parameters folded in, since dxlib reads every parameter of an upload
from X-Var as the dialect folds them into the body of any other
operation (ADR-031). generate go-dxlib reads them in the handler as
it reads a body's, through the parameter values dxlib fills from the
header, and the client it writes sends them as X-Var. extract go
writes the parameters a registration of EndPointTypeHTTPUploadStream
declares as stream.parameters. The TypeScript screens send a task's
fields in X-Var in the dxlib dialect; in the standard dialect, which
names no header, a page that submits to an upload with parameters is
an error at the page. The plain openapi target writes them inside
x-specarch-stream, and the technical specification lists them in a
table under the upload.

An endpoint that reads a raw body whole, not as a stream, with
parameters in X-Var stays outside this word: extract go leaves its
parameters out with the note it writes today.

Consequences: A file goes up with the values that describe it, typed as the
design gives them, and a reader of the specification sees them
beside the upload. A stack other than dxlib that serves an upload
with parameters names its header in its own generator; until one
does, the standard dialect's targets report such an upload rather
than drop its parameters.

**Insight:** OpenAPI 3 can describe a JSON object in one header: a parameter in header whose content holds an application/json schema. The design cannot use it as it is, since that parameter must carry the header's name, which is the stack's; so the design keeps the schema under stream and the dialect writes the name. A query string would carry the values in the URL, where they are logged and bounded in length, and flattens a list, an object or a null into text that each stack parses its own way, so the types the design gives would not survive. A multipart body would carry them typed, but makes the request a different content type that dxlib reads whole rather than streams, which is what stream exists to avoid. Path and query parameters stay what they are in the standard dialect; the dxlib dialect folds them in because dxlib reads nothing else on an upload, the same fold it makes for every other body.

**Note:** From OpenAPI Specification, 3.1.0: A parameter in header may give its schema under content, one media type such as application/json, for a value that is a structure rather than a scalar. <https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0>

**Note:** From RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, 2022: Header fields carry metadata about the message beside its content; the content is the representation itself. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110>

### ADR-163: A handshake may be served in dxlib's persistent-session types V3 or V4, chosen in the implementation file, and specarch's hooks carry the pre-key envelope's bytes through them

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: dxlib has two more envelope types beside the pre-key one (ADR-145):
an endpoint of type EndPointTypeHTTPEndToEndEncryptionV3 hands its
JSON body to a hook the service sets, OnE2EEV3Unpack, which answers
the request's header and body as two length-prefixed elements and a
state of its own, and hands the answer's status, header and body to
OnE2EEV3Pack, which answers the bytes dxlib writes as JSON with the
inner status. V4 is the same with little-endian length prefixes
inside the process. When the unpack hook refuses, dxlib answers a
plain 422 whose reason is REFRESH_SESSION. dxlib fixes nothing else:
not the exchange, the cipher, the session store nor the bytes on the
wire. extract go asked a must question at every such operation, and
no generator served either type, so a service built on them could
not be read back or regenerated.

Decision: The design does not change: a handshake declares its key agreement,
signature, cipher, establishing operation, lifetime and uses, and an
operation names the handshake it travels in. Which of dxlib's types
serves a handshake is the stack's, so the implementation file says
it: the openapi target's settings.envelopes maps a handshake's name
to v2, v3 or v4. A handshake it does not name is v2, so every
specification written before generates as it did. A name that is
not a handshake of the specification, or a value other than those
three, is an error at the implementation file.

Over V3 and V4, specarch's envelope is the one dxlib's V2 carries:
the request is {i, d}, the index of a handshake and the hex envelope
dxlib's datablock packs under the first shared key with the client's
Ed25519 signature, and the answer is {d} under the second shared key
and the service's signature. So a handshake served in V3 or V4 takes
the same primitives as one in V2, x25519, ed25519 and aes-256-cbc,
and is established the same way, by its establishedBy operation, a
plain JSON call of a0, a1 and a2 answered with i, b0, b1 and b2;
dxlib's own bootstrap path through the hook, an unpack that answers
no element, is never used. The hooks keep the handshake in the same
store, so lifetime and uses hold as they do under V2. A client
cannot tell the three apart but by the reason of the plain refusal,
REFRESH_PREKEY or REFRESH_SESSION: the TypeScript screens'
transport establishes a new handshake on either, and the Go client
answers either as it came, for its caller to call Handshake again.

The dxlib dialect writes EndPointTypeHTTPEndToEndEncryptionV3 or V4
for an operation under such a handshake. A download stream under
one is an error at the operation: dxlib's only download type in an
envelope is EndPointTypeHTTPDownloadStreamV2, the pre-key one.
specarch generate hands the setting to every plug-in as
apiEnvelopes, beside apiDialect (ADR-161), since the file that holds
the openapi target need not be one the go-dxlib target reads.
generate go-dxlib sets OnE2EEV3Unpack and OnE2EEV3Pack, or the V4
pair, to hooks that read {i, d} from the body, open it as the V2
hook opens it, hand the shared key and the service's signing key to
the pack hook in the state, and seal the answer as {d}; the V4 hooks
convert the elements to and from the little-endian framing.

extract go reads an endpoint of type V3 or V4 as travelling in the
handshake session when the module sets the matching unpack hook to
a function of the module that opens dxlib's datablock
(datablock.UnpackLVPayload, followed through the functions it calls
up to three deep) and the pack hook to one that seals with it
(datablock.PackLVPayload): the datablock fixes x25519, ed25519 and
aes-256-cbc, inferred, and the establishing operation is found by
a0, a1 and a2 as for preKey, with the same should question on the
lifetime and uses. That the type is V3 or V4 is not held in the
design; it is a could question at the handshake naming the setting
that serves it. A module that sets no such hook, or one that does
not open the datablock, keeps the must question, now saying which
of the two the reader did not find.

Consequences: A service on dxlib's persistent-session types is read into a
specification and regenerated to a service and a client that call
each other, with the same round trip as the pre-key envelope, and a
handshake moves between V2, V3 and V4 by one line of the
implementation file without touching the design. A service whose V3
or V4 hooks make their own bytes, another cipher or a bootstrap
through the hook is still read as a question, since the reader can
say nothing of an envelope it does not recognise.

**Insight:** ADR-145 puts the bytes on the wire in the stack, and the three types differ only there: a client of each runs the same exchange, seals and opens the same way and renews on a refusal. A word in the design for the type would make the design name a library's internals and give two ways to say one handshake. specarch defines no new envelope over the hooks: reusing the datablock keeps one cryptographic construction to implement in each client and to audit, which the round trip already proves against dxlib and the browser, where a second would add a format with nothing the design could say about the difference. The establishing operation stays a plain call, as ADR-145 requires, so a handshake is established one way whatever type serves it.

### ADR-164: The plain JavaScript screens call the service through one transport module, the TypeScript screens' transport in plain JavaScript, in either dialect, with the pre-key handshake and the streams

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: ADR-161 gave the TypeScript screens the dxlib dialect, dxlib's
pre-key envelope and the streams, and left the plain JavaScript
screens on the standard dialect: specarch-gen-ui refused a service
in the dxlib dialect at the root, and a page that loads from,
submits to or runs an operation that travels in a handshake's
envelope or streams a file at the page. Each of its pages called
fetch itself, with the operation's path written into the page as a
template literal, so the call knew nothing of the dialect, and a
service whose operations are encrypted had no plain web front end
at all.

Decision: specarch-gen-ui writes transport.js beside the pages: the TypeScript
screens' transport (ADR-161) in plain JavaScript, with the same
createTransport, call and upload, the same bytes of dxlib's
envelope through the Web Crypto API, the same renewal on
REFRESH_PREKEY and REFRESH_SESSION, and save for a download. It
imports nothing. service.js makes the one transport of the screens
from what the generator was told: the dialect, from apiDialect in
the plug-in request, and each handshake a page's call travels in
with the operation that establishes it.

Every call of a page goes through it: a list's page and its row
actions, a picker's list, a form's record and its submit, a view's
record and its actions. A call is described once in the page's
module as the operation, its method, its path with the {parameters}
left in, and the handshake, the stream, the upload's media type and
in the dxlib dialect each path parameter's snake-case name, where it
applies; the page hands the transport the parameters by name, and
the transport fills the path in the standard dialect or puts them
in the body in the dxlib dialect. In the dxlib dialect a list and a
picker read the paginated-list idiom's dxlib names, the page counted
from 0, a filter a member of the filter object, the records under a
dotted name such as list.rows; those names are dxlib's own, taken as
the idiom writes them and not mapped by info.wireNames, as the
TypeScript screens take them.

A task page whose submit streams an upload shows a file input of
the body's media type, labelled by the request body's description,
and sends the file chosen as the request's body, refusing one above
maxRequestBytes before it is sent; its fields are the stream's
parameters and travel in X-Var in the dxlib dialect (ADR-162), an
error at the page in the standard dialect, which names no header. An
action, on a list's row or on a view, whose operation streams a
download saves the file it answers. A page that loads from, reads or
submits a stream anywhere else is an error at the page, and so is a
call in a handshake's envelope when no implementation file serves
the dxlib dialect, or whose handshake's primitives are not dxlib's
three, as for the TypeScript screens.

Consequences: A service in the dxlib dialect, its operations encrypted or not, gets
plain web screens as it gets TypeScript ones, and the round trip in
internal/gendxlib drives transport.js, as the generator writes it,
against the generated vault on Node beside transport.ts. Every
plain JavaScript page changes shape once, the standard dialect's too:
its calls name an operation and a path in place of fetch with a
template, and the screens gain transport.js and service.js. The
transport is written twice, in TypeScript and in JavaScript; the
round trip runs the same tests against both, so they cannot drift
in what they send. The SwiftUI screens stay on the standard dialect.

**Insight:** One module for every call, rather than the envelope inside each page's fetch, keeps the bytes of the envelope in one place a test can reach, as transport.ts does for the TypeScript screens; a page that calls fetch itself would need a second copy per runtime file. The module is the TypeScript one with its types taken out, rather than a design of its own, so the two web stacks agree on the envelope by construction and a fix to one is the same edit to the other. The plain JavaScript screens need no build step, so the module cannot be compiled from transport.ts at generation time without a TypeScript compiler, a dependency the plug-in does not have. The path stays a template with its {parameters} because the dxlib dialect sends the parameters in the body by name, which a path already filled in no longer says.

### ADR-165: The user manual writes a section per command, from the commands the design already holds, info gains program, the name typed before a command's words, and a command gains remedies, what the person does after each status it fails with

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: ADR-160 wrote the user manual from the flows, menus, pages, roles and
problem types, and left a command-line tool's commands out of it.
The design already says most of what a person needs to run a
command: commands, keyed by the words typed after the program's
name, each with its summary, description, permission, arguments in
order, options, the files it reads and writes, what it prints and
every exit status with what it means. Two things have no home: the
program's name, so no command can be written as a person types it,
and what a person does after a command exits with a status other
than 0, the command's answer to a problem type's remedy.

Decision: info gains program, the name a person types to run the system's
command-line interface; a command gains remedies, keyed by an exit
status its exitCodes lists, what the person who ran it does next, in
their words. Both are optional plain text with no reference in them.
A remedy keyed by status 0, which is success, or by a status the
command's exitCodes does not list is an error at that remedy,
exit_code, the same in both builds.

specarch document manual gains a Commands section after the pages,
a section per command in the order of their words: its summary and
description; its usage line, the program's name, the command's
words, each argument in angle brackets, square brackets around one
that may be left out and ... after one that is repeatable, and each
option, a boolean one as the switch alone; who runs it, anyone for
the permission public, otherwise the roles a person holds that grant
its permission; whether it is deprecated or switched by a setting;
a table of its arguments and one of its options, an option's enum
values named; what it reads and writes, or that it writes no file;
what it prints on standard output and on standard error; and a table
of its exit statuses in number order, each with what it means and
its remedy. A specification with no commands gets the section as one
sentence naming commands, and one with commands and no program
writes each command by its words alone and says that info.program
names the program; either way the section opens with the notation of
the usage lines. A file's path is written as one code span, its fence
longer than any run of backticks in the path, as CommonMark reads a
code span. The manual reads commands, so a question blocking
them makes it a draft and their problems are marked in it.

Consequences: An existing specification reads as before: both keys are optional
and no rule refuses their absence. Every manual gains the Commands
section, a sentence where the specification has no commands, and
its opening line counts the commands beside the tasks and pages.
SpecArch's own specification names its program and gives its
commands their remedies, and its implementation file names an output
folder for the manual, so docs/manual.md is SpecArch's command-line
manual, kept current by CI; its sections for roles, menus, flows and
pages are each one sentence, since SpecArch has none. What is still
not written: an example of a command line with what it answers, and
a command's shorter option names.

**Insight:** program under info rather than on commands or in an implementation file, because the name a person types is part of the interface, the same in every stack, and one name holds for the whole specification; commands keeps its keys the words after it, as it did. remedies as a mapping beside exitCodes rather than an object in place of each exitCodes string, because every specification with commands writes exitCodes as strings, and retyping it would turn each into an error; a mapping keyed by status keeps the strings and gives the rule something to check. Plain text, optional, with no reference, as a problem type's remedy is (ADR-160): it is advice to a person, nothing generates from it, and a status's meaning often already says what to do. Status 0 refused, because a remedy for success would read as a failure in the manual. Commands sorted by their words, because a reader looks a command up by name; the technical specification keeps the design's order. The program's name taken from the specification, not from the binary a stack builds, because the manual is written before any is built. Compiler test: a specification with commands and no program still gets every command, by its words, and the sentence naming the key. Acceptance test: a person reads the usage line, the options and what to do after a failure before the program exists, and a remark on one names the command and the key to change.

**Note:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4.12: The operation process uses the system in its intended environment and supports its users. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

### ADR-166: A job that keeps an item apart says, under deadLetter, the role that handles a kept item, where it is kept and the steps to look at it, try it again or discard it, and the operations guide writes them under the job

Status: accepted, 2026-10-20.

Context: ADR-026 gave a job retries with a limit and what follows the last
try, deadLetter or discard, and ADR-160 wrote the jobs into the
operations guide. For deadLetter the guide could say only that the
item is kept apart for a person: the design had no word for which
person, where the item is, or what they do with it. An operator
who finds a kept item on the daily checklist had nothing to follow.

Decision: A job gains deadLetter, what becomes of an item it keeps apart: role,
the role whose people handle a kept item; description, where a kept
item is, what is kept with it and how a person finds it, in the
design's words; and steps, what the person does, in order, each
with a name, an action and a check, as a monitor's response is
written: look at the item, then try it again or discard it. All
three are required when deadLetter is written. A role that is not a
role of the specification, or a deadLetter on a job whose retries do
not say deadLetter, is an error at that key, job, the same in both
builds.

specarch document operations writes the role in the job's row of
the jobs table, kept apart for that role, and, after the table, a
part per job that keeps an item apart: the description, the role
that handles it and the steps as a table. A job that keeps an item
apart with no deadLetter gets its part as one sentence naming
deadLetter. The daily checklist row of a job with a deadLetter
sends the reader to that part; a job without one keeps the plain
row.

Consequences: An existing specification reads as before: deadLetter is optional,
and a job that keeps an item apart without it gets a sentence, not
an error or a warning. The library lending example's nightly job
says what the desk does with a loan it could not mark, kept current
by CI. What is still not written: the store a stack keeps a kept
item in, such as a queue or a table, which belongs in an
implementation file's deployment as a monitor's tool does, and a
test case derived from the steps.

**Insight:** deadLetter on the job rather than inside retries, because retries says how often and what follows, and the handling is a person's work with its own role and steps; keeping retries to limit and then leaves every existing retries as it is. The same word as the value of then, so a reader finds the handling under the name the retries gave it. The place in words rather than a queue or table name, because the design holds nothing stack-specific (docs/conventions.md) and a person reads where to look before any stack is chosen. steps rather than plain text, unlike a problem type's remedy, because trying an item again or discarding it changes data on the live system, and a check after each step is what tells the operator it worked, as a monitor's response and a rollback do. Required role, description and steps, because a deadLetter with any of them missing leaves the operator where the sentence does, and the schema says which is missing. A deadLetter on a job that discards refused, because the guide would describe kept items that never exist. Compiler test: a job that keeps items apart with no deadLetter still gets its part, as one sentence naming the key. Acceptance test: an operator reads where a kept item is and what to do with it before the system runs, and a remark on a step names the job and the key to change.

**Note:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4.12: The operation process uses the system in its intended environment and supports its users. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

### ADR-167: specarch-gen-scripts writes a guarded script for MariaDB as one compound statement the mariadb client runs, with user variables given in --init-command, each checked against its column's form before anything is read, in a strict session

Status: proposed, 2026-10-21.

Context: ADR-158 wrote the guarded scripts for PostgreSQL only, and the
roadmap's target 8 named another dialect as not built. MariaDB is the
dialect closest to that path among the four specarch-gen-sql writes:
open source, widely run, with transactions, locking reads and a
procedural block a script can run without creating anything. The
steps and their promises stay those of ADR-158; what differs is how
MariaDB and its client take a value, report a refusal and convert a
value.

Decision: A scripts target whose dialect is mariadb gets one script per guarded
entry, derived as ADR-158 says, against the tables specarch-gen-sql
writes for mariadb, with the precondition written as that generator
writes a MariaDB check constraint. Each script is:
- a SET SESSION that adds STRICT_ALL_TABLES to the session's
  sql_mode, keeping the rest of it;
- one compound statement, BEGIN NOT ATOMIC ... END between DELIMITER
  lines, so the file runs through the mariadb client only; inside it
  an exit handler rolls back and raises the error again, the
  transaction, and a labelled inner block the already-applied step
  leaves;
- every value a user variable named after its column (@id), set by
  the operator as mariadb --init-command="SET @id = '...'" <database>
  < script.sql, with @apply = true to commit. A variable that is not
  set is refused by name, except that of a column that may be null,
  which left out sets the column to NULL; before anything is read,
  each variable's text is checked against its column's form, by a
  pattern that ends in \z: a whole number for an integer column (no sign for an
  unsigned one), a decimal with at most the column's scale of
  digits after the point, a number for DOUBLE, true or false
  (or 1 or 0) for BOOLEAN, a date or time of day that CAST also
  reads, hexadecimal for a binary column, a uuid's 36 characters for
  a uuid field, and for a date-time field the type-rendering idiom's
  UTC text with nine fractional digits. Text of any other column is
  taken as it is; @apply must be true, false, 1 or 0 when set;
- the value cast as the column holds it: a whole number or a
  decimal through DECIMAL(65,s) with the column's scale, DOUBLE,
  DATE, TIME(6), UNHEX for binary, a boolean as LOWER(@v) IN
  ('true', '1'), and CHAR without a length for text;
- the five steps of ADR-158, with SELECT COUNT(*) ... FOR UPDATE as
  the locking count, ROW_COUNT() for the count written, <=> for
  IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, a text column compared with its value
  converted to utf8mb4 under utf8mb4_nopad_bin, and an audit instant written as
  DATE_FORMAT(UTC_TIMESTAMP(6), '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%i:%s.%f000Z');
- a refusal raised by SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' with the message ADR-158
  gives, its values joined by CONCAT; a notice is a row the client
  prints under the column message.
gensql.Column carries the format of the field a column holds, so an
audit column is known as an instant whatever type the dialect gives
it. SQL Server and Oracle stay an error at the target.

Consequences: The scripts run through the mariadb client, not through a driver or
another client that does not read DELIMITER.
Compiler test: generate-scripts-mariadb writes the six scripts of
the PostgreSQL case for MariaDB, with the same warnings. Acceptance
test: the scripts were run by hand on MariaDB 11.4 against the
tables specarch-gen-sql writes: an unset variable, a malformed uuid,
a fractional unsigned key and a fractional integer were refused
before reading; a dry run rolled back; an applied run committed; a
second run reported the record already changed or was refused by
the count; a title too long and a state outside the check were
refused and rolled back; a title changed only in case was written,
and one changed only by a trailing space was a change; a value with
a trailing newline, for an integer, a uuid key or an unsigned key,
was refused before reading, with NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES set in the
session too.

**Insight:** The mariadb client has no variables of its own and no conditional lines, so the values come in as user variables and every decision is made inside one compound statement. MariaDB runs a compound statement outside a stored program only as BEGIN NOT ATOMIC, and one that starts with a label is refused, so the label is on the inner block. --init-command rather than a SET followed by SOURCE: tried on MariaDB 11.4, a SOURCE after a SET on one -e line does not parse, and an error inside a SOURCEd file does not stop the client, which went on to the next statement and exited 0; a file read on standard input stops at the first error with exit status 1. The checks before the casts stand in for what PostgreSQL's casts do on their own. MariaDB's CAST converts what it can and warns: 123.7 cast to UNSIGNED is 123 and to DECIMAL(65,0) is 124, a date that does not exist is NULL, and text that is no number is 0, so a key given wrong would name another record. A pattern the text must match refuses it by name instead, before anything is read, and once the text matches, the cast is exact. A decimal key is held to its column's scale for the same reason ADR-158 casts a PostgreSQL key without its scale. Text is cast without a length so a key too long matches no record; a value too long is refused only by a strict session (without one MariaDB cuts it and warns), and STRICT_TRANS_TABLES is the default but a server may run without it, so the script adds STRICT_ALL_TABLES itself, as a statement of its own before the compound statement, so the whole of it runs under the strict mode; tried on MariaDB 11.4 with the session's mode emptied first, the title too long was still refused. The same statement takes NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES out of the session's mode, so the backslash in a pattern and in a message reads alike on every server; the rest of the session's mode is kept, so the precondition reads as the check constraints do. A pattern ends in \z, not $: MariaDB's REGEXP is PCRE2, where $ also matches before a final newline, so a value pasted with one would pass, be stored with it, or be cut by the cast. Tried on MariaDB 11.4, '5' followed by a newline matched '^[0-9]+$' and not '^[0-9]+\z'. Text is compared byte for byte in the already-applied step and the postcondition, since PostgreSQL compares text exactly and a column MariaDB makes without a collation takes the server's, which is case- and accent-insensitive and pads trailing spaces: under it 'the hobbit' equals 'The Hobbit', and a change of case alone would be reported as already made. utf8mb4_nopad_bin compares code points and counts trailing spaces; the value is converted to utf8mb4, which holds every character set a column may have, so the collation fits whatever the column's character set is. A key and a from state are still matched under the column's own collation, as the table's unique and check constraints match them. The locking count holds: tried on MariaDB 11.4, a second session's UPDATE of a row counted with COUNT(*) ... FOR UPDATE waited until it timed out. Under MariaDB's default repeatable read a locking read and an UPDATE read the latest committed row, not the snapshot, and the rows counted are locked, so the change writes what was counted and the postcondition still refuses a short count. ROW_COUNT() counts rows changed rather than rows matched; every change the design derives writes a value the record did not hold (the state leaves a from state, the soft-delete flag turns true, a PUT whose values all match ends at the already-applied step), so the two agree. The audit instant is written in the idiom's text form, whose byte order is time order; MariaDB keeps microseconds, so the last three of the nine digits are zeros.

**Note:** From MariaDB Server documentation, Using Compound Statements Outside of Stored Programs: Compound statements can also be used outside of stored programs. BEGIN must use the BEGIN NOT ATOMIC syntax. A compound statement might not start with a label. <https://mariadb.com/kb/en/using-compound-statements-outside-of-stored-programs/>

**Note:** From MariaDB Server documentation, CAST: The following CAST() gives warnings, because x'aa' and 'X'aa' don't behave as a number: Truncated incorrect INTEGER value. <https://mariadb.com/kb/en/cast/>

### ADR-168: A guard's writes says what a change writes when no keyword of its entry does, set with given or a literal for each field, or delete, and specarch-gen-scripts writes the guarded script from it

Status: proposed, 2026-10-21.

Context: Target 8 of the roadmap. ADR-158 derives what a guarded change
writes by keyword only: a transition its entry triggers, a PUT of the
entity by one path parameter, a DELETE by one path parameter. Every
other guarded entry (a PATCH, a POST that changes records already
there, a command no transition names) is a warning at its guard and
its script is written by hand, since the guard says the entity, the
precondition and the count but not what the change writes. The
corrections an operator runs on a live system are mostly of that
kind: clear a field on the records that hold some state, put a value
back on one record, delete the records left over by a job.

Decision: A guard takes writes, one of:
- set: the fields the change sets, each with its value, one
  expression in SpecArch's subset of CEL: given, the value the
  operator gives when running the change, or a literal of the
  field's type: a string in double quotes (for an enum field, one of
  its values), a whole number, a number with a point (for a decimal
  field, with no more digits after the point than its scale, and no
  exponent), true or false, or null for a field that is not required
  or whose type allows null. A field with no literal (a date, a time,
  a timestamp, a duration, bytes, an object) takes given.
- delete: true: the change deletes the records, or sets their
  soft-delete flag when the entity is deleted softly.
Both validators check it with the rule guard, at the entry it is
wrong in:
- writes on a PUT whose request body is the guard's entity on a path
  with one parameter, or on a DELETE on a path with one parameter, is
  an error: the keyword already says what the change writes;
- delete on an entry that triggers a transition of the entity is an
  error: the transition moves the records the delete removes;
- set naming a field the entity lacks, a field of its primary key, or
  its stateField is an error: the key names the records the change
  writes, and a state is moved by a transition, whose from states
  the script checks;
- a value that is not given or a literal of the field's type is an
  error, which says why.
A transition the entry triggers still moves the state field, and set
adds its fields to that change. specarch-gen-scripts reads writes
when no keyword says the change, keyed as ADR-158 says: on a path
with one parameter the change writes the record by its key and
recordsChanged must be 1; on a command or a path with no parameter
it writes every record for which the precondition holds. A value
given is a variable named after its column, as a PUT's is, and a
literal is written into the script as the specification writes it.
A set with no key also leaves out the records that already hold
every value it writes, so its count is of the records it would
change. What writes leaves a warning at the guard is what no word
says: a POST that makes a record, a PUT that sets a field stored
encrypted or no column a caller may set, transitions of one trigger
with two to states, a transition back to the state it leaves, a
keyed change whose recordsChanged is not 1, and an entity whose key
is not one field; writes setting a field stored encrypted is a
warning too, since a script cannot encrypt the value it writes.

Consequences: The conformance cases generate-scripts and generate-scripts-mariadb
carry a keyed set of a given value and a literal (amendLoan), a set
of null and a set of a string on many records (clear notes, label
returned), a set beside a transition (mark overdue) and a delete of
many records deleted softly (purge returned); validate-guard-writes
shows each error in both builds. The scripts were run by hand
against PostgreSQL 16 and MariaDB 11.4.4: a dry run, an applied run,
a second keyed run reported as already applied, a change of case
alone applied, a value left out set to NULL, a record whose note was
null labelled, and a second run of a set or a transition on many
records refused by its count with nothing changed. A change the
design does not say stays a warning at its guard, which names writes
where writes would say the change.

**Insight:** One way to say one thing: a PUT by its key and a DELETE by its key already say what they write, so writes on them would be a second way that could disagree with the first, and an error keeps one. A transition is said on the entity, where every caller reads it, so writes cannot move the state field around it; it can set other fields beside it, which a transition does not say. The values are kept to given and literals because a guarded script must change nothing when it is run again (ADR-158). A record that already holds every value a set writes is one the change has made, so the script can say so and stop; a value worked out from the record when the change runs (renewals + 1, a field copied from another) gives a different value on each run, so a record changed cannot be told from one not yet changed. A literal is written as the specification writes it, so a decimal keeps its digits rather than passing through a double, and a decimal with more digits than its scale is refused at the guard, since the column would round it and the check that the record holds what was written would then refuse every run. A string is not taken for a date or a timestamp: the subset's comparison does not take one for the other either, and on MariaDB a date-time field is text in the type-rendering idiom's form, which a literal would have to repeat. Without a key a set has no record to find already changed, so the condition leaves out the records that hold every value written: a second run finds none and is refused by the count, as a transition of many records is when none is left in a from state, and nothing changes. The comparison treats two nulls as equal (IS NOT DISTINCT FROM on PostgreSQL, <=> on MariaDB, with text byte for byte as ADR-167 compares it), so a record whose field is null is counted as not yet holding a string: with = the comparison would be null and the record would be left out of the change without a word. A delete with no key needs nothing more: the records it deleted no longer meet its condition, or carry the soft-delete flag the condition excludes. A POST that makes a record has no record to count before the change or to find already made, so it stays the project's own script; the warning at its guard says that a POST that changes records already there says what it writes with writes.

### ADR-169: extract swift, javascript and dart read the client, signature, application, caller and audience checks and the event writers the implementation file names, where each finds its permission checks, and write and ask about them in the words extract go uses

Status: accepted, 2026-10-21.

Context: Roadmap 5, caller context. ADR-154 and ADR-159 named the gates
that read no permission under the http binding, clientChecks with
clientArgument, signatureChecks, applicationChecks, callerChecks,
audienceChecks and eventWriters, and only extract go read them; the
swift, javascript and dart readers read permissionChecks only, so
the same estate written in another language read its client,
caller and audience checks as nothing and its operations as open
to any caller.

Decision: The swift, javascript and dart readers read the six lists as extract
go does and find a gate where each finds a permission check, matched
the same way: for swift, a middleware a group is given, made by the
check's function; for javascript, middleware of the route, of a
mount above it or of an earlier use on the same router, called with
its argument or named without a call, and a call in the handler; for
dart, a check wrapping the handler, the wrappers nested one in
another followed to the handler, a call in the handler, and a call
in a dart_frog _middleware.dart above the route or in its onRequest
in the branch of its method. The names an argument gives are a
string or a list of strings: an array literal in swift and
javascript, a list literal in dart, and in javascript a const the
permission is read through too. A gate is never read as a
permission check. What is written and asked follows ADR-154 and
ADR-159 word for word: callers and via from literals, the questions
for declarations, the names from a setting, the through, the
audience, the strings after the named argument and two checks of
one kind in turn; the four readers share the one code that writes
them. The question for a client or caller check whose argument
gives literals cites each call of it at its own line with the names
that call passes.

Consequences: An implementation file without the gate keys reads as before in
every reader. The Txn-Token header read stays with extract go: the
other readers do not read a handler's headers yet, so an operation
whose handler reads it is not asked about there. The facts dumps are
unchanged, since they already carry calls with their arguments and
array and list literals. The cases extract-swift-caller-checks,
extract-javascript-caller-checks and extract-dart-caller-checks hold
the readings.

**Insight:** One meaning per key: a check named under clientChecks admits only clients whatever the language it is written in, so each reader reads it and writes the same callers and the same questions, and a specification extracted from a service in Swift, TypeScript or Dart shows who may call it as one in Go does. Found where the permission checks are found, because a project writes its gates the way it writes its permission checks, and a reader that looked elsewhere would read one and miss the other. Shared code for the writing, because two copies of the same questions drift apart in wording, and the merge joins questions by their words. A citation is read as what that line says, so one line cited for the names of every call would send the reader to a line that does not pass them. Compiler test: a gate named in part or twice is a must question at the paths in every reader, and every name read is written or asked at its entry. Acceptance test: the first techspec of a service in any of the four languages shows who may call each route and which question names the clients still to declare.

### ADR-170: A rule of the permission table may name through, the one client its row holds through, and extract permissions writes it on the role's grant as it writes a grant's

Status: accepted, 2026-10-21.

Context: Roadmap 5, caller context. ADR-106 lets a grant hold through one
application, and the permission table's grants carry it as
through; a check that reads a policy of path patterns prints rules
(ADR-100), and a rule had no way to say it, so a policy whose rows
admit a role only from one application was read as admitting it
from every client.

Decision: A rule of the permission table may name through: the software_id
of the one client its row holds through, in kebab-case, as a
grant's through is; a rule without it reads as before. Each
permission the rules give is granted to the row's role through
that client, and written under the role's through, the client
declared as an application, with the questions a grant's through
gives: what each client is, which token carries the application,
and, where one row of a role holds a permission through a client
and another holds it with none, a must question at the role's
through, the permission left out of it. Two rows that differ only
in through are two rows; a row listed twice with the same through
is refused, and so is a through that is not kebab-case, naming the
rule. A row's citation names the client it holds through.

Consequences: A policy of path patterns says who may call from where as a table
of grants does, and the matrix shows it. The operations a route
table gives are unchanged: through is the role's, never the
operation's (ADR-106). The case extract-permissions-pattern-through
holds the reading.

**Insight:** One meaning per key: through is the one client a grant holds through whatever row gives the grant, so a rule says it with the same key and the reader writes it with the same code, and the questions read the same in both. A row with no through beside one with it is asked, never read as either, because the check reads them in an order the table does not show and through is never guessed. Compiler test: a rule through a client is written on the role, a disagreeing pair is a must question at the role's through, and a malformed through is refused naming the rule. Acceptance test: the first techspec of a service whose policy narrows rows to one application shows the narrowing in the matrix.

### ADR-171: A module's derived cases read the identity module given in the same run, for the through of its roles and for the security events and trust domain it holds, and each event names its identifier under the trust domain

Status: accepted, 2026-10-21.

Context: Roadmap 5, caller context. ADR-107 keeps the roles, their through
and the trust domain in the identity module, and ADR-109 has the
identity module declare securityEvents. The derived cases read one
specification: a module whose roles and security events live in the
identity module derived no case for a caller through a client the
role's through does not list, and its refusals named no security
event, although validate resolved the same references in the same
run. The event clause named the rule and the severity, and not the
identifier <trustDomain>/events/<rule> that ADR-109 gives each
event.

Decision: The derived cases of a specification read the identity module when
it is given in the same run: the dependency of kind
identityProvider, resolved as every reference is, in an estate or
among the folders given. A role of the identity module whose through
names a permission of the module by reference,
<dependency>#/permissions/<name>, derives at each route or command
that permission guards the case refused through a client not listed
for <role> of <identity module>, as a role of the module's own does.
A refusal's then names its security event when the module or the
identity module declares securityEvents, and the event's identifier,
the trust domain with /events/<rule> after it, when the module or
the identity module declares trustDomain, the module's own first:
"it is refused as not allowed, and the security event through
(medium), https://estate.example.org/events/through, is written".
validate, derive, the documents' cases left out and the problems
target read the cases so; validate does in both builds. A module checked alone,
without the identity module, accepts a test that covers a through
case of a role of the identity module named so, as waiting for that
module, as a reference into it waits.

Consequences: derive over an estate, or over the folders of a module and its
identity module, writes the through cases of the identity module's
roles into the module's tests, and the security event and its
identifier in each refusal's then; the drafts carry no problem mark,
since the check that marks them is given the same modules. A module
with neither key and no identity module given derives as before.
A test that covers a through case of a role of the identity module
is checked against the derived cases when the identity module is
given, and waits when it is not.

**Insight:** One meaning per key: a role's through narrows its grant wherever the role is written, so a refusal the validator derives from a local role is derived from a referenced one too, and a specification split into modules by ADR-107 gets the cases it would have had in one file. Read from the run, not from a path the dependency names, because the references already resolve only against the specifications given together, and a second way of finding the identity module would find another one. The role is named with its module because a module may have a role of the same name, and two cases of one name would be one test for two refusals. The identifier in the then, because ADR-109 makes it the name a reviewer and the event store use, and a test that checks the refusal wrote the event checks it under that name. The case waits when the module is alone, as ADR-107's references do, because the compiler reads an incomplete estate: a test the estate run checks is not an error in a run that cannot tell. Compiler test: a module validated alone keeps its tests of the identity module's cases and reports nothing of them; the estate run checks them at the entry. Acceptance test: derive over an estate writes the drafts of every refusal a role of the identity module narrows, each naming the event a security reviewer looks for.

| merge-printed-parsed | command merge | system | golden | a tree extract openapi wrote from a document wholly in dxlib's dialect, a code source with reading: printed, holding two operations; a route tree printed from the code repository, reading: printed, holding one of them; and a tree extract go wrote from that repository's source, reading: parsed, holding that operation under another operationId and one operation no printed tree has | merge is run on the three trees | it joins the operation all give into one with every citation and asks a must question on the operationId they disagree on; it leaves out the parsed tree's question whether the running system registers the joined operation, which the printed trees answer, and its question on the operation only it declares, which it asks again as a must question citing the source's line; it asks a could question on the operation only the printed trees have, citing the document; it keeps reading on the document's source and leaves it out of the repository's source, which one tree read printed and another parsed; and exits 0 |
